ARTS. a. Maggie could bake, Maggie could brew, ••••• Maggie could spin, ay! an' milk the coo, And mend the class. Whaur can ye meet wi' sic lassies noo, Or hamely ways? Maggie could dress hersel' unco braw, Could sweep up the hoose, or dust the ha', Fu' neat an' clean. t Yet aye keep a han', as white as gnaw, Tae gae a frien'. / • Maggie was woo'd an' Maggie was won, An claithed her bairnies wi' what she spun For meny years. ; She never was fleyed at wind or sun, Or fractious fears. • She made her man happy, a' can tell, Her held was clear an' soond as a bell. An' aye she tried Tae mak' a' richt, as wed l as herser- -1-- That was her pride.
Ilia) 'Maggie grows aulder ilka day, But hauds love's art, though her hair is gray;

_ As spinnin' yarn; ; She thinks, noo, kimmers are no worth strao To man or bairn. • • Maggie is richt, withoot muckle doot;— The way tae darn, an' the way tee doot, In mony parts, An' mak' folk happy a' roond aboot, Are a' lost arts. —Leeds Hereury Supplement. 1-7617:: Poet, tell Me what thou see'st In the earth and sea and sky; In the lovely flowerets blooming, And the shining orbs on high; In the world where men are striving, Changing with each fleeting breath, Mirth and childhood, age and manhood, Changing till the change of death; • In the Courts of gilded splendour • Low ambition's hollow heart; In the cottage, pure but lowly, Canst thou find a letter part ? • In the scenes of dissipation, Full of vain and empty show; In the work of truthful manhoo • Dost thou something better know? • In falsehood, selfishness, deceit, And dark ways where truth is not; In affection, love, and friendship, Canst thou find more happy lot? In the sea, whose surface changes As the winds inconstant blow; In the creatures deep and wondrous, Poet, canst thou little know? In huge rocks that tell of ages, Of the countless fleeting years; In the life deep rocks betoken To thy vision what appears? In the microscopic creatures That a few brief moments live; In the force so strange and hidden 4 Which the power of life can give. t In the reptiles lowly creeping Or burrowing in the ground; In eniless insect tribes that there In myriad forms abound; In birds, delightful birds, that sing, Warbling sweetly as they fly; In forests, rivers, lakes, and mountains, Rugged, sombre, dark, and high; 111 stars that gem the vaulted sky, And ever bright in splendour shine; In the vast universe beyond, Poet, what ca•ast thou divine? In star of earth 'mid other stars, 10•14'•• " And man's life 'mid other life ; !our In the changes that surround us, _ To what purpose tends the strife? - In all nature is there wisdom, Is there goodness we may bless? In the infinite eteinal Canst thou look for happiness? In the creatures just existing, - When the change of death is o'er; • In some other form returning Do they taste of life once more? With the hero, freely giving Life that others may be blest, In belief in an hereafter, Poet, may thy spirit rest? Warrington.

Justice is truth in action. Those who never retract their opinions love them- selves more than they love truth. With some writers the style grows out of the thoughts; with others the thoughts grow out of the style. There is about neat and clean clothing a sort of youth- fulness in which it is well for old age to envelop itself. What a wonderfully small matter suffices to hinder a verse, a poem, a picture, a feature, a face, an address, a word, an accent, a gesture, from touching the heart! 1 Politeness is a sort of guard Which covers the rough edges of our character, and prevents them from wound- ing others. We should never throw it off, even in our conflicts with coarse people. Mathematics make the mind mathematically exact, while literature (les lettres) makes it morally exact. Mathematics will teach a ~man to build a bridge: the humanities will teach him to live.

STRATEGIC VALUE OF HERAT.-A glance at the record of the past will show that from time immemorial Herat seas regarded a.s an outlying bulwark, the poesessign of which was necessary prior to attempting the conquest of India; the holding of which by India, or by impos- sible Powers dependent on India, would render an invasion of . that country. The hasty reader may object—What can the possession of one city sig- nify? A question of this nature touches the real point of the argument. Herat is called the gate of India, be- cause through it, and through it alone, the valleys can WO entered which lead to the only vulnerable part of Inclia. Those valleys, running nearly north and south, are protected tethe east by inaccessible ranges, to the west by impracticable deserts. No invading army could dare to attempt to traverse the great salt desert, and the desert immediately south of it, the Dasht-i-Naubad, whilst a British army held Herat. The possession of Herat by Russia means the possession of that one line by which India can be invaded; the posiession of Herat by England means the annihilation of all the Russian hopes of an invasion of India. Let the reader imagine that Kandahar is the frontier British station; that between Herat and Kandahar is a long lane, so protected on both sides that the man who may wish to traverse any part of it to Kandahar must enter by Herat. Is it not ob- vious that the Power which shall hold Herat will COM- pletely dominate the lane? It is this which makes the possession of Herat by England a matter of vital conse- quence. Another fact illustrates the enormous value of Herat. Place an army there, and nothing need be brought to it from Europe. Within the limits of the Herati territory all the great roads leading on India con- verge. The mines of the Herati district supply lead, iron, and sulphur; the surface of many parts of the country is laden with saltpetre; the willow and the Poplar, which make the best charcoal, abound; the I,eids produce in abundance corn, and wine; and oil. From the population, attracted to its new rulers by good government, splendid soldiers might be obtained. Such are the military advantages presented by Herat to the Power that shall occupy it. Should that Power be an enemy, Herat would be to him an eye to see and an arm to strike— an eye to pry into every native Court of Hindustan, to watch the discontents and the broodings of the rulers, the heartburnings of their subordinates. , Yr' watching and noting to fermenting and stirring up, there is but one short step. Every Court, every bazaar, in India would note the presence on the frontier, in a position not only unsssailable, but becoming every day more and more capable of assailing, of a first-class Power, the secret enemy of England, and professing the most unselfish anxiety to relieve them in then distress. An arm to strike, because a few years of intelligent rule would render the valley of the Hari Rud capable of sup- porting and equipping an army strong enough even to invade India. In a third sense, likewise, the possession of Herat by an enemy would be not less dangerous to England. The roads converging on it, already alluded to, are traversed by caravans to which no other route is available. The European Power whose influence shall , be paramount in Herat will rule the markets of Central Asia. More even than that. The possession of Herat by Russia means the exclusion of England from the markets of Central Asia.—Frorn " The Russians at the Gates of Herat." _ .

4' Woinan is made to perform every kind of degrading labour. She prepares the fields for planting, she drives the oxen and holds the plaugh„ and not unfrequently she takes the place of the ox before the plough. She sows the seed and tills the soil, she shovels, she hoes, she reaps, she gathers the harvest, she thrashes the grain and carries it to the mill, she grinds it at the mill, she markets the products of her small strip of land to buy bread for her children arid beer fdit her lord and master. She does the work and the drudgery in the factories; she is the scavenger for cleaning the streets and gather- ing offal in the cities and highways for enriching the land. She does everything but play soldier and hang around beershops and drink beer from early morning until late at night, like the German men, and these occu- pations would be assignekto her provided they required bard labour or drudgery of any kind. Yet they are strong and robust, and perform what is called a man's labour.' While at work in the fields, and it is only during the warm months of the year that they can, they are only paid ten or twelve cents for a day's labour of twelve hours. When tfiey board themselves they re- helve from twenty to twenty-eight or thirty cents a pay.,, . • WHY DOESN'T THE BMW WALE ?-70/10 inquiry which Is often asked the physician is Why does-not my baby Walk ?" In answer, we (Babyhood) may say, first of all, that delay in walking does not necessarily imply 'physi- cal disease or weakness. A child's disposition may have much to do with its; courage and self-confidence make he infant forward, while timidity will make him back- Ward. The example of other, especially older children, ktimulates the enterprise of an infant;- while, on the ,bther hand, too constant attention from nurses relieves hn indolent child from the necessity of exertion. When he tardiness passes beyond the ordinary limits, it may be due to some weakness, either natural to the child, or perhaps the result of some definite disease. Any severe ailment may entail such debility as to interrupt the natural development of the child in this direction. Even the process of dentition may have such an effect. Many times we have been told at clinic that the child, who bad already begun to get about, "lost his walk," as the result of teething or of some disease. Moreover any lowering of the general condition, without a special fit of illness, may have a like result. Some- times a paralysis of limb may be at the bottom of the trouble, but this isUgly to Ito recognised from the fact of the illness that predllided it, or from the powerlessness of the limbs for other purposes than walking. So, too, injuries, such as fractures and dislocations, have some- times been overlooked, although it would hardly seem that they could be by persons of ordinary observation and intelligence. To anyone anxious &bent the tardi- ness of a ''chnd in walking, we would-say/first of all, do not hurry and do not worry... Try to ascertain if the -child is well as to digestion, nutrition, sleep; arid all ,the matters-that go to make u general good health. If you are convinced that your child is inlierfect health, and your opinion is confirmed by your medical adviser, it would be perfectly proper to encourage him in every way, as the tardiness is probably due to mental pecu- liarities alone. If he has had an illness, do your best to bring about his complete restoration. Observe closely whether he uses his lower limbs freely and strongly when sitting and lying, and whether he uses the two with equal freedom and force. If he does so the limbs are probably sound. If the examinatioa leaves any doubt in your mind, ask your family physician to decide the point for you. AN ARTICLE cay AMERICANIB3IB,—Much has been written on the other side of the Atlantic to show that many expressions commonly called Americanisms are merely survivals of good old English forms-that have died out on their native soil. In the February number of the Andover Review (London: Ward, Lock, and Co.) there is an article on forms and expressions that have been manufactured in America within the memory of men still living, have crept slowly into the language, and are more easily noticed by those who have for a length of time been absent from the country. Around is some- times used for round. A book has been published in Philadelphia with the title "Around the World," which, according to pure English, could be predicated only of the equator, parallels, and meridians. The expressions f! on the street,' on tne cars," for in, have come into vogue within 30 years. "I remember during a prolonged absence abroad, hearing a lady lately arrived from the United States speak of having been at a certain time on the street, and gathering at first that she had been lying .there !" "Badly whipped," "badly defeated," are now used where people used to say "well whipped," "com- pletely defeated." While bids fair to oust such words as aldttntgh, in spite of, admitting that, granted, &c. - This form reached its acme about the time of President Gar- 'field's wound. Now it not only usurps the place of though, but is even followed by yet. One of the best journals has, "While he felt obliged to meet Mr. Clay, yet he had determined," &c. Quite has a peculiar usage in America. "A well-known Bolton clergyman, a good deal of a purist, and priding himself on drawing only from the pure well of English undefiled, met a chance companion while travelling in England, and had an agreeable conversation for half an hour. At the end of that time the Englishman said, ',,Now I have found you out! I have been in donlat all the time as to your na- tionality; but when you said, It is quite a fine day, all my doubts as to your being an American cased." A novel use of occur has started up within two or three years. _A funeral will occur; a battle occurred. But an occurrence is rather what is accidental or incidental, not ' what is matter of arrangement. The. insertion of an adverb between the infinitive and its sign has led to much discussion. "The scourge' has rebounded to England, and our ally, the Daily News, has done much towards spreading it. Mr. Irving's late farewell speech to the English, as reported by that journal, though very short, has two instances of this form—namely, to again 'renew," to permanently settle down.'" A common error of some good journals is found in such a sentence as "Korsakoff is one of those Russians who believes," &c. The verb ought to be plural. Very has of late been used with the past participle, instead of much—" Very pleased." We might as well say, "Very loved, very hated." Public Analysts have submitted CADBUIty'S COCOA. to blose tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining- and nourishing .beverage. Beware of Imitations.— ..Add,

He says that he would utilise all green crops in the form of manure by ploughing them In, and thus do away with sheep and the necessity of an outlay of a large amount of capital. In many districts Sheep have been in the past year absolutely disastrous, frequently fetching lower prices than they cost to buy in. The system of ploughing in green crops is an Old one, and has frequently been revived with advantage. Mr. Biendell says that a year or two ago he read a paper upon 'tills subject before a South Hants Farmers' Club, when several of his neighbours tried an experireent, with a most favourable result, upon all soils, especially upon light land—whether the subsoil was chalk, gravel, or sand,—and the result was the more favourable when lt was compared with what had previously been done with sheep. , The chief points are stated to lie in the fact that the land has yielded a crop for sale and for manuring the same season, as instanced by the growth of mustard or cole seed and turnip seed mixed upon land from which white Canadian oats, early peas, Tale- Vera wheat, rye, and other early crops have been grown; also crops of beans, with the cola seed and turnip seed sown between for the purpose of ploughing in; and also mangolds and turnips, drilled three feet apart in the rows, with cole seed and turnip seed sown between at the time of the second horse-hoeing. Upon the removal of the main crop of these roots these green crops yield most valuable manure upon ploughing. There is in addition the green crop of mangold leaves, which many farmers make a practice of leaving upon the ground, although there are others who prefer the very old sys- tem of plucking them for the consumption of cattle. Upon the face of it, it almost seems wasteful and con- trary to nature to produce a crop and afterwards to plough it in the land, but experience has shown that there is much sound argument in the practice of Mr. Blundell, more particularly when, as in his -and other cases, it has been found to answer and to do away with the necessity of heavy -artificial manuring or of sheep feeding on the land. NITRATE OF SODA.--I have an impression that amongst the general body of farmers, science; as applied to farm- ing, is as yet in its infancy, and to many it is a wholly sealed book. Supposing men like these, possessing no previous training, were permitted to experiment in the laboratory, we should naturally expect a speedy blow- up. And so it has been on the farm where artificfala have been -used promiscuously, not farm, whether the soils needed this or that, and the blow-up„unfor- tunately, has been in the farmers' pockets. The land upon which we used nitrate as an experiment is a thin, hungry soil, on the limestone formation. It requires a lot of manure, or soon becomes poor. Sir John Lawes says that in the case of a tenant leaving he would do a wise thing to use nitrate of soda so long as he was only getting out his own unexhausted fertility. Does not this bear out the northern acceptation of it?—" When one of our farmers is known to be using nitrate of soda it is taken as a hint that he is preparing to leave his farm, and is also getting all out of the land that he can." I fully 'agree with Sir John B. Lewes that, from the tenant's point of view, this is much "preferable to claiming compensation under the Agricultural Holdings Act, with the doubtful success which may attend his efforts "—especially this latter, when viewed by the light of recent claims for compensation under the Act. But it is a delicate and difficult question, rendered much more difficult in present times of agricultural depression, for a tenant to determine within himself when he has reached the point of exhausting his own fertility and when, he is trenching on the inherent fertility of the soil, the Pro- perty of the landlord. On soils such as ours I feel as- sured that a couple of years' liberal use of nitrate of soda would leave a wretched prospect for the succeeding tenant; and thus nitrate of soda has come to be known with us as the "robber of the soil." On heavy lands, and clay lands, I should fancy its use would be bene- ficial as releasing locked-up fertility. Contrasting these heavy lands with light, poor, and porous soils, the fol- lowing simile seems to illustrate the contrast. A sPonge is easily filled with water, and as easily squeezed out; but a log that has long laid in water requires con- siderable pressure before it can be drained of its ac- cumulations. But the land on which we used the nitrate of soda did not exactly correspond with the sponge, be- cause it had an under backing to prevent the escape of the nitrate. It was in oats and seeds following a crop of swedes grown with superphosphate solely, farmyard manure being 'scarce. It had been treated to a liberal application of well-rotted manure; and, a dry time setting in, the oats looked badly, hence the dressing of nitrate over a portion as an experiment. The seeds would thus arrest the nitrate of soda, and the corn crop would have its full value; but, as I said before, the portion of the field so dressed was very poor afterwards In contrast to the rest of the field, and as we allow our grass-seeds to remain down two years the result was plainly seen. On the other hand, the surcharged log ' would require a considerable time, like the strong or clay land, before its moisture (fertility) was extracted.---,' R.

aft, of s., Jill there is restriction; in pts,ce of natural food, i.e., the food which the bird chooses for itself, there is artificial; we take away the condition that would make the, fowl hardy, to resist unfavourable Circumstances, and leave it enfeebled phy- sically; and we do not see how any other result can be arrived at. Domestication of any animal has a: ten- dency to weaken the powers; the, savage is nearly always stronger in body than the civilised man. The conditions of his life are in the direction of strength. Therefore, when we domesticate fowls we must prepare for the result, and seek by a careful study of the question to attain that happy mean, by which we can keep fowls healthy, and yet guard them by such conditions that when unfavourable circumstances arise—circumstances they would be able to meet themselves when in a state of nature—they may be protected therefrom. The strength and hardihood of a fowl is it reserve force. If we weaken these we must substitute some other reserve outside the fowl itself. It will be seen from what we have here ,stated how Important the question of housing is,. Given that we put a fowl into a house, it is imperative upon us to see that the house will be a real protection to it; and, on the other hand, it is equally imperative that in our seeking tb protect we do not carry this too far and weaken the fowl by over much care. To do one or the other will be fatal to success. There is a point between these two extremes which can be chosen, and it ought to be our object to find that point. The first point to be regarded in housing is that there shall be sufficient air space for the number of fowls to be kept therein. Overcrowding is always an economic mis- take. Something can be done 'by a proper system of ventilation to overcome the evils of overcrowding, but oven perfect ventilation will not make a house only capable of holdintg a dozen fowls comfortably suitable for tw ice that number. • • If too many birds are put into a house they exhaust the oxygen in the air and it rapidly becomes foul. By creating a strong draught this might be prevented; but then draughts are dangerous, and great evils would follow the adoption of such a plan. A gentle current of air, imperceptible except when tested, is all that can be safely applied, and only as many fowls should be kept in tho house that such a current can deal with. We do not like very largo houses, for in these during the' winter season there is a great bank of cold air the fowls cannot contend against, and which starves them all the night long. We all know what it is to go into a great cold room in winter, and the chill we feel is just what birds in a house far too big for them have to bear. Neither too large nor too small should be the object desired. A house 6ft. by 4ft. 6in. is a good size for a score %owls of the ordinary size. The next point le ventilation. Now, ventilation means a current of fresh air constantly passing through the house, but a current of air properly directed in its course. We have seen in France summer poultry houses, which consisted simply of a thatched roof and lattice wood sides. The latter were merely a protection against night marauders, and could be no shelter. But, whilst suit- able for a warm country in the summer season we could not recommend them on this side the English Channel. Such houses would be far better than many we have seen, every board in which is ill-jointed, and the whole house more like a sieve than anything else, letting in both wind and water. Draughty buildings of this kind are far worse than no houses at all, and it is small won- der that fowls kept in them are not free from disease, much less thrive. The walls, windows, door, and roof of the house should be taut—air and water tight; and the ventilation so arranged that the birds will never roost in the direct current of air. A simple way is to put louver boards at each end of the gable, and of course higher than the perches, so that when the foul air rises, as it will do, it can, be carried away at once. Another, way is to put one or two ventilators in the walls, level with the roosting places, but covered on the inside by a box or spout with the upper side only open to send the I air upwards. • The questions of damp and dirt need but few words at our hands. Dampness, either from defective walls or a bad floor, is an evil that must be combatted. It can be prevented. If neglected, it will be fatal to success, for to it is due many of the diseases affecting the re- spiratory organs. And from the accumulation of dirt we have diseases affecting the stomach and bowels, as well as respiration. Foul odours rising from a floor covered with droppings poison the air, and thus make the birds breathing it ready subjects for the first trouble that may appear. Insects, too, are encouraged by dirt, and where they are numerous fowls can never thrive. SEASONABLE HINTS. Eggs 'should now begin to get plentiful, and chickens also. The latter bring trouble, in that they crowd the ' runs, so that extra room is very desirable. Upon farms, and where abundance of ground space is available, there is no difficulty whatever, as the coops can then be widely-, scattered. But where the space is limited, then it if necessary to make some other arrangements, and this had better soon be in the direction of breaking up the breeding pens, so as to give the space occupied by them to the older chick. It may appear early to do this, but we are now a third through April, and, in well managed yards, by the end of the month all the eggs required for breeding should be in the nests. .

It will be in the recollection at the Guardians that the Board have frequently asked them to obtain from the vaccination officers explanations reepecting the default shown in their respective returns, and as recently as the 17th November last the Board expressed their opinion that the explanation of the vaccination Officers ferwerded with your letter of the sth November are not satisfactory. I ant to request that the Guardians will call upon Misers HaHord and Cooper to for- ward to the Beard on the 18th May next fresh returns on the enclosed fortes, showing the then atate of vaccination in their respective districts as far as relates to the children whose births were registered therein during 1883 and the first half of 1884, and that the returns may be accompanied by stateetente showing as regards each child not finally ac- counted for as to vaccination, what steps the vaccination officer has taken to procwe its vaceination."—The CLERK acid Mr Belford had been communicated with, and be would make the necessary return for the Warrington dis- trict, and Mr Cooper had been communicated with also. As they were aware Mr Cooper was only a new officer, and that he met with an amount of opposition and difficulty that few men would be prepared to continue to meet if they *meld kelp it. Tirey had no doubt read of the scenes that took !lace in cenneolion with the reale of goods at Newton distrained for vaccination penalties. Public meetings had been held, and there was no doubt that it was most dieicult to perform Mr Cooper's deities. The Clerk then read a letter from Mr Cooper, in which he informed the Board that he had not got the Hest of births from February until March 28th, although they were due on the 3rd. This was regu- lar *recurrence, he reoneequence of which he was always be- hind with his work. He had repeatedly spoken to the registrar (Mr Appleton) about this delay, but he did not take any notice, and he (Mr Cooper) trusted the Board would cause inquiries to be made in the matter. Having regard, the Clerk said, to all the difficulties Mr Cooper met with in the performance of his duties it was certainly most essential that every other offieer should do all he could to assist. He (the Clerk) then mentioned that so far back as 1881 ,Dr Beard had complained of the way in which Mr Appleton discharged EU duties and he (the Clerk) was bound to say ' that even prior to 1881 Mr Appleton had not discharged his dirties in that regular and punctual manner which he once did; and since than he had himeelf been much incon- venienced by Mr Appleton's delays.—The Crteurceer then asked Mr Appleton (who was in the room) if he had any explanation to give in regard to these complaints.--Mr AP. 'PLETON stid he did not wish to offer any explanation. He was very sorry he had neglected his duties to that extent, and he promised faithfully that it should not occur again. —The CHAIRMAN Said as it was the first complaint they had had of that kind he hoped it would be the last.—Mr DARBYSIIIRE said that was scarcely the first complaint be- cause they had had complaints from private individuals who had wished to have their children vaccinated at the proper time, and had not been able to do It through the neglect of Mr Appletog.—Mr Elletensow thought it was due from Mr Appleton ndt only to promise that it would not occur again, but also to offer some explanation as to the cause of the neglect. When an officer WAS guilty of a dereliction of duty he ought to offer some explanation.—ln answer to a further question, Mr ArrEwrow said he had had the forms ready but for oee or two reasons he did not deliver them to Mr Cooper. If Mr Cooper had called for them he could have got them—The CLERK Kid they coald be posted, but he was afraid that was not the reason. Mr Appleton had sent him the eame letter every third month, yet it happened again next time.—Mr APPLETON said he did not offer any excuse ;it was entirely neglect on his part. In answer to Mr Jame, Mr Appleton said his neglect had not beep due to his having any sympathy with the anti-vaccinators because it was not the case.—After some further conversation, the CHAIRMAN informed Mr Appleton that if the same neglect occurred again the Board would consider the matter very seriously.—The matter then dropped.—ln answer to Mr Rateliffe, Mr COOPER, the vaccination officer, said that when children which had not been vaccinated were removed from his district he endeavoured to find out where they had gone to. and when he had done that he informed the vaccination officer of that place of the fact.—The CLERK said it would be necessary to eummon more of the anti-vaceinatore. There were 400 of them at Earlestowne, and he was afraid the Board must give a general order to pursue the matter.—The CHAIR/dew said they must carry the law out.—With regard to the contents of the letter given above, Mr COOPHR said he thought the Local Government Board were not aware of the difficulties he had to contend with in respect of these vaccinations.—'Fhe CHAIRMAN said he ehold tell them.— The subject then dropped.

The Chairman, having intreduced Mr Henley, the new Local Government Board inspector, who was:present, to the rest of the members, Mr HENLEY having referred in eulo- gistic terms to his predecessor' Mr Cane, said he should en- deavour to do there as he had done elsewhere, allow as far as he could the Guardians to .elanage their own affairs. As long as they kept within the law and within the rules they would find no interference from him, and if he could at any time be of any assistance to them his services would be at their disposal. (Hear, hear.) He then threw out somesug- gestions as to the management of the workhouse, dm. He said there was one thing In connection sith their work- house which astonished him, and which he did not remem- ber to have Been before, and that was the great number of women in the workhouse who got tobacco. He had never known a workhouse, he thought, in which women were per- mitted to smoke by order of the medical officer. He, how- ever, did not offer any opinion on it himself, as it was a matter between them and their medical officer. He com- mended the practice at the workhouse of keeping the in- mates engaged at light work, and also approved of the Guardians having removed the children from the workhouse. —The CHAIRMAN, on behalf of the Board, thanked Mr Henley for his remarks and for the hints he had thrown out.—Mr JEANS cilled the attention of the inspector to the difficulty of carrying out the Vaccination Act in that dis- trict, Earlestown in particular. He would urge upon him to read of the recent proceedings which took place in Earles- town, which would give him some idea of the difficulty they had to contend with. He ehould wish also that the inspector might bring to the notice of the Local Govern- ' ment Board as to whether some little modification of the law ought not to be introduced. He thought any person reading the account of those proceedings at Earlestown must be convinced that it was utterly impossible for a Board of Guardians to enforce the Vaccination Act in that dis- trict. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WIMNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty miaatee after twelve o'clock. Tun Slurs BILL.—The House went into Committee on the Redistribution Bill, resuming the consideratior of the seventh schedule, which deals with the divisions of coun- ties, and which was under discussion whex progress was re- ported on Tuesday. The desire of Sir R Peel to retain the name of Tamworth, which borough is to be disfranchised, as the name of one of the divisions of Warwickshire, on account of the distinction which Tanaworth acquired through the services of his late father, gave rise to an in- teresting discussion. Ultimately a proposal to substitute Tamworth for Coleshill as the name of a Warwickshire division was carried by an overwhelming majority; and Richmond was substituted for Northallerton as the name of one of the Yorkshire divisions, by a vote of 113 to 73. A proposal to substitute the name of Batley for the sug- gested Morley division of Yorkshire was talked out by Mr Warton. MISCELLANFOUS.—The Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday Bill having been postponed until June 17, the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday No. 2 Bill, together with the similar bill relating to Durham and Northumber- land, were deferred to Wednesday next.—On the motion of Mr Stuart Wortley, the Burial Boards (Contested Elections) Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock.

The Earl of'it-ed-e-sdale took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter after four o'clock. BILLS FORWARDED.—The reports of amendments to the Election (Hours of Poll) Bill and the Educational Endow- ments (Ireland) Bill were received and agreed to. The Municipal Voters (Relief) Bill and the Army (Annual) Bill were read a third time and passed. THE AFGHAN QUESTION. Earl GnANyILLs informed the Marquis of Salisbury that the Government had not yet received any reply to the queries which had been addressed to Sir P. Lumsden, and our Ambassador at St Petersburg had stated that it was not likely that the Russian Govern- ment would receive for a few days any answers to the ques- tions which had been put to their General.—The Earl of JERSEY desired to know whether the Government had, as stated in the newspapers, agreed to give up Panjdeh to the Russians, but the FOREIGN SECRETARY replied that he must decline to make a statement as to " the un-author- ised. and nearly always inaccurate, accounts of the pro- ceedings of the Government upon these difficult questions which appear in the newspapers." COLONIAL FEDERA'TION.—The Earl of DERRY presented a bill to constitute a Federal Council of Australasia' and stated that it would be more convenient to their Lordships if he made a statement on the subject on the motion for the second reading.—The bill was read a first time, and the second reading fixed for Thursday next. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TnnasnAv.

-- The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. 'Tug MALLOW DISTURBANCES.—Mr CAMPBELL-BANNER- MAN, is reply to a long series of questions respecting the re- cent disturbance at Mellow station, gave to the House full details of what had taken place. It had been arranged that upon the departure of a certain train the platforms should be cleared to prepare for the reception of the Royal party. A party of police was, upon the application of the railway authorities, told off to clear the platform. They directed the people to leave, and the greater portion complied at once, but some who refused were ejected. In a few cases where resistance was offered the police had recourse to their batons, but they used no more force than was necessary. The railway company had a right to make what arrangements they thought fit for the admission of persons to the platform. THE Russo-AFGHAN DISPUTH.—Mr A Bartlett desired to know what steps the Government were taking to counteract the injurious effects of General Kornareff's aggression on the people of Central Asia. To this Mr Gladstone replied that the matter named had received the careful attention of her Majesty's Government. Mr Gladstone, replying to Sir Northcote, said that no further communication had been received from Sir P Lurneden, and added that it was neces- sary to give a warning- on this point, as there was a very great uncertainty icdeed as to the time which was now re- quired, either from St Petersburg or from London, to com- municate with the officers on the spot, and he had an appre- hension that we must be content ta put up with some further delay before receiving replies either from St Peters- burg as to the questions mired, or from Sir P Lumeden as to important questions sent to him. A telegram had been received that afternoon from Sir B Thornton which stated in a few words that a provisional administration bad been ea- tablishedat Penjdeh. Ae to the rumour about the cession of Penjdeh, not only was the statement without authority, but no assurance had been given or received on the part of either Government on the subject of particular points on the frontier. Replying to Sir W Hart Dyke, the Prime Minister said Sir 1i; Thornton did not mention by whom the administration of Penjdeh had been taken over, but he could net doubt that it was established under Raseian auspices. Later in the evening Mr Healy ir.qaired it there was any truth in the statement that the Czar had sent a letter to her Majesty's Government containing assurances of an extremely pacific character, and Lord Hartington re- plied that no snob letter had been received at the Foreign Office. THE EGYPTIAN Lome GLAINYTONE, in mov- ing that the House go into Committee en the Egyptian Loan Bill, pointed out the consequences that would cer- tainly follow should the House reject er refuel, CO pass the bill. There was no oonnectian, be said, between the bill and the subject of the amendment ef Sir 11. Cross. The nectssity for the bill was extreme ; for a fortnight the House had—thanks to the leader of the Oppoeition—shown a great deal of self-restraint and tetnperano in relation to critical matters of Imperial policy, and 'fie hoped they would continue to exhibit that feeling —Sir B. A. Cuoss moved that the House, taking into consideratiten the terms of the declaration of the Great Powers sof the 17th March, declinee to proceed to the discussion of the details of this bill until it shalt have before it the Convention which is to be concluded with regard to the Suez Canal. The right hon, gentleman conten- ded that the question of the Saes Canal could not be separated from the general financial question of the Convention, and that any mietake made at this time might be fatal to our commerce fot a long time. It behoved mem- bers to be cautious that no Convention was made behind their backs.—Lord R Ctacructrmz oontended that an attack wee being made upon the Government which, both argu- mentatively and numerically, would be weak and baeffee- tive, and that Sir B. Creel was prejudicing the object he had in view by mixing up the financial agreement with the Suez Canal.—The debate was continued hy Mr Norwood, Mr S Hill, Mr D Davies, Mr Warton, Mr Northcote, Mr Farquharson, Mr A Bartlett, Mr Elton, Mr Mat:leer, and Mr Forster.--Sir S Noarwaora thought that under the cir- cumstances his right hon. friend might be satisfied with the discussion —The amendment was then withdrawn, and the bill passed through Committee. THE SEArs BILL—The House then resumed, and Imme- diately afterwards went into Committee on the Redistribu- tion of Se Its Bill, taking it up at the seventh schedule, which divides the counties, and resuming with that part of the schedule which related to Yorkshire.—An amendment, moved by Mr W Leatham, to substitute the name of Holm- forth for that of the proposed Penieton Division, was carried on a division by 125 against 63. The Committee proceeded to discuss amendments respecting the Parliamentary divi- sions in Scotland and Ireland.—Pregreers was reported at 1-30, and the House resumed. The House was counted out at 145.

Nauman CowDucr.—At Chester, OR Tuesday, a woman named Harrison was committed to gaol for three months. Ten days ago she passed through Rainow, and left her five- 1 year-old boy in a quiet lane, where he was found at mid- night nearly dead. The Glasgow barque River Leven was on Tuesday night sunk in the English Channel], off Dover, by collision with a Swedish steamer. Three of the crew of the Glasgow vessel were lost; the remainder were landed at Weymouth on Wed- nesday evening. SHOCKING AOCIDENT TO • BOY.—Harry Woodward, a boy. on Monday was sent to Halesowen Railway Station. Whilst proceeding he was induced to ride in a handcart he and others had with them. When travelling at a good speed, the wheel collided with a stone, and the decease was thrown violently against the kerbstone. His head was battered in, and he bled to death. _ . _

_ TERRIBLE MIIRDEIL9.—On Friday night, a Welsh farmer residing near Carmarthen, who has recently been drinking heavily, cut his wife's throat and inflicted a number of terrible wounds on various parte of her body. He was found in the room with the dead bxlv of his wife some hours after the attack, and upon the po:ice entering he inflicted several wounds upon his own throat --On Saturday a pensioner, who is said to be suffering from sunstroke, cut his wife's throat at Oldbrook Farm, near Foleshill. Warwickshire. The man inflicted a terrible wound upon himself, and both he and his wife were removed to the hospital at Coventry. MERIC AN HORSES.—Dr. William A. of the Russian Government is expected, as the inevitable result of a great war. SPEECH OF THE VICEROY OF INDIA. LAHORE, WEDNESDAY, 2-45 P.M.—Lord Dahlia arrived here to-day. Replying to the address of welcome from the municipality, his Excellency spoke as follows :—" Coming freshly from an important interview with the Ameer, whose dominions have, so far as I have been able to ascertain, been the scene of an unprovoked attack, it is a grog satisfaction to me to find the Princes and the people of India ready with one accord to rally round the standard of Great Britain, even at a distance from their own frontier. As yet it is impossible to say in what the present grave crisis will end, but be sure that if war breaks out it will be ha spite of the earnest and anxious endeavours of the British Go- vernment to avert so dire a result, and in &fiance of the most moderate and conciliatory conduct on their part." MELBOURNE, WEDNESDAY.—Active military preparations are being made in all the Australian colonies,

A Portsmouth telegram states that orders were received on Wednesday that the Indian troopship Malabar, expected there this week from Bombay on her concluding voyage for the present season, is to prepare immediately for further and indefilite military transport service Contrary to expectation another meeting of the Cabinet —the third this week—was held at the Premier's official residence in Downing-street, at half-past two on Wednesday afternoon, and continued sitting until five o'clock. In the House of Commons no question was asked as to the Minis- terial deliberations, nor about the crisis with regard to Af- ghanistan, it being privately understood .on the front Oppo- sition bench that the Government had no further informa- tion to commanicate. Generally there was a more hopeful feeling at the House of Commons on Wednesday, though no substantial reason for this view was forthcoming. All the Ministers except Earl Spencer, attended the Cabinet meeting. ____

div.head: AFGHAN CRISIS.
div.p: THE AFGHAN CRISIS.

THE BATTLE OF PENJDEH. GEN. KOMAROFF'S EXPLANATION. Si'. PETERSBURG, StiNDAY.—The Official Messenger of this morning publishes a telegram from General Kornaroff to the Minister of War, dated "Dash-Kepsi, April Ist," ex- plaining the circumstances which led to the engagement on the Kuelak river. General Kornaroff says:—" On the 25th ult, our detachment approached Dash-Kepsi, on our side of the Kushk river. When near the bridge I saw an entrench- ment occupied by the Afghans. In order to avoid a conflict I stationed my troops at a distance of five vents from the Afghan position. On the 20th ult. negotiations commenced with Captain Yates. When the Afghans were convinced that we had no intention of attacking them, they daily , drew nearer to our camp. On the 27th they despatched against us one company, intrusted with covering a 'aeon- noitering party, three companies, with one gun and some cavalry. Their audacity and arrogance went on increasing little by little anti' the following day, when they occupied the height which commanded the left fl tnk of our camp. They commenced to throw up intrenchments, establishal a cavalry force to the rear of our line, and placed a picket at gunshot distance from our ford. On the 29th I sent to the commander of the Afghan detachment an energetic sum- moos giving him till evening to evacuate the left bank of the Kuehk, and the left bank of the Murghab as far as the mouth of the Knshk. The reply from him was that, acting upon the advice of the English, he refused to retire behind the Kushk. I then sent him a private letter coached in amicable terms. On the 30th nit, in order to support my demand, I marched with my detachment against the Afghan position, still counting upon a pacific issue of the difficulty, but the fire of the Afghan artillery and the attack of their cavalry compelled me to accept the combat, the results of which are already known." TEHERAN, MONDAT.—The battle near Penjdeh occupied one hour, but it seems to have been of a very sanguinary character while it lasted, for the Afghan loss s are now stated to have been 900. It was while traversing the pass in the Safari Koh range, on the 4th iost, that Sir P Lumsden and the British Commissioners were overtaken by a severe snow- storm. Seventeen camp followers and 50 transport animals perished. The Englishmen of the Commission are all safe Many tents and a large quantity of officers' baggage were lost, and have not yet been recovered. It is hoped, however, that the principal records will be saved.— Standard. The Press Association understands that Sir Peter Lunn- den has taken up a strong strategical position on the Heri- itud, a: Tirpul, which will, it is believed, prevent a Russian coop de main on Herat. THE RUSSIAN FLEET. NAPLES, MONDAY.—The Russian frigate General Admiral left here early this morning, the commander having re- ceived orders to proceed to the Baltic, ani to send all the other ships of the Bearden Mediterranean Squadron to the same destination. Thanes, SAvranAv.—At Odessa the greatest activity has prevailed in all military circles and departments during the last few days. The whole garrison and other troops ean- toned in the district, also numerous Cossack battalions, are daily paraded. Within the formidable new battery at Kertea the gen ieon are at present engaged night and day in eomplet- ing the works. Two neighbouring steatn flour mills are similarly engaged for the immediate and abundant provision of the fortress. THE RA.WUL PINDI CONFERENCE. DEPARTURE OF THE AMEER. RAWVL PINGS, SUNDAY.—The Viceroy bade farewell yes- terday to the Ameer, who left here this morning, being es- corted to the railway station by the Foreign Secretary and Lord Duffelin's private secretary. Troops lined the rout to the station. The Ammer was Invested with the Grand Cross of the Star of India prior to his departure, with which mark of distinction he was highly gratified. Itawrx. PINDI, Mmamtr.—Tha Viceroy will leave to-night via Attock and Khusaltur, for Lahore, where his Excel- lency will meet the Maharajah of Cashmere. ARREST OF AYOUB KHAN.

TEHERAN, Sarnetnair.—Ayoub Khan was arrested this morning and removed to the Citadel, In consequence of the discovery of correspondence relating to the arrangements for his intended escape. The Persian authorities have taken possession of hie house. TEHERAN, M0NDAY,.....1t is said that the paper found in Ayoub Khan'a rooms confirm unmistakably the suspicious of his complicity in anti-English intrigues in Herat, which led to his arrest. He is now elosely confined in the Citadel of Teheran. The Russian authorities are using all their , influence to obtain his release. 11 WAR PREPARATIONS IN ENGLAND. It is stated that Great Britain could, if necessary, send out at once an extra fleet of nearly thirty vessels, of which there are nine or ten in waiting at Portsmouth, nearly a dozen at Chatham, and seven at Davonport. Those at Devonport are known to be ready to go to sea within twenty four hours. Late on Saturday telegrams were despatched from the Admiralty to the commanders-in-chief of the British squad- rons in foreign waters, and the fleets under their respective commands are as soon as possible to be strengthened. The Baltic Fleet, to be commissioned within a few days, will be very strong, and will, it is understood, be commanded by Admiral Hornbv, who will hoist his flag on beard the Hercules, with Rear-Admiral Seymour as second in com- mand. The Treasury on Monday granted an additional vote of £22,500 to the Portsmouth dockyard to prepare various ships for commission, £2O 000 to Devonport, and lesser sums to smaller yards, amounting in the aggregate to be- tween £50,000 and £60,000. The money. in to be epent at the discretion of the executive officers in engaging extra 'About or employing in overtime the present staff. The America is new ready at Liverpool to receive her armament. The Government have chartered a third; stea- mer from the Cunard Company, the Utnbria, which will arrive in Liverpool next Sunday. The Intelligence Department is closely watching the movements of Russian war ships abroad. The authorities at Woolwich Arsenal were reluctantly compelled to order several departments to continue wok throughout Sunday. The department in which the greatest activity has prevailed was the Royal Gun Factory, where efforts are being concentrated to supply the sinch Woolwich guns for the America and Oregon. The War Office authorities have issued a circular to Municipal Corporations suggesting that their Watch Com- mittees should allow Army Reserve men from their re- spective constabulary forces full credit for superannuation of such period as they may be required for military service. and should receive them back into the police service. Several Corporations have notified their compliance. A computation of the troops that could be at once des- patched, including only those medically fit for service, , show! a total of 52,672 men of all bitinches of the service, composed of 30,660 infantry, 1,752 horse artillery, 4,950 field ' artillery, 4,270 garrison artillery, and 1,972 Royal Engineers. The total number of horses available Is estimated at 6,712. The Morning Post says:—The financial difficulties of Rusia in known to be extreme, and the formal bankruptcy

Sr. PirrEasnt.ino, THIIRSDAY.—The Official Messenger to-day states that according to a despatch from General Komaroff, dated, Dash Kepri, tith inst, the remnant of the Afghan detachment which was defeated in the engagement on the Kushk River has lied to Herat. General Komaroff states that the Afghan losses considerably exceeded the first estimate. litany perished through cold and hanger. Rain and snow have been falling for the last 12 days. The camp iaAla Marghab which was abandoned by Sir Peter Lums- den has been burnt by the Afghans. The camels with the provisions and baggage, as wall as part of the British escort, were driven away by the Sarahks. In order to prevent an- archy a provisional administration is being organised in Penkieh. A Russian detachment remains at Dash Kepri. The despatch concluded by stating that there is no necessity for a forward movement at present. REPORTED AFGHAN RISING.

Sr. PBTEI2BBURG, THUSISDAT.—.The NetWe Vretnici this morning publiehefl particulars of a rising of Afghan tribes on the Kushk, whick followed directly after the defeat of the Afghan forces by the Russians. It is staled that this insurrection is the result of general discontent at the Rawnl Pludl Conference. The Afghans, the Noyes Vrentjs alleges, are apprehensive of another English invasion.

div.head: SIR P. LUMSD.EN'S FORCE.
div.p: SIR P. LUMSD.EN'S FORCE.

Sr. PSTERSHUNG, TUESDAY. 10 £.M.—lt is asserted bore on the authority of telegrams from officials in Central Asia, that Sir Peter Lumsden left his late camp in a piti- able plight.. Many of his followers succumbed to hunger while others were frozen to death. After the English left. the Afghans burnt the camp, while the Barak/is pillaged the abandoned baggage. The weather in Central Asia is still reported most severe. Intense cold with heavy downpours of snow and sleet prevail.

div.head: WAR PREPARATIONS.
div.p: WAR PREPARATIONS.

It is announced that the Admiralty has decided to take up all ships that they have contracted for frem the marcher:l- - marine as armed craisers for a period of six months car tale, instal of by the month as at first intended. An Englishman who has just arrived at Varna from Russia reports that during last week not less than 120,000 men named along the railways from Odessa, Sebas- topol, and Taganrog for the south of the Volga, whence thir destination was understood to be by the Caspian to the Caucasus.

A fire occurred on Tuesday at Messrs Stevens' warehouse, Glasgow. Six hundred barrels of rosin were consumed. The damage amounted to £B,OOO. Loup Ripon ow TRH CRISIS. Speaking at York on Monday, in connection with the unveiling of a statue of the late Mr. George Leeman, M.P., the Marquis of Ripon said he should not discuss the merits of the Afghan frontier dispute, believing that it was the duty of all public men to refrain at present from exciting popular passion or fanning the warlike feeling which existed. Should a conflict with Russia unhappily become inevitable, however, England would enter upon it with the consciousness of having a loyal India and a friendly Afghanistan enlisted with her, together with the promise of material assistance from her great colonies.

DEATH OF THE LORD MAYOR OF LONDON.—The Right Hon. George Swan Nottage, Lord Mayor of Lon don, died on Saturday morning at 20 minutes to eight o'clock. He had been suffering lately from pleurisy. Alderman Not- tage, who was widely knows as chief of the London Stere- oscopic Company. was chosen as alderman for the ward of Cordwainers in 1875. No other Lord Mayor of London has died during his year of office this century. In the middle of the 18th century there was a succession of deaths in the civic chair which must have impressed the supersti- tions. In 1741 the Lord Mayor died ; next year the holder of the office also died; and from 1749 three Lord Mayors died at intervals Of a year, i.e., 1749, 1751, and 1753. The neat death occurred in 1770, which was the last for 115 years. On Wednesday morning the new Lord Mayor of London (Mr Alderman Fowler) was received by the Lord Chief Justice, in the &bones through bereavement of the Lord Chancellor, at his private room in the Royal Courts of Justice when the Queen's approval of the choice of the citizens was formally signified to Mr. Alderman Fowler.

Scots Guards move to liandoub with squad- ron Lancers end large convoy."—" 4-5 p.m.: Inspected line rail and. Handoab to-day. Convoy 1,100 camels, 35 Carts, water supplies, engineers' stores arrived here with Soots guards. Working parties head railway covered by East Surrey and squadron Bengal Cavalry scouting. Railway advanoed to No 1 station. Berkshire and Marines at camp near No 1 station, with one company in blockhouse there; East Surrey and Shropshire camp in rear. All satisfactory at Handoub, excellent work done in cutting wood, and on defensible posts and camp. In force 1,600, only five sick. Water plentiful for cattle and washing purposes, found only 3ft. below dry bed watercourse. Mabmoud Ali on friendly mission to Amaraars to try and get them over." 1 HaNuorn, MONDAY.—About 150 friendly natives made a reconnaissance among tbe mountains. To-day they encoun- tered a small force of the enemy, whom they defeated, taking some prisoners. The Mounted Infantry reconnoitred in the direction of Otao To-day General Graham reviewed the New South Wales Artillery. THE MAHDI'S DIFFICULTIES.

Canto, SCNDAY.—Lord Wolseley will leave very shortly for Suakim, but says be has no idea of abandoning the autumn campaign in the Soudan, for which he is makicg every preparatios. Canto, MoNray.—lt is stated that the French Govern- ment threatens to suepend diplomatic relatictvi if the order for the suppression of the Bosphore Eyvytien is not rescinded. liabat Pasha, however, firmly refuses to yield.

DONOOLA, SUNDAY.—The insurrection against the Mandi in Kordofan is reported te be headed by Abdel Hamed Waled Essafia, and to be spreading widely. The Mandi himself has gone to the scene of hostilities, leaving an Etnir to go- vern Khartoum and district. Down:nat., MONDAY.—A deserter reports that the rebels have left Berti and retreated to Berber, while those who were at Metemmeh have withdrawn to Khartoum. Large num- bers ci the Bishareen Arabs, who had joined Osman Dignia, received such a severe lesson in their several defeats at the hands of the British troops that they are leaving Digma's country with their families, and are retreating to Berber.

div.head: SEIZURE OF OSMAN DIGAIA'S CATTLE.
div.p: SEIZURE OF OSMAN DIGAIA'S CATTLE.
The following despatch was issued from the War Office on Tuesday evening :

From Lieutenant-General Sir G Graham to Secretary of State for War.--'inakim, 14th April, 4.55 p m.—Reconnais- sauce yesterday from Randoub to Otay, a distance of eight miles. No enemy was visible. Two wells; water supply can be developed. The road is easy for construction of railway, there being little scrub. The Eat Surrey and Shropshire Regiments moved yesterday to head of railway. 11 miles beyond No. 1 bl.ckhouse. Protective precau- tions are taken. Osman Digma is endeavouring to collect followers, and to compel the tribes to bring him supplies. Native scouts went out on the 12th to Handoub, and inter- cepted cattle on the way to Osman. The sick and wounded are progressing favourably. The percentage of sick in the whole force is a little over four.
SUAKIN, TCESDAY -It i 9 intended to form a camel corps here, consisting of 400 British and 100 Indian soldiers, under MAjor JAmeg The advance on Otao is expected to be made about the 18tb inst.

CAPTURE OF A CONVOY.-SCARCITY OF FOOD IN BERBER. The following is a telegram from Sir G. Graham to the Sec- retary of State for Wa.., dated Suakim, the 14th of April : —" Mounted Infantry from Handoub made successful re- connaieance to-day through the hills beyond Haeheen to Deboret. They have brought in 40 prisoners, including women and children. They also captured 12 camels and over 500 sheep. They were evidently on their way to Oman Digna. No fighting. The men in the 31abeli's camp either ran away or gave themselves up." Screitur, WEnsnesnay.—Deserters who have arrived here report that Osman Digma has retreated to Erkowit with a few followers. Traders from Berber state that Arabs in the vicinity of that place dread the British advance, and are convinced that the Mandi is a false prophet. They add that food is very scarce in Berber. The Intelligence De- partment has ascertained that the enemy are willing to sur- render for a heavy ransom the prisoners taken from the Indian contingent.

div.head: EXTENSION OF THE NILE RAILWAY.
div.p: EXTENSION OF THE NILE RAILWAY.

ALEXANDRIA, WEDNESDAY.—A large consignment of railway plant, eufficient to cover a distance 0150 miles, ar- rived yesterday from England. It is to be used in the ex- tension of the present Nile line running between the Wady Haiti, Same, and Farik, a place not far from Dal. It is ex- pected that the rail way will be completed some time in July. It will greatly facilitate communication. The diffi- cult passage up the Nile, with its numerous cataracts, will be avoided. Cam, WEDNISDAY.—Lord Wolseley will not proceed to Suakirn this week. INDIAN COOLIES FOR RAILWAY SERVICE.

EVAKIM,THIIRSDLY.—TweIve hundred coolies are coming from India to assist in the construction of the railway, which will reach Handout, to-morrow, and will be carried on to Otao without delay. The railway has already proved of great service in the conveyance of military stores to the front.

- - - ALEXANDRIA, TIMM/Y.—One hundred and My tents which were sent to shelter the inhabitants et the town of tofelig have been completely destroyed by fire. About fifty persona were burnt to death. THE RISING IN CANADA.

Orraws. FRIDAY.—In yesterday's sitting of the Do- minion House of Commons, Sir John Macdonald, the Pre- mier, gated that he had received no confirmation of the reported movement of Indians from American to Canadian territory. He believed that the report was invented by in- tereeted raffles. According to intelligence received this morning from other sources, the Crows, Kooteray, and Gros Ventres Indiana have sent a large fighting party via Bear's Paw mountains in the United States to Cypress Hill on the Canadian side. The party Is now encamped on the Milk River, which is on the way to Cypress Hill. The Indians in other districts are adopting an insolent attitude. OTTAWA, Scrwmay.—Crowfoot, chief of the Black Feet, has telegraphed to Sir John Macdonald, the Premier, that he will keep faith with the great mother, and will not make war upon the whites. The young braves, he says, shall spill no blood and will keep on their farms. Gen. Middle- ton telegraphs that be is approaching Humboldt, having marched an average of 21 miles per day. He has SOO men, and expects to reach the river and to meet the enemy on Wednesday or Thursday, A force of 350 men left Swift Current last night for the river, an will embark on tke steamers at Scow. on Monday morning, taking Gatling guns with them. The force at Prince Albert Is quite safe. Strag- gling bands of Indians from the American side have entered Southern Manitoba, pillaging and burning several houses. Troops have been despatched from Winnipeg to repulse them.

LARGE DEFALCATIONS.—A commercial traveller named John Alderson, of Stockton-on-Tees, was Indicted at the as- sizes held at Carlisle on Wednesday for embezzling the moneys of his employers, Messrs Carr and Co., biscuit manufacturers. The prisoner's defalcations amounted to over 11,200. lie was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment with hard labour. THE MI=DER OF AN ENCILISHHAN IN AMERICA.-00 in- quiry at Scotland•vard it has been ascertained that the American authorities had not yet communicated with that department respecting the supposed murder of an English- man at St. Louis. Little doubt is entertained by the rela- tives of Mr C A Preller that the remains discovered are these of the young traveller representing the house of Mr J H Dixon, worsted manufacturer, Bradford. Mr Preller's father, who is in business in London, first heard of the tragic centreline through the newspapers. He afterwards received a cablegram confirming his worst fears.

div.head: ! THE ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.
div.p: ! THE ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.
SATURDIY.

lAt one o'clock on Saturday the P ince and Prin- tees of Wales and party proceeded to the new dock constructed at the North Wall extension, Dub- lin, for the purpose of naming it. Everywhere great crowds were gathered in the streets. The ar- rival at the deek of the Royal pair, with their brilliant eecort of the 10th Lancers, was the signal for a great cheer from the company, and a musical salute by the band of the Highland Light Infantry. The Princess then named the dock "Alexandra," amid loud cheers, and at a signal the guns at the Pigeon House Fort bellowed out a salute of 21 guns. After luncheon, their Royal Highnesses and suite left the Castle for Trinity College. An address was presented by the Provost. The Prince, in replying, made a feeling reference to the loss the University had sus- tained by the death of its Chancellor. Their Royal High- nesses then drove round the New Square, followed by the students, cheering lustily. The Artave Industrial Schools, near Closter!, were next visited. A few kindly words were ' spoken to them by the Prince, who then left with the Princess and Prince Albert Victor for Dublin, which wa• reached soon after six, the same manifestations of popular favour being exhibited en the return. In the evening a state dinner party was given at the Castle, to which the leading judges, professors, and other distinguished citizens were invited.

div.head: SUNDAY.
div.p: SUNDAY.

On Sunday, at liantua—,;;;;;; Cork, an open-air meet- ing was held, attended by over 6,000 persons. The follow- ing resolation was adopted :—"That while we were willing to adopt Mr Parnell's advice and extend to the I'rince of Wales the elurtesy of our silence, we are of opinion that , the ruffianly attempts now being made by the English press to abuse the forbearance of the Mak people and to construe their silence into a disregard of the advice of the Irish leaders, renders it absolutely necessary for the people from this time for th, whelever the Prince of Wales presents himself, to proclaim their detestation of the English and their unspeakable confidence in Charles Stuart Parnell."— Mr W O'Brien, M.P., delivered a violent speech. He said they were bound to remind the Prince of Wales that the wrongs of Ireland were too solemn for the mockery of Royal visits.—ln Cork Park on Sunday afternoon a mass meeting was held. Several bands were in attendance.—Mr John O'Connor, M.P., proposed a resolution similar in terms to that mentioned above.

MONDAY. Cu Monday morning the Prince presented new colours to the Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry. The regiment, numbering 800, assembled in the Viceregal Gardens at tha rear of the Castle, in the form of a squire, an open space at one of • its sides being left for the keyal party and tee officers of the staff. His It -iyal Highness delivered an ad- dress, stating that he was proud to be connected with the regiment, and adding that be was sure the roll of honour- able distinctions on their colours would ever increase.— Colonel Stabb briefly thanked his Royal Highness en behalf of the men.—The Royal visitors left at midday by a special train for the South, and were loudly cheered. Prior to their departure from the Castle the Lord Mayor drove up to the City Hall to attend a meeting of the Corporation, and the crowd assembled to cheer the Prince and Priacess heartily groaned him. He turned and said warmly, "I will tele- graph to Cork and Mallow about this. I will give three cheers for Parnell." Here he waved his hat and celled for three cheers for Parnell. His requcet was but feebly re- sponded to. He continued: " I was determined to let the Prince go in peace, but you have hissed me to-day, and I was hissed by Orangemen, Freemasons, landlords, and bailiffs. I will remember it all the days of my life, and von will be sorry to-morrow." He then entered the hall. 'the Royal visitors passed immediately afterwards, on their way to the station, and were loudly cheered. At the station a company et the Grenadier Guards was:draet n up as a guard of honour. The train did not remain long in the station after the Royal party bad taken their swats. , At Mallow Junction the Town Commissioners had deoided to present an address to the Prince, and this was taken exception to by certain individuals. The aid of the local member, Mr. Win. O'Brien, was invoked in the direction of organising a counter-demonstration. Mr. John O'Connor, the recently elected member for Tipperary ; Mr. Deasy, the junior member for Cork ; aid Mr. Timothy Harring- ton, the representative in Parliament of Westmeath, also went down to Mallow, and bands of music ware collected from Cork, Charleville, and Kantutk to form the nucleus of the demonstration. These bands marched to Mallow sta- tion a short time before the royal train was due, and were followed by about two hundred persons. A train was sig- nalled, and this being taken by the crowd to be the royal train, the bands began to play " God save Itelar.d." A company of the Royal Irish Constabulary was told off to clear the station. The crowd refused to go and had to be expelled hoee. the platform. Exactly at six o'clock the royal train steamed into Mallow station, which was then filled by a crowd of orderly country people, who gave the Prince a hearty welcome. A counter reception on the part of the Nationalists outside was not heard amid the shouis of the more enthusiastic people inside the station. The I address was handed to the Prince, who deferred his reply. The Royal party then proceeded for Couvarnore, the seat of Lord Listowel, near Ballyhooly. A Cork correepondent says that on the return of the bands from Mallow consider- able disturbances took place. Several houses at which bunting was displayed were wrecked, including that of Mr. B. Shelia°, ex-Mayor, and other houses also suffered.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

_ The Prince and Princess of Wales remained at Conva- more, Lord Listowel's seat, on Monday evening, and early on Tuesday morning they left by special train for Kilmea- dow, County Waterford, and drove thence to Carraghmore, the seat of the Marquis of Waterford. The Royal parry stopped at Lismore for about five minutes on their journey to Curreghmore, and had an enthusiastic reception. At Dungaryan all the vessels in the harbour had their flags hauled down. At Kilmacthomas black flags, with the Nationalist inscription, were displayed, but there was a cordial Royalist welcome. At Cork flags were freely dis- played and triumphal arehea erected. The Prince's journey lay along the valley of the Blackwatar, and crowds of peasantry gathered at railway statioas and other points A party of Villierstown labourers were gathered at Cappoquln, while at Lismore and Fermoy addresses were presented by local bodies amid the cheers of large crowds. At Ballyduff, Dungaryan, and elsewhere there were assemblages of peasantry who manifested no feeling whatever. At Kilma- doon, from which place the Royal party drove to Currach- snore, through Portlaw, several thousands of persons filled the roads and gave the Prince as enthusiastic welcome. After lunching at Lord Waterford's mansion, the Royal party returned by the same route to Convamon.

WEDNESDAY. On Wednesday morning the Prince and Princess of Wa aocompanied by Prince Albert Victor and the Royal suite, made their State entry inte Cork. As has been the cam throughout the Royal tour in the island, the day was beauti- fully fine, and the sun shone with more than vernal warmth. The Prince and Princess entered the special train at Bally. bode, at a quarter past ten, accompanied by the Marquis and Marchioness of Ormonde, Lord Suffield, Sir Dighton Probrn, and the remainder of the Royal suite, and a rapid ran of an hour brought them to Cori. Here an enthusiastic recuiplon had been prepared for the Prince and Princess by a large company et the citizens of Cork. The West Surrey Regiment formed a guard of honour, and saluted the Royal party with the customary honours. Lord Bandon, as deputy lieutenant of the county, presented the Prince with an address of welcome from the city and county magistrates. In reply the Prince said he hoped that all those who had influence on their affairs would avoid those dissensions which impeded the progress of a city and unite in earnest efforts to promote the real welfare and further the true in- terests of the inhabitants. His Royal Highness afterwards proceeded to the Convent of the Good Shepherd, a Roman Catholic institution founded as a refuge far adult females and a reformatory for girls. A way of half an hour was made here. After taking leave of the Bishop and the Sisters, the Royal party drove down Sunday's Well Hill, across the Wellington Bridge, and back to the Cathedral. At most points of the route the reception given to the Prince was very cordial. At 5-20 p.m. with the sounds of the National Anthem and the cannonading of the ironclads ringing in in their ears the Royal party left Queenstown. At night parts of the town and the ships of the Channel Squadron were illuminated and a grand display of fireworks took phoe.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

The Prince and Princess of Weles left Convamore, near Mallow, on Thursday morning for Killarney. Before leav- ing, their Royal Highnesses each planted a tree in front of the !muse as a memento of their visit. Small crowds, who gathered at Ballahooly Station, offered a respectful recep- tion, while at Killarnev Station and within the town a cot, dial greeting was extended. Their Royal Highnesses drove to Kenmare House, and will remain guests of the Earl if Spenoer until Monday.

At Dublin, a number of forged £l.O Bank of England notes are in circulation. The Salford Stipendiary on Wednesday committed to tle assizes on the eapital charge the two youths Murphy and Grant, who are charged with the murder of Christophir Sheffield,

_ At Oldham on Wednesday John Taylor was remanded on a charge of shooting Mr Whittaker, iron merchant, with in. tent to murder him. The injured man, who received a bullet wound in the neck, is recovering satisfactorily.

Om:smug DISPETE.—On Tuesday night district meet- ings of the operatives on the wages qustion were held in Oldham. The employers have proposed 5 per cent. reduc- tion in the operatives' wages, including spinners and card. roam hands. A resolution was carried to resist the reduc- tion, the operatives saying they preferred stopping a month, two months, or even three months than having a reduction, or have short time. SHOCKING MPEOEII.—A young woman of weak intellect. named Alice Goodwin, was committed for trial by the Wol- verhampton magistrates, on Wednesday, for the manslaugh- ter of Archibald Bennett, a boy aged six, the son of a packer. The prisoner, on being teased by several children, seised the deceased, and knocked his forehead against a lamp poet, causing injuries which resulted in tbe child's death shortly afterwards. ATTEMPT TO UPSET a M&NCRESTER Exrmess.—The ether day George Barton, a labourer, of Barpender!, was anew to place a large stone and a Bleeper on the Midland Railway lines between St. Albans and ilirpenden. Almost Immediately afterwards an express goods train :Arne towards 'Harpenden. It passed over some obstruction, and the driver, looking out, found that a large stone. had been plead on his line. The prisoner has been committed to the Mnonbeliew Assizes. He is believed to be humus.

EARL&STOWN WAN.. nErtnns.—This match, the last of the season, was played at earlestown on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the. visitors by three goals to one, P Davies, J and T Foster. and Faram (forwards), and Kachen and Slater ,back) de- Qerve great praise for their play for the winners; while hi' the Wanderers, Champion, Harrison, and Thompson ougl to be mentioned. RUNCORN v. Torriscercne.—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday, and ended in favour of Runcorn as follows :—Ruacorn : One try, two minor points; Tottino. ton : One try, one minor point. Ftqgg kicked off, and Speakman returned the ball. Spencer made a litttle head- way and passed to Barlow, who finished a nice run with a punt, which Lewis neutralised with a Hying kick. Lewis kept up the attack, and finally scored a try. Woods took the place kick, but was not succr:ssful. Johnson returned the drop out, Wright, Ford, Joule, and Hoffland, aided by Woods and H Hughes, taking the play into the Tottington twenty-five. Ellison and Barlow got the ball back into Raucorn quarters, and W Hughes, not having time to pick up, dribbled into the pack, the Tottington forwards getting past him, and folk grounded the ball. Fogg kicked at goal, out did not register the major point. Wright, after half-time, re-s'arted the ball, Holding and Wilkinson lodg- ing play in neutral ground. Ford and Gatley broke away in go d style, and Fogg tried to beat Speakman, but the latter player brouglit him down. Roberts now got the ball nicely away, and Andrews passed to Johnson, he in turn transferring it to Clark. The Tottington lines were threatened, where a hard scrimmage or two took place, and Tottington getting the ball ran back and touched down. Teams :—Tottington: Dawson, back; Fogg (captain), Ellison, Barlow, three-quarter beck,; R Hartnett, Spencer, half backs; Walker, It Hannett, A Holding, Wilkinson, Meadowcroft, Booth, Masser, Holt:, forwards.
