EARLBSTOWN V. LIVERPOOL STANLEY.—Earlestewn, win- ners or tile Liverpool and Dietrict,Vhallenge Cup, visited the new ground of the Stanley Club at Walton Stiles, Liverpool, on Saturday. The visitors were announced as the "Cap Learn," but this title sadly belied the Earlesto- , nians. who arrived with °My ten men, an these did not I include Appleton, Whalley (captain), Dagnall (vice-cap- tain), Rich, and Ellison, whose places were filled by second eleven men. Tolls weakened, it could not be expected that the cup-holders would score a victory. The game had scarcely proceeded ere it was noticed that the home team were much too fast for the visitors, though the Earlestown for- wards during the first portion of the game occasionally pressed their opponents. Stanley undoubtedly had the beet of a very uninteresting struggle, but up to half-time neither side had scored. During the first half Eettley. of Cambrian Football Club, had been assisting Earlestown, but in consequence of an injury he retired, and for the whole of the second half Earlestown played with ten men. After crossing over the home forwards fastened on the ball, and Brown lotssing to Morris, the latter player notched the first goal within a minute from the restart. This ad- vantage imparted some life into the game, and after re- peated corners Brown neatly rcored again for Stanley. Evi- dently the cupholders' play had now became disorganised. and Stanley penned them to their own quarters. From a corner kick by Brown, Morris notched a third point. The EArlystohians.substquently played in better form, and after some good passing amonzst the forwards Holcroft managed to score for the cupholders. When time was called Stanley had won by three goals to one. Tsarrs :—Earlestown—J Harrison, goal : R Green and J Green, backs ; R Bow- ker, J Duxbury, and A Clayton, half-backs ; J Sims and J Ogden, left wing,; C M Ketley, centre ; H Hol- croft and W Murray, right wing. Stanley—Kerr, goal ; G Dovy and A Pd•Calluin, backs; F Walsh, P Owen. and W Wilson. half-backs; W George and Grant, rigkt wing; T Morris. centre; G Wright and Brown, left wing.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The qaestlon of professionalism bids fair, taking into ac count the construction of the committee recently appointed to be settled before the commencement of next season. A meeting of the committee has b3m called for next week, to be held in London. The full committee, appointed with the officials of the association, is as follows, with the side they I are expected to take in regard to the legislation of pates. sianalietn :—Messrs. Betts (for), Sudell (for). Gregson (for) Crump (against), Lawrie (against). Hunter (for), Lymberry (for), Beardshaw (against), J U Clark (for). W C Alcock (for), W Pierce-Dix (against), Hon. A F Xinaird (for), and Major Marindin (for). On Saturday. Wales beat Ireland at Belfast ; Glasgow and Edinburgh played a drawn game at Edinburgh; rheale aod Windsor played a drawn gams in the final tie of the Berke and Bucks Junior Cup Competition ; in the Bolton Charity Cup Competition, Great Lever beat Belli- well ; in the semi-final tie of the Derbyshire Charity Cap Competition, Spital beat Derby County ; in the Glasgow Charity Cup Competition the Rangers awl Dumbarton played a drawn game; Aston Villa beat Corinthians ; at Sheffield. Wenesday beat Lockwood Brothers; Staveley beat Derby and District, at Staveley.

nansccrr BOARD OF GUARDIANI.—The first meeting of the new Board was held on Thursday. Mr John Leather- barrow was unanimously elected chairman, and Messrs Lowe and James Fisher, vice-chairmen.—The Clerk ex. plained that the Local Government Board bad been asked by the Guardians to sanction the sinking of a well in the neighbourhood, but they had not done so.) Two experts had since recommendei that some other source should be found 1 or rather that a well should be sunk in a different situation !to that recommended previously. Tha matter WAS referred to the Visiting Committee.—Dr. Wood, medical oaicer for the Wool ton district, tendered his resignation, and Dr. Chia. ! holm was elected hie successor pro tern —Mr. J. G . Dann I tendered his resignation as @Assistant overseer for the Eccles- ! ton district. It WAS decided to advertise for a successor, who would be required to find security to the amount of £5OO, under bond from a guarantee society.—Mr. Fisher, in accordance with his notice,i moved that the vaccination con- tract with Dr. Ricketts, n t'le Parr and Sutton districts, he determined, in the ground that Dr. Casey, who was a Union medical officer, resided in the district, and Dr. Ricketts did not. The motion was carried by fifteen votes to two. I The PHYIieOY HIGHWAY Bosun held its last meeting for the year on Monday forenoon, when there ware present— Messrs W L Evans (in the chair), J Leatberbarrow, M Lowe, Newton, H Cross (clerk), W Goldsworth (surveyor), and IT Goldsworth, jun. (assistant surveyor) The Clerk I said the first business was the making of the calls for ! the ensuing year, and the surveyor remarked that according to the estimate submitted at the last meeting the amount was £2,100. As they wished to have a little money to they had made the sum £2,200. Asto the position of the townships Whision was £43 iu arrear, Reinbill £125 to the I good, Knowsley £B6 to the good, and Bold £232 to the I bad. The Chairman observed that last year the calls were —Bold .£530, Knowsley £1336, Barnhill £5OO, and Whistoa £736, This year the surveyor proposed to make Bold £5OO, a decrease of £3O; Knowsley £6OO, decrease of £36; Eats- ' hill £4OO, a decrease ef 1100 ; and Winston £7OO, a de- crease of £3O. After some iliscassion it was agreed that the call for Bold should he £550, for Wbiston £6.50, and let Rainhill and Knowsley the amounts stated. A motion was also passed that the calls be payable within one month. The Lancaehire and Cheshire Telephonic Exchanee Company ' applied for permission to erect poles in Longbarrow-ronl. Knowsley. and Comber.lano, Masten, to connect the water- works at Knowsley, and the matter was left In the hands of Mr Evans, Mr Leatherbarrow, and the Surveyor to make the best terms they contd. The Surveyor's statement of ex- penditure for the month showed—Bold £6 13s 91, Knows- Isv gd, Rainhill £1 12s od, Whisten £.3 185 3d, team labour £52 Os sd, new materials £2l 19s, incidentals £2 103 10d, total £95 12s sd.—On the motion of Mr Lowe, seconded by Mr Leatherbarrcw, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to the chairman for his services during the past year, and a similar compliment was also paid to the vice-chair- man (Mr Leatherbarrow).—This was the only business.

DESIONWRATION OF THE LONDON UNEMPLOYED.-41. demonstration of the employed and unemployed in London took place on Sunday afternoon, in Hyde Park, for the pur- pose of urging upon the Government the absolute necessity of giving emvloyment to the thousands out of work by re. ducing the Working day to one of eight hours, and by tbe carrying out of public works such as canals, aqueducts, aid embankments. Some 20,000 people assembled. spew," were delivered from five platforms. The proceedings, which throughout were mast orderly, lasted about an hour and 6 quarter. SUDDEN DEATH OF TUB LORD CHANCELLOR OF LAND —On Monday evening the Right Hon. Edward Sulli- van, Lord Chancellor of Ireland, died suddenly at his resi- dence. Early in the morning he attended at the Castle, and remained there some time. On returning home he was se:zed with an attack of rheumatic gout in the stomach. which shortly proved fatal. He was 63 years old, and was appointed Lord Chancellor a little more than twelve months ago. Sir Edward Sullivan was admitted to the bar in Ire- land in 1843, and became a QC. in 1858. From 1866 tor 1870 he at a! a Liberal member for Mallow. He was ap- pointed Solicitor-General for Ireland in 1865, and Attorney- General in 1868. In 1870 he became Master of the Rolle, and in 1383 Lord Chincellor of Ireland. The death of sit Edward Sullivan is the third within 18 mooths of eminent men who have held the office of Lord Chancellor of Ireland—Mr. 15w, Lard O'Llagan, and the latest incum- bent of the office.

THE Liberty and Property Defence League have issued a smart little pamphlet on "Drink," which has been written by Lord BRAMWELL. His lordship is always incisive and interesting when he puts pen to paper ; but he is so anxious to make a point whatever subject, or phase of a subject, he deals with, that he attempts as a rule to prove too much. It is so in the treatise before us ; he goes in so strongly for liberty that carrying his argument to a logical conclusion—there ought to be no interference at all on the part. of the law in the sale of intoxicatinz liquor. Perhaps he is prepared to go this length, but if that be the case, it is obvious that he is very far behind, or, as he might put it, a long way in advance of the rest of the corn munity. Let it be assumed that there is some risk of hardship arising out of total prohibition; this, surely, may be admitted without rushing to the conclusion that there should be "free trade" in the sale of drink. We rather think there are sundry brewers —some even pretty near home—who would be horrified at a proposal on the part of the Government to throw "the trade" open. They believe in legislation up to a certain point— the point at which they are enabled to secure a monoply in particular localities, Whatever Lord BRAMWELL may think, it may be taken 1, as settled, 9fr AS En.alltiri;..,,r, tte masi Ate tinC'erned, that it is the duty of the State to exercise control over the liquor traffic. The moot point is as to the extent of this ' control; and, this being so, much of Lord 1, BRAMWELL'S reasoning is wholly besides the mark. He asks—" Can nothing be done by law to diminish the mischief caused by drink ? " and he gives an emphatic "No." What an utterly hopeless Prospect I Happily the majority of the p .ople of this country— irrespective of party—are of a different , opinion, and there can be no question that the next Parliament will undertake a reform of the licensing laws. The matter is one which is undoubtedly beset with difficulties; but this is certain, that working-men who suffer so much from drink shops being placed at their doors are determined to have a voice in the number and distribution of licensed houses. It is all very well for aris- tocratic politicians like Lord BRAMWELL to urge that the law can do nothing; they are far enough removed in their country resi- dences and West end mansions from the evil influences of "the trade." But let them be surrounded with public-houses and beer- ' shops ; let their sons and daughters be sub- ject to their influence as are the children of their less fortunate fellow-men, and we venture to predict that another tale would be told as to what can be "done by law to diminish the mischief caused by drink." The law cannot do everything, but it can do something; it can and ought to make it easier to keep sober, and harder to get drunk,

THE Liberals of the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire, held a meeting of the " 300 " at Earlestown, on Monday, at which Colonel MCCORQUODALE was adop- ted as the Liberal candidate. Members.of the Press were excluded from the meeting, a circumstance much to be regretted, for the result is that a necessarily imperfect, and possibly inaccurate report of the candidate's address iS all we can lay before our readers It may be desirable to treat minor tran- sactions of the Council as private or semi- private ; but it is surely unwise to close the door upon the Press when a candidate is giv- ing an all-important address. We are glad to learn that Colonel MCCORQUODALE met with a cordial reception ; and, although it is impossible that he should please everybody, there is reason to believe that he will receive the enthusiastic support of the Libera's of the Division. It must not be overlooked that, from a personal point of view, he is making some sacrifice in putting himself in the hands of the Liberal party as their candi- date. He has, however, placed duty before personal convenience, and, if the Liberal electors will follow his example in this re- spect, they will see him at the close of the next contest at the head of the poll. They must be prepared for a hard fight ; for his opponent, Sir RICHARD CROSS, has the pres- tige of possession of a seat, it he has nothing else to recommend him. The new electors who are alive to their own interests will cer- tainly not be tempted to vote for the El- i-lONE SECRETARY, seeing that, if he had had I his way, they would have hid no vote at all. rhe Bill so dear to their hearts which has now become law was, on one occasion, it is well to remember, referred to by Sir RICHARD CROSS as "that wretched Franchise Bill." Wretched," indeed, if it should result as we trust it may. in his being left, so far as the new Parliament is concerned. out in the cold. What is there to hope from a House of Commons composed of such men as Sir RICHARD CROSS ? What has he to offer that working-men can regard as a benefit ? Nothing, absolutely nothing. Colonel MC - CORQUODALE, on the other hand, comes be- fore the electors with a full programtne of reforms. .He sees the evils of the law of primogeniture, and is prepared to abolish that remnant of a barbarous age; and, fur- ther, he would ,remove the obstacles which now stand in the way of the sale and transfer of land. He advocates changes in the licen- sing acts ; and perceives the necessity of amending the Employers' Liability Act, so as to make it a still greater benefit to the working classes. He has no sympathy with perpetual pensions, and will support any

div.head: LAL
div.p: LAL
TR

well-considered measure for getting rid of these monstrous burdens upon the nation. He has not forgotten that the House of Lords, backed up by such members of the House of Commons as Sir RICHARD CROSS, recently sought to prevent Two Millions of capable citizens being admitted within the pale of' the constitution ; and that, as at present con- stituted, the House of Lords is a menace to the State. By way of letting their lordships ! know that they are vulnerable, and as a means of weeding out the worst of them, Colonel MCCORQUODALE would suspend for a number of years those who were ' guilty of acts of immorality ; or else remove them altogether from the list, as is sometimes done with Justices of the Peace. He is not insensible either to the need of reform in the House of Commons, for he is like other practical men in desiring that for the future there may be less talk and more work. Colonel MCCORQUODALE is an excellent candidate, and as such we commend him to the electors of the Newton Division of South West Lancashire.

As no news is good news, we are glad to be . in a position to say that there is a growing hope of a peaceful solution of the dispute with Russia as to the Afghan frontier. Mr. GLADSTONE referred complacently, in the House of Commons last evening, to the in- telligence that had come to hand of the Rus- sian occupation and administration of Penj- deh, from which it is perhaps not unreason- able to infer that there is truth in the current report that it is a matter of indifference to the AMEER whether Penjdeh goes to Russia or is retained as a part of his own territory. If he is not concerned, there is no .reason why we should trouble ourselves in the matter, unless on the supposition—a disagreeable one to entertain in view of the recent conference with the VICEROY—that ABDUR RAHMAN is playing into the hands of the EMPEROR of RUSSIA. It is some satisfaction to know that the CZAR has this week evinced an anxiety to keep on good terms with the British Government, and we must decline, on the facts before us, to believe that it is even probable that Afghan and Muscovite are alike false to us and to their own professions It may be that, in the first instance, Russia meant war, and that she has changed her mind on finding that England was ready if not eager for the fray. If this be so, it will give force to the saying that preparedness for war is the best guarantee for peace.

The proceedings were very enjoyable, and reflected great credit upon Mr J Farrant, who had trained the children. • • Ce/Mentkf Ildt4eoaN.---The mern!€! ¶ the singing closes, conducted by Mr John Holier& gatfa condert in Ellesmere-street schoolroom on Thursday evening. The at- I tondance of the public was not very encouraging, but the concert was of a very enjoyable character. The programme embraced an attractive selection of sacred and secular music from the works of Handel, Mendelssobn, Spohr, and Bette, and the manner in which the choir performed the somewhat difficult pieces set down, showed careful and in- telligent teaching. The following ',scalier' took part : Mrs Newell, Mrs Burrows, Mies Catena, Miss Janes, Messrs J Holford, A Fox; W Howard, T Fox, and Marlow. Mrs Turnbull presided at the piano, Comenvorsa Onclimirielot; Ay RUNCORS.—A meet- ing of the Conservatives was held in Holy Trinity School- room en Thursday evening, under the presidency of the Rev IV Preston Mr I W Lightbarn explained that it had been decided to form a General Council, consisting of lice represeatatives to every thousand of the population, and this Council would meet at Northwich to-day to select a candidate. LABOUR REPRESENTATION —A "pit set" conference of miners' delegates, convened by the Lancashile and Ckeahire I Miners' Federation, was held at Wigan on Saturday to de- cide as to what steps should be taken to secure the repre- sentation of the mining interest in the ceunty at the next general election. There VIM a large attendance. 'After a lengthy discussion, it was unanimously resolved that the Inca division of South-West Lancsshire should be contested by a candidate in the labour interest. Various names were mentioned, and it was decided that another conference be held to settle this important point. The Conservatives in the Ince division of South-West Lancashire have decided to request Mr N Eekersley, one of the representatives of the borough of Wigan, to become the candidate of the party in the new division. The Liberal electors of Stoke have de- cided to guarantee the election expenses of Mr Broadhurst. A POTATO DEALER'S DISPUTE.—At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, his Honour Judge Vol:tikes heard a case of some interest to farmers and potato dealers.—Mr Walton. barrister, appeared for the plaintiff, Samuel Clarke, potato dealer and innkeeper, Frodsham, and Mr Pickford, barrister, for defendant, Samuel Rowland, a farmer, of Whitley.—Mr Walton said that action was brought to re- cover damages in respect of certain potatoes delivered by the defendant to the plaintiff, and In respect of certain potatoes that were not delivered according to contract. The potatoes that were delivered were of an inferior quality, and the amount claimed in that respect was a odd. A fur- ther quantity of 100 loads were not delivered at all, and damages were claimed on that account to the amount of £2 10s. There was also a small item as to soma potatoes that were paid for and not del(vered.—Evidence was then given as to the quality of the potatoes and their marketable price, it being contended that they were not of the quality represented to plaintiff when he agreed to purchase.—Mr Pickford admitted an *meant ef Ss for potatoes paid for, but net delivered. With regard to the claim of damages for non-delivery, Mr Pickford commented on letters written by plaintiff, which, be urged, put him oat of court, as be (plain- tiff) had agreed that the bargain should be put an end to, and that the 100 loads should not be delivered. He also claimed that the potatoes had been properly riddled, and were of a good quality. The agreement was that they , should be made into good marketable etuff, and that had been fulfilled.—After a long hearing his Honour gave judg- ment for plaintiff for £4 15s 3d. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTRORITY.—The fort- nightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tues- day. Mr John Ashton presided, and there were also present the Revs J W N Tanner and J Lockwood, Messrs Stokes, Aaron, T Lewis, W Pickeriog,ll Linaker kclerk), W II Lina ker (deputy clerk), and Dr Adams (medical officer of health). —ln regard to Weston sewerage, Messrs C E Linaker and Davies wrote from Frodsham, under date 13th inst., saying that in commenting upon the letter of April 7th from the Local Government Board they had to report that they had given the matter consideration, and in addition to reducing the size of the sewer they had also reduced the number of manholes and lampholes. An amended estimate for the entire work, of £396 lie 6d, was enclosed. The letter of the Local Government Board referred to was read, and stated that the report of the inspector of the inquiry held by him in refer- ence to the application of the Authority to borrow £6OO for works of sewage for Weston had been considered. The Board, it said, were a twitted that if the new sewer was constructed of 15 inch pipes it would probebly suffice for many years for the requirements of that part part of the township to be sewered, and that the number of manholes and lampholes along its course might b, considerably reduced. They were also advised that means for flushing the sewer should be provided, and that the detached blocks of houses along the road to the south of the existing sower, which at present are without means of drainage, should be connected with it wherever practicable. It woe reqaested that in this respect the scheme should be revis,d tied again submitted to the Board, together with an amended estimate showing in detail how the amount proposed to be borrowed would b 3 spent. Further information was also asked an the subj,ct gener- ally.--The report of Ike Medical Officer of Health for the quarter ending 31st March, 1885, stated that the Registrars' returns recorded 154 births and 115 deaths in the four registratien districts comprised in the literal Sanitary dis- trict of the Runcorn Union. Of the Itirthe 73 were male and 78 females, and of the deaths 62 were m ales and 53 females. The death rate for the quarter had been unusually large for a rural p3pt,' lien. There had occurred 22 deaths (torn bronelaTs and inil ammation of the tunes, and measles accounted for 14 deaths, thus testifying to the fatal import- ance of the outbreak of measles upon which he had from time to time reported. No less than 10 deaths had formed the subject of coroners' intricate. These three causes alone accounted for 40 per c ,nt. of all the deaths occurring during the quarter. No deaths had occurred from scerlet fever, Ind only one each from typheid fever and whooping coagh. Sir Adams rem irked to the meeting that it had been reported to him that Stockton Heath schools, had been closed in con- sequence of measles; but 51r Farriegton sanitary inspector, said that on the day previous he was at Stockton Heath and did not hear it inentioned.—This ryas all the business.

WESTON POINT NATIONAL SCHOOLS.--The COIRMITtee of Me Et ayal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Liverpool Branch) have awarded a prize and certificate each to Annie Riding and Richard C Rosenberg, both at- tending these schools:for the excellence of their respective essays oa " Reasons for kindness to Animals," sent in at the competition held a month ago. The Mayor and Mayoress of Liverpool (Alderman and Mns Radcliffe) pre- sented the prizes to the recipients. Sroarrs AT WIDNES.—The members of the Widnes Har- riers' Club held an athletic festival on Milldeld Recreation Grounde on Saturday. There was only a moderate attend- ance of spectators. Mr H Quinn officiated as starter, and Messrs Gerrard, Coops, and Wright as judges. The first event was a 220 yards handicap d-cided in five beats, the winners of the heats being T Brassendale (14 yards). P McMahon (11 yards), J Wright (13 yards), add W Bate (14 yards). In the final J Wright was first, J Roscoe 2nd, and P Mcliakenßrd won by a yard and a half. The three mike handicap brought out 14 starters and a good race resulted as followsl-41 Wright, 80 yards, 1 ; T Laws, 210 yards, 2; U Evans, 273 yards, 3. SAD DRAM OF AN INFANT AT WIDNES.—Mr W T Hus- band, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Sea View Inn, Farnworth, on Monday, on the body of an infant, the son of Richard and Charlotte Harris.—Dr O'Neill deposed that internally all the organs were healthy, but the body bad a blanched appearance indicating an'absence of blood. Death bad resulted from hcemorrage.—Alice Ducker said she was present at the birth of the child, which took place on Thursday night. After the midwife left she had the child upon her lap, but about 8 o'clock she laid It down. At half-past one o'clock she found it was dead. All its night drawl was saturated with blood.—The jury returned a verdict that the child died from hoemorrage. SWINI FEVER IN WIDNES: POLICE PROSECITTIONS.—

Joseph Shuffiebotham, a young man was summosed to Widnes Police Court on Wednesday, charged under the Con- tagious Diseases (Animals) Act with having oil the 6:11 inst removed a pig in a swine fever infected area without license.—lnspector Wood proved that the district of Widnes and Ditton had been declared an infected area for swine

fever, and that placards bad been posted upon the walls, and handbills distributed.—P.S. Savory proved the removal of the pig along Widnes-road —E nrna Hatton, the owner of the animal, pleaded guilty to causing its removal.—Francis Houghton and Patrick Connor also pleaded guilty to re- moving pigs without licenses.—Henry Copplok was charged with removing, and Hannah Wood with causing to be re- moved, a pig without a license.—P.C. Cummins admitted that at the time he saw the pig he was delivering handbills relating to the matter.—The Bench dismissed the two latter cases on the ground that it was rather "quick work," and ordered each of the other defendants to pay costs, 75 ad. Future offenders, the Bench stated, would be severely dealt with.

RIINCORFI BOARD OF GIJARDIANB.—The fortnightly meet- ing was held on Tuesday, Mr John Ashton presiding. There were also present the Revs J Lockwood and J W N Tanner, Messrs W Handley, Stokes, Aaron, T Lewis, W Pickering, T Norman, Whittaker, and W Fisher.—The Local Govern- ment board wrote approving the appointment of school at- tendance officer for the Union.—The accounts of the Finance Committee, showing an expenditure of £282 La 6d, were submitted by Mr Handley and passed.—The Chairman said he bad a resolution to move that would he cordially approved, and at the same time receive] with regret. They were aware that the RV, Canon Barclay had nQt sought re-election as a Guardian, and ha was expressing their stll-1 timents in saying how sorry they were that he had felt that I he could not do so. Canon Barclay had presided over them for many years and had been most courteous and kind. He was well versed in laws relating to the poor, knew well the duties and responsibilities of a Guardian, and his absence from the Board would be felt not only by the members but the whole Union, and the poor especially. They would hope with him that Canon Barclay would speedily be restored to health and be long spared to enjoy the fruits of his la- bours. He then moved a resolution expressing those senti- ments, which was seconded in suitable terms by the Rev W N Tanner, supported by Mr Handley, and unanimously carried.—A cordial vote of thanks was also accorded the vice-chairman, Mr Ashton, who briefly responded.—The Board then proceeded to relief business. CONCIIRT AT WIDSTES.—In aid of the fends of the Rail- way Servants' Society's Orphan Fund a concert took place in Lacey-street Schocl-room, on Monday evening ; and there was a good attendance. Mr E Carey presided, and in a brief address contrasted the railway system in England with that of America. During his journeyings on that eon- tinent about twelve months ago he seldom received a civil answer from the railway officials, Miilet in England the railway letVardi Were it a rule cArtentis and obliging, lie expressed his pleasure at the satisfactory c nlition of the finances of the society they were nt-t together to aid, Tile programme comsaenced with the quartett "In abstnce " rendered by St Paul's qusrtett party in go,l style. Mr R Moore sang " Once again" in a capital manner, ant he was warmly applauded. He was also highly successful in the song "Dog Help," when the handsome Scotch collie dog beating that name appeared on the platform by his side. Miss Cools contributed the claesical excerpt "Should He upbraid " in a most pleasing and tasteful manner, and she was loudly applauded. " Golden L-ive" was sung by Miss N Handley, whose voice, was heard to great advantage, and she was recalled. She was also associated with Mr R Moore in Verdi's charming duet "Home to our mountains." The singing of the comic song "Mrs Jot' s Musical Nay " by Mr R Morris was heartily appreciated, and he had to answer to an encore. He also contributed "The While Squall." Mr A Fox, who possesses a full deep voice, sang "Every bullet has its billet" with good expression. Much amusement was caused by the duet "The upper ten and lower five " sung by Mr R Morris and Mr A Fox 111 character. Mr Bibby sang "My native home" very taste- fully. A euphonium solo by Mr J Outhwait performed with much skill, was heartily enjoyed. Mr Kitto gave a couple of readings. The Widnes Soap Works Band perfor- med selections of music, and the concert concluded with the rinartett "When evening's twilight" by tire St Paul's quartets party.

THR RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. Ott Thursday even-! log a meeting of ratepayers wis h-ld in Bethesde Lecture ' Hall for the purpose of receiving the annual statement of the ancounts of the Runcorn Burial Board. Mr W Handley occupied the chair, and there were present—Messrs W F I Salkeld, C Cooke, J J Speaktnan, W Brookes. W Dobson, and W Sutton (assistant overseer.)-11r W F Selkeld read the report of the auditors (Messrs J J Speakman and C Cooke) which was to the effect that the accounts were cor- rect in every particular. Mr Salkeld aloe read the balance sheet, which will be found in oar advertising columns. It was adopted on the motion of Mr W Broakes, seconded by Mr Dabson.—Mr Speakman and Mr Cooke bore testimony to the correct and efficient way in which the accounts were kept, the former gentleman remarking that they reflected great credit upon Mr Salkeld.—The Chairman said what- ever Mr Salkeld had to do he tried to do it well, aed he always accomplished his aim. In the matter of figures he was always correct. From the time that he accepted the position of actuary to the Savings Bank, there had been the greatest confidence reposed in him by the managers. He had ably filled many public positions in the town. (Ap- plauee.)—Mr Salkehl suitably acknawledged the observa- tions with regard to himself, and suggested that the balance sheet should be advertised in the local pap-rs.—On the pro- position of Mr Suttee seconded by Mr Brookes, the stag- gestion was adopted.2Toe Chairman observed that during the pest year, the Burial Board had required a less sum from the, rates than in any previous year. For a great number of years the amount hat been between MOO and £4OO, but last year there had only been £l2O required, and he was of opinion that in future never more than £2OO would be required each year. The cemetery was, therefore, nearly self-supporting.—Mr Speakman : May we take it that it is through the heavy death rate P—The Chairman : No ; but because there were extra expenses this year that would not be incurred :elect year, the population'had in- creased, and the cemetery was fast becoming the only plane of sepulture in the town. The cemetery in future would not be a burden to the rate.—A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings.

SEAMEN'S DISPUTE AT RUNCORN —At Runcorn Petty See- alone on Monday, E•lward Ellis, master of the brigantine Caroline' was summoned by George Sherratt for btlance of wages. Mr Burton appeared for the complainant and Mr Lake for the defendant. It appeared that on the 7th No- vember, 1833, the complainant joined the vessel in New-1 foundland at £5 15s per month. He sailed to various parts of the globe and on the 4th April the vessel arrived at Runcorn, where the complainant, whose articles said he was to leave at the first English port of discharge, left the vessel. He had served 16 months 28 days, mahing his wages £97 7s 4d. There was a further claim of eight days' pay at 34 101 per day and 5s per day. "table money," bring- ing the total amount to £lOO 18s. The wile of the Corn- plainant, bad, however, received £4B, and the complainant himself bad received £9 103 31 for tobacco, ctc. Upoa arriv- ing in port the plaintiff left the vessel, as h 5 was permitted to do according to his articles, and the captain never gave him an account of hie wages nor told him where he could 'draw his money.—ln answer to Mr Lake, the p'aintiff said the captain ordered him to come bank on Monday. and ad- mitted that it was unusual to a leave a vessel immediately on arrival in port. He had been alongside the vessel several times, and met the defendant in the street, but he bad not asked tor his wages.—Mr Lake pointed out that the Custom House, according to the Shipping Act, was the proper place for the prisoner to receive his wages, and if a man could sum- mon his master for wages befere he had applied for them that court would be made a medium for the gratific,ition of pa- sonal spite and spleen.—After an argument between the advocates, the Bench suggested that the case should be settled, and the parties retired into the magistrates' room. The result' *as that the Bench made an order for the pay- ment of £37 15s ad.—The defendant MS then charged with assaulting ate co uplainant on the high seas off the Wes- tern Islands os the 30th March.—The complainant alleged that the defendant found fault with the manner in which he was doing some work and struck hhn on the face and head with his fists. Be fell to the deck and the defendant struck him whilst there, causing •hi a eye to become black and marking his ear.--.A.f ter hearing .the evidence the Beach dismissed the charge.

' Pons Rens FOR Drrron.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the magistrates consented to the levying of a poor rate of 91in thee to realise fe41.45 His Si for the town- ship of Dinar). Drsgy MINSTRELS AT RCNCORN.—The dusky minstrels In connection with the Widnes C.E.T.S. gave an entertain- ment in Runcorn Public Hall on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance, and the proceeds will be added to the fund for beautifying Holy Trinity Church. CAMDEN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—The anniversary sermons in aid of this school will be preached in St. Paul's Church on Sunday by the Rev Dr Nicholson, of Liverpool. An interesting feature will be the singing of hymns to the old Methodist tunes by the congregation. Further particulars will be found In our advertising columns. Assam:two A NEWSBOY AT WlDNES,—Edward Gorden, a young man, was charged at Widnes Petty Sessions en Wed- nesday witk assaulting a boy named James Gaekell. The boy sells evening papers, and on the 7th inet the defendant asked him what had won the "Great Lancashire Handicap" race, and upon his refusing to tell struck him on the head and face.—Mr J P Morewood, the agent to the paper, said these assaults were becoming very common, 20 or 30 cases having occurred within a very short time. One boy was now suffering from a very large wound on the back of the head, the result of maltreatment he had received at Crow Wood.—The defendant was fined 515 and costs, 9s 01. RESCOED BY • WOMAN AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Catherine Milton, a young woman, was charged with resisting P.C. McDonald and rescuing a prisoner named Moran. It appeared that on the 30th ult the officer arrested a man in Elmund-street on a charge of felony. The prisoner struggled violently, and the woman, saying the constable should not take him attempted to drag him away. The constable retained him, hold of a neckerchief, but whilst getting the handcuffs from his pocket the woman nntied the neckerchief and the prisoner made his escape He was with difficulty afterwards appre- hended.—The woman was sentenced to seven days' hard la- bour.

WIDNIES PABLILMINTAIIY DITISION.-Sir Edward Sulli- van haying declined to contest the constituency in the Con- servative interest, the party is again on the look out for a candidate. The subject was discussed at a meeting held in Liverpool on Wednesday, Major Cross presiding, but noth- ing definite was arrived at. The names of Colonel Ireland Blackburne, M P., and Mr T B Boyden were freely men- tioned as likely candidates. The Libzrals will not consi- der the selection of a candidate until the party organisation is complete. Rumour is making free with the names of Mr Gaskell, senr, J.P., Mr F U Gossage, J.P., and Mr E K Muspratt, J P., as probable candidates, but there is no official authority for mentioning these names.

ASSAIILT ar DITTON :-LJames Devine, a young man, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of assaulting Mary McMahan, a young woman.—Complainant said she was on her way to Dillon Church on Sunday miming, when the defendant came be- hind her, made use of disgusting language to her, seized her by the throat, and knocked her hat off. She picked up a stone to throw it at him after his conduct, but had given him no provocation.—The Defendant alleged that as he was walking along the road the complainnt asked " Whose father stole the money out of church ? " and said she would "Knock smoke" out of him. He retorted by saying" You little bitch." and the complainant picked up a stone, which he took off her. He never assaalted ber.—After hearing the , witnesses, the Bench said the defendant had no right to ' take the LOW irate his own hands, and mast pay a fine of is and costs Ils 61. Rl:Neoax POLICE COURT.—Yesterday, before Mr James Handley and Mr U L Davies, Victor Ramsey, a powerfully. built seaman, was charged with bring drank ant dis• orderly in Lock street. and isso with wilfully damaging the , house door of the Sloop Inn, occupied by Joseph Pegg. It ' appeared that the prisoner was a b 'larder at the inn, and about eleven o'clock on the night of the 15.. n inst. he went Into the house in a state of drunkenness. In conioquence of his noisy and disorderly cmduct he was turned into the street, and he retaliated by smashing the door with his foot. He was fined in the total sum of £l. 46 101, or 14 days' hard labour. P.C. Harper proved this case. The money' was paid.—Mary Jane Ann Gallagher, who made her 32nd appearance, was sentenced to a month's hard labour for being -drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on ; the 10th inst.—For a like offence Lucy Bates was sentenced 1 to 14 days' bard labour, in default of paying a ale of 10s and costs, 7s 44, The Citatiort A.OAINST A WIDNES INSORANCE Angler.— At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, James Gaghan, I shoemaker, and Widnes agent to the United Assurance company, Liverpool, again appeared before the magistrates ; to answers charge of unlawfully withholding £2B 8s Bd, the ; monies of the society.—Mr W H Quill iam (Liverpool), pro, secuted, and Mr W 'l' Husband defended. The case was proved a week ago is order that it might if possible be set- tied ; but no agree nent had been arrived at between the parties—Mr Husband admitted that his client Was civilly but not criminally indebted to the society to the extent of £25. Tue society, he argued, knew the defendant was in arrears, arid had acceptcd payments on account, and the action ought to have been taken in the Conety Court.— Mr Quilllam replied that that was at the prosecutor's option, but be would ac:ept £25 to save the time of the court.— The Bench therefore made an order for the payment of that ' amount at the rate of £1 per month. INHUMAN TREATMENT OF CHILDREN AT WICHES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Patrick McMahon was , brought up under a warrant charged with deserting his chit. I dren, Patrick and M'cbael, aged respec ively 11 and 7 I years.—Mr Scannell, the relieving officer, stated that in July 1881 the prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard ladour for neglect of family. At that time the children were sheltered in an empty house in Oxford-street, but they I were provided with neither food nor fire, and were almost naked. The children were removed to the Workhouv, hut I were again placed in the care of the father when he was released, but in September they were again in a state of destitution, the father haying left the neighbourhood, and I since then the Workhouse had bees the home of ihe unfelt- tanate bor. Their maintenance hot cost the ratepayers ; £lO4 Bs.—The prisoner, who, as a labourer, could earn from I 22s to 246 per werk, preferred to lead the idle, dissolute life of a vagabond, tramping from place to place.—The prisoner was remanded until Wednesday.—The prisoner was brought lop before Mr J C Gamble and Mr J Brock at IN'idnes I [Petty Sessions on Wednesday, and sentenced to two months' , hard labour. _ .

A. DRINK Daisy AT Wrottsts —At Widnes Petty SIUSIODS on Wednesday Jtne Thompson, wife of a man who keeps a beerhouse in Water-erreet, was summoned for u-in 4 de- famatory language to Mary Sullivan, a married won an liv- ing in the sante neighbourhood.—Mrs Sullivan stated her mother kept five lodgers and she kept two. On Saturday the sum of £2 was owing to Mrs Thompson for drink sup- plied to the !tabors during the week, and the complaisant took Mrs Thompson 18s. promising to pay the remainder oa Saturday next. Subsequently Mrs Thompson went into Mrs Sullivan's house athl benaved in such a violent fashion that it was a hard task for two lodgers to restrain her !torn c mitting an assault. The landlerd of the beerhouse then ap- peared on the scene and blows were exchanged. It was al- leged that Mrs Thompson called the complainant, rogue, rubber, and other epitheta—A cross-summons was then betrd against Mrs Sullivan, and Mr J W Knowles, who re- presented Mrs Thompson, proved by witnesses that Mrs Sul- livan had had some liquor, and that the two lodgers were tt tipsy," and that Mrs Sullivan made use of most disgrace- ful language. AS Mrs Sullivan's name had occurred fre- quently on the police hooks, she was bound over to keep the peace, herself in £lO, and one surety in LS. The ease against Mrs Thompson was dismissed.

LIBERAL ORGANISATION AT WIDNES.

A mee-ing of Widnes Liberals was held in Lacey-streee I schoolroom on Tuesday evening under the presidency of Mr E K Muspratt. There was a good attendance, amongst those present being Captain Brunner, Captain Wareing. Messers E Carey. J Morrison, F 11 Pankhurst, S Owen. S B Stringer, J L Muspratt, J H Lewis, 1) Wright, J Mid. wood, J Taylor, F Reyes, J E Johnson, S Robinson, R Webster, W W Gossige, R Fogg, T Sadler, 8 Sadler, &c. The Chairman, who received a cordial greeting, referred to the extension of the franchise and the scheme of redis- tribution now before Parliament. He was glad to see that , this scheme was formulated to a great extent upon the prin- ciple of electoral districts, which had for so long a time been one of the aims of the Radical patty of this country. (Ap- plause.) In dividing South-West Lancashire into electoral districts one of them had been formed with Widnes as its centre and to which Widnes gave its name. (Applause.) He had no doubt that the boundaries as fixed by the Com- missioners would be accepted by Parliament.—(bear, hear) —and as the general election would most likely take place .in the autumn of this year, it wan desirable not to lose any time in formiug an organisation of the Liberals of the divi- edm. A meeting of Liberal representatives had met in Liverpool for the purpose of formulating an organisation, and it was decided that it Wet desirable 0 make that '.rant- action as democratic and tepresentative as possible, I ! (Hear, hear.) For their guidance they took the ! organisation which was firet adopted in Diming-1 barn, known as the caucus, and which was the great bugbear of the lory party. (Hear, hear.) He trusted the scheme of organisation that would be presented to them would be adopted in its entirety. Part of the or- ganisation was a general. council of 418 members, which would have to perform the important function of selectina a candidate; and therefore they would see how necessary it ' was that that council should be as large and representative as possible, because they desired to tuvo a candidate, who would unite all the Liberals of the Division. (Hear, bear. and applause.) There would be an Executive Council of 52 members selected from the General Council for the pur- pose of carrying on the business of the Association: lithe Liberals were to succeed at the coming election, they must take In hand the registration of the new voters, and he could assure them there would be considerable difficulty in seeing that the registration was properly carried out. He had no particalar r,sp:ct for that part of the Reform Bill relating to what was calla' the "service franchise." Unless care- fully guarded against this would give great power to gen- tlemen who lad many men servants to give them, the right t) the franchise. Undoubtedly it extended the franchise in one sense, but from his point of view it would have been far" better to have manhood suffrage at once. It was necessary for that reason that the franchise should not be given to wrong people, and that an end was, put to faggot voting. (Hear, bear, and applause.) He congratulated the workiog=men of Widnes upon the fact that they.would now have an opportunity of voting for a member of Parlia- ment—(applauee)—who should represent then); and be hoped they would be largely represented on the General Council: They did not want the association to be cons-

. _ Prised of masters, employerr, or "bosses," as they were Bometimes called, but a real association of the Liberals of the district, working together for a common end—that was, beneficial legislation for tke country. (Applause.) Mr 11 B Shores then read the proposed scheme, and it was unanimously adopted on the motion of Mr E Carey, seconded by Mr F Heyea. 208 members of the General Council were then elected, and a ballot took for members of the Executive Council. The result was that the following gentlemen were appointed on the executive :—Messrs H Brunner, E Carey, T Crosier, it Fogg. Frank Gaskell. F H Gossage, W W Gossage, Francis Meyer' 8 Kidd, J H Lewis, F Lowing); J Midwood. J Morrisen,.E K Muspratt, S K Muspratt, Dr O'Keeffe, 8 Owens, S Sadler, T Sadler, Piers Tal lon. John Taylor, Harry Tirnmis, J W Wareing, H Web. ster, and 1) Wright ; for Ditton, Mr W Clarke; for Cron- ton, Mr T Snipe.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held at Alforde Chambers, on Tuesday, Mr F HGessage presiding. Present —Dr o.Keeffe, Messrs S Sadler, E Manley, Li Gaskell, D Wright, E Carey, F if Pankhuret, J Midwood, J Hough- ton, B Dutton, J T Allen (clerk), J Carr (engineer), and Higginison (surveyor). SUOORSTED EXTENSIVE PORCHISE OF LAND. A dis- cussion took place upon the advisability of pa chasing 1,148 square yards of land, situate in the locality of Peel- house-lane, Albert--oad, and Mill-lane (belonging to the trustees of the late J Pearson), for the purpose of public improvement.—Mr Midwool moved, and Mr S Sadler seconded that the land be purchased at a price not exceeding 4s per yard. —Mr Dutton moved, and Mr Houghton moved a direct negative, which was carried by 5 votes to 4. PROPOSED INCORPORATION.— The Chairman aaid the next business was the sonsideration of the incorporation of the town. He did not see any advantage that the town would derive by incorporation, and he did not think this was a good time to take such a momentous step considering that this was the last meeting of that Board.—Mr Webster said incorporation was often aimed at by Local Boiirde, but he could not say whether they would be better or worse. He had no objection to incorporation himself.—The Chairman said it had been stated that one of the benefits of incorpora- tion would be that a town council could borrow money cheaper, but that had been disproved. Another objection was that they very seldom got incorporation without intro- ducing politics Into local administration matters which was hardly pessible while they remained a LORA! Board, the members being selected at present without party prejudice at all; and as long as everybody were perfectly free and unbiassed it would ba an advantage to the town. Then they would have to have a mayor, to whom they would have to make an allowance, bat that Amount would be by no means corameneurate to the amount he would be expected to spend. lie moved that the censideration of the in Mee be postponed until the meeting of the new Board.—Dr O'Keeffe seconded the motion, which was carried unanim- ously. THE EtvcrioN.—The Chairman read the offieal return of the election. Lie said the number of voting papers de- livered by the constables in 1884 was 4.188, and in 1885, 4,345. In 1884 the number of papers filled tip in the pre- sence of the returning officer was 339, and in 1885, 26. The total number of papers Issued in 1884 was 4,527, and in 1885, 4,371. There were ago many more bad papers this year than lest ; for what reason he could not make out.—(Dr. O'Keeffe : The absence of bribery, sir )—The amount of expense incurred was £74 6a 63, and he asked that a cheque should be signed for that sum.—The cheque was paesed on the motion of Mr D Wright, seconded by Mr F U Penichurat.

_ STREET MAKING, &C. The Highway Committee recommended that the following streets be made under the previsions of the Public Health Act, 1875, and that the surveyor he instructed to prepare plans and estimates for the same :—Witt-road, Tic- toria-street (Newtown), Farrant (late John) street, and New. street (Simms Crone.) It was recommended that the charge for hire of the steam roller be 30a per day and the cost of fuel. At a later meeting the committee recommen- ded that the unadopted portion of Wellington-street and Irwell-street be made under the provisions of the Public Health Act, and reported that 812 square yards of land bad been conveyed from Mr J Dutton for the widening of Lugs- ' dale-road.—A vote of thanks was passed to Mr Midwood for his services as chairman.—Mr Midwood moved, and Mr Dutton seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr Hough- ton said the streets recommended to be made led to nowhere, and be was of opinion this was not the time to do the work.—Mr Webefer asked what the committee had done with regard to the better lighting of Widnes-read.—Mr Wright wished to know why Oaklaad-street was not men- tioned in the list of streets to be made. If there was a street wanted making more than another it was Oakland- street—Dr O'Keeffe observed that the streets in the list were those where most of the Eases of infectious uiseese originated, and he completely agreed with the recommends- tion.—Mr Webster said John-street was in good order.—Mr Dutton said he WM inlividually in favour of Oakland- street being m.de. He hoped Mr Wright did not insinuate that there was any inflaence brought to bear upon the committee to prevent that street being made.—Mr Wright : OA no, no.—Mr Midwood, in reply to the various questions, sa'd he had had that Boardroom packed with owners, who had agreed that they would do anything that the commit- tee wished then to do as Vroporary repairs to defer the expense of making the streets for the present, but he was sorry to sty that promises was all the committee had re- ceived yet. The Health Committee and the Medical Officer of Heath had reported these streets to be in a very instni- tary condition, and the Highway Committee had been com- pelled to make Ulla recommendation. With reference to the lighting of Widnes-road, a lamp had been placed opposite St Paul's Church, and the committee were of opinion that the road was as well lighted as any other part of the town. The reason Daklen I-street was not recommended to be made was that the cammitt-,e had never been called upon to do no. —Mr Midwood mentioned that dating the past veer the Highway Committee had exceeded the estimate by £258 lOs 6d, in consequence of the heavy work they had had to do.—The minutes were then adopted. THE BLOCKING OF Misr BANK-STIFEI.— The Clerk ; reed a letter dated let April, hem Messrs Bolton and Sop, ' with reference to the closing of a portion of West Bank- street. They argued that the alteration would be of value to the firm, would not de any injure to any individual rate- payer nor to the ratepayers generally, and would be a con- siderable advantage to the pockets of the rreepayers gener- ally, and the property owners in the neighbourhood. Any I extension of their works was impossible if this portion of the street could not he enclosed, and their oaly alterna- tive would be to place the mechanical portion of their works: I elsewhere, end certainly not in Widnes. The letter stated that at the meeting of property owners upon the question, they all consented to the closing of the street ; and it was admitted on all heads that the street could not now be of Ins. for traffic, ae it merely leads into that end of Hutchin- son-street, which could never be anything but a cut de sac, and its maintenance would merely be a melees expense to the tawn. Farther, Major Cross, on behalf of Hutchinaon Trustees, agreed to improve the approach to Hulcbinson• street by Peel-street, and thus the communication would be nearer to any part of the town than through the portion of West Bank-street which they wished to close. It was con- tended that the schools wedd not be in any way affected by the actual closing of the street, and the misunderstanding between the school trustees and those of Hutchineon'seetete did not appear to be a reason for the Board to refuse their applicatien, unless on the ground that they con• eider it a sufficient reason to make it their diity to bitsle• , the development of the works to the detriment ef the I, ratepayers generally and of the firm, who had taken the ground simply for the purpose of works. With the street Iclosed employment would probably be shortly found for an additional 150 workmen of a superior class, which meant the occupation of at least 103 houses, which, while in- creasing the value of the house property in the neighbour- hood. would prove a material assistance to the ratepayers in various ways, which it must be unnecessary for them to Ipoint out; while if the street was to be open not only was the above benefit lost to the ratepayers, but they also lost what benefit they may derive from their present mill, which they should be compelled to remove, leaving enly fur- naces, which were the Nest Important of their present works, and employed a lower class of men.—Mr Midwood said the Highway Committee, considering the opposition to M-ssrs Bolton's wish, thought it advisable to formulate some scheme veletreby they could substitute another inlet and outlet to West Bank-street if this street were stopped up. The committee made a recemmendation, but the firm would hear of ncehing that would bring expense about. They simply wished to close up the street. The commit- tee could do nothing mo:e than they had done. There was a great deal of opposition to Messrs Bolton's wish that the firm knew nothing of. He (Mr Midwood) looked upon the Board as the custodian of the rights of the township, and if they failed to protect those rights, the ratepayers would have their remedy and conk' go to quarter sessions in oppo- oition to the Board or MiIRIBII Bolton, Tax Tlosinget..—Mr Sadler, iti moving the adop'ion of the Hospital Committee's minutes, said he was glad to say the patients in the hospital during the past year had not been very numerous, which he thought was cause for Con- gratulation. Although there hid been considerable repairs done to the buildhig during the year, the committee had kept £33 within their estimate.—Mr Houghton seconded the motion, and the ml utes were passed. SEWERAGE COMIIITTEE.—The' Sewerage Committee had given instructions that the attention of Mr J Evans should be called to (he silting up of the sewer outlet, also to leak- age under the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany's archer, and is ask for prompt attention. The Lan- don and North-Western Railway Company's account for expenses incurred through the sewer (No. 1 contract) pass- ing under their lines. Instructions given to employ Mr Copland to examine account and prepare contra account.— Mr Carey, in reply to Mr Sadler, said it was intended to em- ploy Mr Copland because he was the engineer in charge at tho time, and they thought they would get a more setis• factory result if Mr Copland checked the bill. The ventil- ating shaft in Witt-road was creating a nuisance, and if it could not be remedied the shsft would have to be removed. mini:Vas were adopted. HEALTH COMMITTRE.—The minutes of the Health Com- mittee contained the medical officer's report for March, which elated that during lidarch there were 95 births and 36 deaths, beiog respectively 44 22 and 160 p=r thouund. Zymotld diszases caused two deaths. A vote of thinks was accorded to Dr O'Kei ffa for his services as chairman of the committee.—The minuted were approved, on the proposition of Dr °lied% seconded by Mr Carey. Tan FINANCES 07 THE BOARD.—Tbe Finance Committee pubmitted the following estimates for the six months end- ing the 30th.S.:ptember next :—lrghway, £21201 1.5. s

health, £479 51 ; finence, £2,271 7e; and a credit from the market of £l9 14s 6d, making a total estimated expenditure of £3,057 2561. The committee recammeuded that a rate of Is in the / be laid, e.tirnated to predict £4,620.-I,jr Gaskell moved 4he adoption of the micutes. He remarked that the rate recommended would not cover the expenditure,. but there was a balance in hand of £453. The estimate of the Highway Committee for the half year showed that for the year it would be £636 more than lest year. This increase was equal in itself to an increase of 24.1 in the £, and un- fortunately it was an increase that Mr Midwood said would he permanent, in consequence of work the Board had sanc- tioned and which wart in hand. The Board would also have to provide for the Public Offices and Infectious Diseases Hospital, the interest and principal to be re-paid upon the loans of these being equal to a rate of lid in the X. It seemed to him that the Board WB9 commitred to a rate of 61.1 in the X for the year.—Mr Wright seconded the mo- tion, which was carried —A formal resoltion sanctioning tic laying of the rate was also passed. Tree PCBLIC OFFICFS.—Tbe General Purposes Committee repotted that a letter had been received from the Local Go- vernment Board stating that it would be necessary to hold a paiblic inquiry before determining the number of years for which the loan would be sanctioned for the ertction of pub- lic cfsces.—lt was recommended that the tender of Mr Both- well, £.5,905,.be accepted subject to his entering into the ne- cessary contract, and the sanction of the Local Government Board being obtained, and that application he made to the Local Government Board to sanction borrowing powers not exceeding £lo,ooo.—The minutes were adopted on the mo- tley' of Ir Carey. seconded by Mr Sadler. Mr Putten, in accordance with notice be had given, . meved that the following resolution passed at the last meet- , lee ef the Beard be rescinded :—"That in consequence of the exist iug preva'cece of measles in Runcorn—tbere being ~but 390 children absent from school and the disease still epreadine—the clerk be Instructed to write to such manu- facturers in Widnes as employ man living in Runcorn to request them either to compel tbobe employee to live in Widee or to cease employing them, in order not to endan- ger the health of the township of Widnes.' He remarked that the Ile erd had no right and no power to enforce such a request.—Mr Houghton seconded the motion —Dr O'Keeffe contended that the notices sent to the members raised a false issue, but the Chairman ruled that tlev were gaits sufficient.—Dr O'Keefe said when he mated that resolu- tion he was simply tilting about infectious disease. There was nobody that would be less inclined to interfere between manufacturers and the men they employed than himself, and his motion was taken with that view, as far as he could, of preserving the public health .of Widnes.—The Chairmen considered the Dr. lead explained very openly and properly that his intention was not to coerce anybody, but as the resolutioa conveyed the idea of coercion, perhaps the best thing would be to rescind it.—Mr Dutton made comie4nentery reference to the zeal and care and watch- falnees exercised over the sanitary condition of the town by Dr O'Ke fie as chairman of the Health Committee. In moving the reseindicg, of the resolution he had no wish to reflect upon Dr O'Keeffe.—Dr O'Keefe said he was ex- ceedingly sorry that the words of the resolption were in any way obnoxious and disigreeable, or if it were thought that the manufacturers had not been paid that deference to which they were entitled. They had had gentlemen living in the county of Cheshire who had been speaking about IVidnes Local Board and treating Widnes itself with abso- lute contempt. He cared very little indeed akent what they said regarding himself. He could hurl their c)ntempt back upon them with scorn. Pshaw I By the holy devil, sir ! (Sensation.) After a pause the docter went on to say that he wished the town to he protected from an invasion of measles, smallpox, or any other infectious disease, and reasoned that if the Local Government Board took so much care about swine fever and other diseases of cattle, sorely the lives of human beings were not less precious, and the Local Board ought to do its duty and take every means in their power to prevent disease from being spread amongst the inhabitants of Widnes.—Mr Wright said he seconded the resolution at the last Board meeting fer the sake of raising a discussion. He aleo voted for it with the idea of preserving the health of the people. He had no wish to coerce the manufacturers became such a course was totally against his principles, and in the second place, he knew that the Board had no, power to do it.—Dr O'Keefe Bow moved as an amendment, that the resaution after the words still spreading should be—" and the Board take such steps as may be necessary to prevent- the importation of disease into Widnes." He observed that the mortality in Runcorn last month was 39 per 1,000, and in Widnes only 17 per 1,000, whilst in _the month previous the death rate
„ was only 12. He therefore said they had one of the health- iest towns in the klngdorn.. They had in_lttincern those
beautiful esuitarians! -Glory bs to .God !—Tile ainer;cfm—e—n—t
was then carried. THANES TO THE cHAIRMAN.—Mr Midwoecl said it affor- ded him very great pleasure to move that the but thanks of the Board be accorded to the chairman. He had had tweve

years experience upon public Boards, and ria-th-alti;--e he had sat under four chairmen, but he was gratified to state that he had greeter pleasure in sitting under Mr Gossage than any of them. He had always been kind, courteous, and consider- ate, end had conduated the operations of the Board in a business-like manner. (Hear, hear.)—Mr Webster, as one of the retiring members, seconded tha reaolution.—Tho motion was carried by acclamation, and the Chairman ac- knowledged the compliment__

THE ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.—Mr Forster moved that Mr F H Gossage be re•elected chairman for the ensuing year. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATIIRDAT.—There was 120 business. ,Monnay—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Mr John Fairclough, and Mr John Greening. Distrnitmenss.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—William Connor. at Market-gate on Satur- day, discharged; Mary Towey, in Buckley-street on Sunday morning, fined 101 and costa; Thomas Flynn, in Cloth Hall- yard on Monday morning, fined 103 and costs ; Margaret Woods, in Winwick-street on the 7th last, dismissed on payment of costs; John Finn, in Union-street, fined Sc in- cluding costs ' • John Harrop, in Rolleston-street, fined 51 and costs ; Thomas Miskell, in Bridge-street (33rd appear- ance). fined 10a and costs; Mary Fearns, in Old-road, Latchford, fined 5s and costs. MISCELLANEOLS.—Patrick Connolly, charged with fight- ing in Wilderspool lord on the Bth mat, was discharged on payment of costa.—John Broadhurst was fined 103 and costs for furiously driving a horse and trap in Irlam-street, on the 4th inst.--Edwarel Smith, a young man, was charged with playing at " peggy " in Napier-street ; he was dismissed. WIFE BEATING.—FmiIy Wells charged her husband, Geo Wells, with assaulting her on the 7th inst. She said that her husband kicked her violently and at Christmas knocked fhree of her teeth cut. He was bound over to keep the peace or six months. UNREGISTERED LODGING-HOLISM—WiII lam Heaton was charged with lipping lodgers without having his house— No. 2, Mottram's-yard— registered. The house is adapted for three persons and seven persons were found there by Mr Norman, sanitary inspector. It was in a dirty state. De- fendant, who had been previously convicted of a like offence, was fined 20s and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment in default.

TUESDAY—Before Messrs John Greening and E .1 Guest. DEUNEENNESS.—Matthew Williams was fined 5a and costs for being drunk in Winwick-street on the previous evening. REFUSING TO WM/IL—Thomas Smith was charged with refusing to perform his task ot work whilat a casual inmate of the vagrant ward of the Union, and with damaging his cell to the amount of ea.—Prisoner said that he wished to be sent to prison. He had been three months in this country. having come from Ireland, and could not get work. He wished to go to prison to earn as much money as would take him back. (Liughter.)—Chief Constable Hunt : How long will it take you 2—Prisoner : I should like to get twelve months. Laughter.)—He was sent to prison for seven days.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandiey and Mr. John Pairclough. WIFH A ssarr..T.—Samuel Smith, an elderley man, was sent to prison for two months, and ordered to afterwards find sureties to be of good behaviour, for assaulting his wife, Margaret, who complained that he constantly ill-used her when he was drunk. FRAUDULENT EmAsTunrr.—Patrick Marr, alias Thomas Murphy, was charged with fraudulently enlisting in the 3rd Battalion Liverpool Regiment, while belonging to the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. Prisoner had been up for thining at Warrington and drew his bounty. Be enlisted again in the first-named regiment at Liverpool, and was sent to Warrington, where he was recognised as belonging to the S .utit Lancashire Regiment. He was sent to prison for three months. BECKIING.—George Gerard, described on the charge sheet as a" drone," was sent to prison for a month for begging in White-street on the previous day. THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. DRUNIENNESS.—EIiza Smith was charged with being drunk and indecent in Brown-street on the previous even- ' ing. It was her 19th appearance, and she Was committed to prison fora month. Patnay.—Before Major Litton and Mr John White. SCHOOL ATTENDANCH.—John Fleming was charged on a warrant with neglecting to send his child to school, and was fined Ss including costs. Mr George Riley, school attend- ance officer, proved the case.
