A PILOT KILLED.—TWO pilots were rowing round the breakwater m Troon, N.B , when a large German steamer, the Armin, which WAIS hzarivg down on the wall, having allowed herself too little room on entering the harbour, dropped her anchor, with the view of preventing a collision. The anchor fell on the pilot's boat, smashing it to pieces, and killing one of the occupant..

NORTHWICII PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION. SELECTION OF A LIBERAL CANDIDATE. An adjourned meeting of the General Council of the Liberal Association for the Northwich Parliamentary Divi- sion was held at the Drill Hall, Nertlawieh, on Saturday afternoon. There were over 300 present, and great interest was manifested in the proceedings, from the fact that the I principal business was the selection of a candidate to con- test the division in the Liberal interest at the nest election. —On the motion of Mr James Handley,Runcorn, seconded _ _

---- - by Mr T Norman, of Runcorn, Mr E 11 Moss, of Ravens- croft Mall, Middlewich, was unanimously elected chairman. —The minates of the previous meeting were read by Mr 0 Leak, of Ruacorn, and passed.—The meeting then elected 30 vice-presidents on recommendations of the Execu- tive ; co optated 28 members of the Council from lists prepared by toed delegates ; and filled up the vacancies in the Couneil caused by the elec- tion of 30 vice-presidents.— The Chairman said the next business was to receive the candidates, Mr R Verdin and Mr

J T Brunner. Mr Brunner, after some introductory observations said : To my mind no man ought to accept such a position as frankly I am seeking at your ,hands to-day —no man ought to accept that responsibility unless he is determined, as I are ready to tell you that I are determined, to devote the best that is in me to your service. (Cheers.) It shall be my aim as far as it is possible fcr my exertions to bring it about that Englishmen shall have a fuller and higher freedom, and the nation shall live a more righteous and more moral life. (Hear, hear.) Well, novr, I have spoken on a recent occasion about what rconsider is to be the key-note of our Liberal policy of the future, and I stated that that key-note had bean struck by a man who has risen by his efforts and his own abilities in a career like that of a comet to one of the highest positions in the land—l mean Mr Joseph Chamberlain. (Cheers.) He has told us that we ought to take this as our motto," That all men born in this land have a free birth-right "—(hear, hear) —and I would say a word or two about what I consider that birth-right is. Ills not an equal division amongst us of this world's goods. That I consider a chimerical object —an object wh,ch it is not possible or even desirable to attain—but that birth-right is this, that each child that is born in this country shall have the opportunity of attain- ing the best that is possible to attain with the intellect and abilities that are granted to it by God. (Cheers.) Gentle- men, that involves free schools, and I shall strive to attain that the schools throughout the length and breadth of this land for the poor, middle class, and the rich alike shall be free. As to foreign policy, we have been considering the foreign policy of England, to my mind, ad *aaseum Now my aim in this .-ection of tbeliational life that concerns our relations to foreign nations would be this—that I would to the utmost promote freedom of intercourse and freedom of trade. Our idea as Liberals, the idea which was given to us by Richard Cobden—(cheers)—is this, that the free in- terchange of goods between nation and nation tenrls to pro- mote a free interchange of friendly feeling and of thought. Now that freedom of trade I shall fight for, in your interest and in the interest of your fellow-countrymen, as long as I remain a politician, and that I trust will be as long as I draw breath. Gentlemen, "Peace hate her victories no less renowned than war." (Cheers ) Now, gentlemen, with re- gard to the colonies. It would be my wish that the colonies should be bound to us in bonds as strong as iron-(hear, hear) —but those bonds shall be. if you please, bonds of love. To my mind such cruel deeds as are daily done in South Africa are not for the benefit of the colonies, are not for the benefit of humanity, are not for the benefit of Christendom. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, it has hitherto very often been con- sidered a delicate matter for a candidate to express his opinions with regard to our relations to the Green Isle. Now, all my life I have bad very good Irish friends, and I trust that I shall find many an Irish friend as I go through the world hereafter. I am not now prepared to support the party of ebstruction in the House of Commons as you will readily suppose. (Hear, hear.) I fact, in parenthesis I might say that I shall fight that obstruction as I would fight a pig-headed man who opposed me in a busineas mat- ter at home. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) But I would— and I trust that I shall be able to help—l would grant to Ireland a very full measure of home rule—(hear, hear)— and I am not afraid to say that to you chosen Liberals, nor shall Ibe afraid to say it to any audience of men threugh- oat this constituency. I believe, gentlemen, that the future electors will view this matter amongst others from a very much higher standpoint than the electors of the past. I believe from the bottom of my heart that the two millions will add to the electorate of this kingdom an element of righteousness, an element of fair play, which will do this nation an enormous amount of good. (Cheers) Now, the land of this country of ours has not, hitherto, been considered by the law-makers in any sense as an instru- ment for the public good, but it has been maintained almost solely for the benefit of the few and for the maintenance in dignified positions of wealthy families. The result of that Is that land is held in enormous masses by comparatively few individuals. For instance, you find the Duke and Duchess of Sutherland—for the Duchess is a very large landed proprietress in her own right—holding between them from two to three millions of acres of land. Gentlemen, to my mind that is a crying shame. (Hear. hear.) Do you know why that has been broaght about? Three generations ago there were far up in Scotland a number of industrious thrifty families living upon land which their fathers and grandfathers had tilled, and who looked forward to spending their days there and to see their children grow up around them as they had grown up, but these people have been cleared off as you might talk of clearing off some scrubby underwood. It is a very distinct loss to the country that those hardy, honest, God-fearing folk should be replaced by wild animals which serve only for selfish pleasure. (Hear, hear.) That is one phase. But there is another of which I spoke two or three days ago, which to my mind is very much more important and exceedingly sad in its results. There are now in many parts of London 1 houses which are rapidly decaying. These houses did not ; keep out the weather and they don't keep out the sewer gases; and the result is a great deal of sickness, very short wages, and very short lives for the people-who live there. Now, bow does this come about? Mr. Henry Broadhurst —(cheers)—let me say, has taken a great interest in this matter. Mr. Broadhurst is a gentleman whose accoaintance I have had the pleasure to enjoy furs good many years past, and with him I hope to work. (Cheers.) Now, this shocking state of affairs is due se the fact that the houses have been built upon short leases, and that at the end of these short leases, by the provisions of the leases themselves, the houses go back to the man who let the land for the purpose of building them upon. This system 11 of short leases obtains in England and in Ireland almost I alone throughout the whole of this globe, and I say that you and I, go Alemen, owe nothing to the men who have maintained that law—we owe nothing to the House of Lords which maintains this law—(cheers)—and being a hater of all class monopolies I declare to you that I shall consider it—and I shall consider it whether you elect me or not—to fight until I get that law amended with alt the energy of which I am possessed. (Cheers) Well, gentlemen, I am a Nonconformist. (Cheers) Being a Nonconformist, I consider I come be- fore you with clean hands, and I have never claimed for myself an unjust privilege. Now, an unjust privilege does not go well with Christianity. I have been taught all my life to look at thie matter from this stasdpoint, that what- ever change we make it shall be a change which shall tend towards the benefit of the Christian religion, and I have to tell you frankly that if I see that the advocacy of religions equality in this year 1885 will breed an amount of bitter- ness, which will show me Mat I cannot attain that good without going through some evil, I mean to hold my hand; but I promise you this, that wherever I am I shall try and persuade my fellow countrymen that this oountry will be far more Christian when the Church is disestablished than it is to-day. (Loud obeers.) Now I shall fight for equality before law for every man, and I will ably@ is order to carry out that view to have the Employers' Liability Act amended so that no wealthy employer or any great corporation or railway company shall be in the position to compel a man who works for him or for it to contract himself out of that Act. (Hear, near.) I further am opposed entirely to the right which is claimed by the son of a peer to make the laws for us. (Cheers.) I would have no man making laws who was not an elected re- presentative by somebody or other. Gentlemen, lam a rich man, and it is possible that because I are a rich man I alti in this position; in fact, I could not be here with nine chil- dren. (Loud laughter.) However, I have done more for , the country in that line than my friend Mr Verdin. (Ap- , plause and great laughter.) Well, I don't consider it an advantage, but a disadvantage, for you know it is an ex- tremely difficult thing, indeed almost an impossible thing, for a poor man to get into the House of Commons and repre- sent you. I consider that worth, that high character and ability, should be the only requisites is a rspresentative— (hear, bear)—and I shall do my hest to smooth the way into the House of Legislature for poor men. (Hear, hear.) N 3W, I do want this: that the position of serving you in local mat- ters shall be made so dignified and honourable that the best men amongst you shall strive to attain to thet position. (Hear, hear.) I would put more responsibility, and very much greater power, into the hands of these men when you have got the right sort. It is an utter absurdity when you think how excessively ill adapted to your needs is your pre- sent system. I sit here as a member of the Sanitary Authority, and to that authority of which I sin a member a man building a house has to come for permission to connect that house with our sewer. There is another authority that sits at Cheater, 17 miles away, which has jurisdiction over the surface of the road, and the man who wants to break into the road has to apply to that authority at Chester for permission. Now is it not an ab- surdity that one authority should command the sueace of the ground and another authority should command the! ground three feet below. To these local authorities, which I will endeavour to make as good as they can possibly be made, I would delegate the whole of the local work, To these local authorities, elected with absolute freedom by all the men and women in the neighbourhood, I would depute the distribution of the number of the public-houses in the district. As I said only a few days ago, I have a passion for common sense and for common justice, and to my mind it is neither common sense nor common justice to let magis- trates manage these matters. (Cheers.) The magistrates do not use the public-houses, and they have no business to say how many there shall be. They don't suffer from pub- lic-housee, and they have no right to say how few there shall be. I have suffered myself at the hands of the jus- tices. I know how they can hunt and how they do hunt many and many a decent man and woman. (Hear, hear.) I have done. The matter now lies in your hands. I ask you
THE

to do your duty so that your consciences will be free when you have given your decision. (Hear, hear.) I ask you, gentlemen, to decide, as far as it is possible for men to de- cide, with absolute unselfishness and with a single-minded desire to do the right thing... (Cheers.) '

Mr Verdin afterwards -addressed the meeting at some length, and both candidates delivered speeches giving their views of political questions, and were severely " heckled" by the delegates. With regard to compensation for damages through the pumping of brine, Mr Brunner promised to support a bill which would deal equitably with the ques- tion. Salt already paid to lighten the eounty rates, and that was unjust. Mr Verdin declined to support a com- pensation bill, but said he would ask for a Royal Commis- sion to take evidence loyally and report to Parliament. Each pledged himself to accept the decision of the meet- ing, which ultimately decided for Mr Brunner by 36 of a majority, the numbers being—For Mr Brunner, 166; for Mr Verdin, 130. A scene followed the declaration of the re- sult. Mr Terdin accused Mr Brunner of untaimqes in pro- moting the selection of particular delegates, and the meet- ing broke up in confusion.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

" Cassell's Magazine " for April is in no wise lacking There is an interesting summary of Sergeant Ballantine's experiences in the United States; the Family Doctor con- tributes an excellent paper on "Reform in Diet and Cookery," and there is a chatty article with the title of "On the Tramp." The serial stories keep their hold, and the finished stories are above the average. The prize song, "When Martins Follow Spring," is beautifully written; bat it will be found rather lengthy for vocal purposes when set to music. "The Gatherer" keeps the reader posted as to the latest useful inventions.—" The Quiver" has some- thing practical on" Sunday School Addresses" by a super- intendent. "A plan for public play grounds" is from the pen of Lord Brabazon ; it is to be hoped it will be brought before city authorities throughout the Kingdom. The shop- boy's story, " Nothing to learn," carries with it a useful lesson, and there is some good verse, and excellent illustra- tions of the various articles.—" Little Folks" has a pretty frontispiece in Daisy Bell. The child's "Story ef a ship- wreck" is capital, and it is capitally illustrated ; and the same may be said of "Knuckle Down." The number is a strong one in every respect, the new features which have been introduced being exceedingly attractive. "The Family Physician" is a new serial which is being issued by Messrs Cassell, and, judging from the first part to hand, it is likely to become very popular. It will form a complete manual of domestic medicine' and, as it is compre- hensive and practical, it will enable that stitch in time to be taken which—especially as to disease—so often saves nine. The work is being issued in a handy size, and the price of each part (61.) makes it generally accessible. The Book of -Health " has reached part 12, and there is happily no falling off in merit or interest. The valuable article on Education and the nervous system" is continued, and such important matters are dealt with as school headaches, competitive examinations, corporal punishment, and family life and parental responsibility. " Cassel's Popular Gar- dening," with its numerous highly finished illustrations, also reaches pert 12. Among the contents of the current ssue are : rock, fern, and wild gardening, decor- ative use of flowers, greenhouse plants, common gar- den flowers, ferns, and orchids. Part 15 of the Encycloreelic Dictionary carries the reader to the letter "C," and leaves him marvelling as usual at the fulness of the work and the wealth of its illustra- tion. This month's issue (part 81 of the fine art edition of the works of Longfellevr is occupied with " The Story of Hiawatha," the illustrations being alike appropriate and charming. The frontispiece is a fine engraving of a paint- ing by Mr F Dicksee, A.R A. Part 6of 'Recent battles on sea and land" is particularly interesting. It gives in gra- phic style the incidents of the Zulu war ; and amongst 1 the illustrations are portraits of Prince Napoleon, Lord Chelmsford, Colonel Redvers Buller, and Sir Evelyn I Wood. " The English Illustrated Magazine," which is just noW exceptionally strong in fiction, continues "A ship of '47 by Bret Harte, and " A family affair" -by Hugh Conway. "Interviewed by an emperor " is a capital paper by Archi- bald Forbes. " The Sirens Three," written and illustrated by W Crane, is such a wonder in its way that it is pleas- ing to know that it is to be continued. " Ward and Lock's Technical Journal" is admirably answering its aim. It is profusely illustrated, and the contents are most varied. There will be no room for sneering at "the British workman " who makes himself thoroughly familiar with this work. Wha,ever his trade, he will find that it has something to teach him. "The Grants to Royalty" (John Heywoxl), is a useful little work, and as it is published at one penny none need be without it. "The Season" and "The Moniteur de la Mods " for April

are brilliant with coloured plates of the fashions for spring. There are besides, valuable patterns, and quite a crowd of illustrations. We have also to band those other popular ladies' papers—" Myra's Journal" and " rdyra's Three- penny Journal."

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

CONOREOATIONAL SCHOOL —A public lecture was deliv• eked in the Congregational School before a large audience, on Monday night, by the Rev J T Camm, resident pastor. The subject was "The Catacombs of Rome; or the early Christian Churches unveiled." The chair was occupied by Mr Williarason. The lecture was rendered additionally in- structive by the use of a number of diagrams. The cus- tomary votes of thanks were passed to the lecturer and chairman. By special request, the lecture was repeated on Wednesday night, when there was again a good audi- ence.

TUB Corrox TRADE.—Consjderable uneasiness has ex- isted in the minds of the Golborne people since Messrs S Breeds and Company posted the notice respecting the pro- bable closing of their new mills. The firm has for many years employed about 500 workpeople in this one mill alone, and the prospect of such a large concern corning to a standstill even for a short time only, is a serious matt9r, both to the Golborne people generally and those living in the ad- joining townships of Lowton and Ashton-in-Makerfield. After the fortnight's notice expired, portions of the mill were allowed to stand and accordingly hands began to drop out et work. This has gone on for several weeks, looms be- ing stopped as the cotton was worked through, until now a considerable number of hands have had to look for employ- ment elsewhere. The old mill and weaving sheds belonging to the same firm are running as usual.

CAUTION TO COLLIERS.—Before Colonel George McCor- quodale, Messrs R Houghton, T J Gillespie, C Pilkington, an W F Gooch, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Satur- day, James Morris, a booker-on at the Golborne Colliery, was summoned by Messrs Richard Evans and Co., for a breach of the Coal Mines' Regulation Act, and also a con- travention of one of the special ruled in force at that cal- liery.—Mr J 0 Swift, of St Helens, who appeared for Messrs Evans, stated that the defendant was a respectable young man, and the firm did not wish to punish him un- duly. Rule 42 stated that no workman should be at the bottom of the pit shaft while the cage was in motion. The cage could descend from the top to the bottom of the shaft in 18 seconds, and therefore it was extremely dangerous for any person to pass under. The defendant was a hooker-on, and on the 25th ult the defendant passed across the bottom of the shaft while the cage was in motion.—The Bench re- marked that the complainants bad no wish to be severe on the defendant, who would be fined Sc and costs. They hoped, however, it would serve as a warning to the defend- ant and others,

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. lII.PORTA.Nr DECISION.

The Select Committee of the House of Lords on the Manchester Ship Canal at on Wednesday, under the presi- dency of Earl Cowper. There was a large attendance of the public, because of the anticipated decision of the Coin- mittes on the engineering evidence. I Mr. Sarnipaiss, on behtlf of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, said he represented an interest whose traffic amounted to a million and a half tons per annum, and he desired to impress on their lordships abs importance either of preserving unimpaired the approach to the lower estuary or of providing an equivalent channel, which should ba permanently main,ained for the purpose of securing access to the inland navigation of the conntry down to Liver- pool. Mr. Pt mann submitted, in reply, that the interests of the Bridgewater Navigation Company were sufficiently safe- guarded in the Bill. Passing to the opposition of the Mer- sey Dock Board, he said that from what he had heard during the inquiry he was perfectly convinced that had his clients taken a tracing of Mr. Lyster's plan, without varying a hair's•breadth in ally particular, they would have been op- posed with precisely the same hostility as they cow were. A revolution in transit was in question, and it was this fear which agitated the cotton brokers of Liverpool and the Lon- don and North-western Railway Company. He asked would Manchester have no intereat in the bar after spending £8,000,000 or £te,ooo,ooo on this scheme ? The fact was Liverpool was now rich and apathetic; the authoritits thoaght they could grub along, and would do nothing to mend the bar. Give the promoters their Bill and there would soon be no bar to maunder over. After all the bar was a mere ridge, and not nearly in so bad a condition as the opponents, to suit their own purpose!, painted It. As regarded Gyp question of the abstraction of tidal capacity caused by the works, he pointod out that the opponents had declined to submit their figures to vecificatien, and be must refuse to accept them. Mr Leader Williams's estimate of the abstraction ranged from nearly 6,000,000 cubic yards to over 2,000,000, accuding to the tide. That abstraction. the learned counsel maintained, occurred at a time when for the purposes of the bar the tidal flow was least operative. and was brought down to a minimum when the flow was most valuable. The learned counsel commented on the fact that Mr Stevenson, the chief engineer of the London and North-Western Railway Company, had not this year been called, and slid his evidence entitled him to assume that Mr Stevenson could not honestly onpose the scheme. Ile referred also with confidence to the fact that Mr Vernon Harcourt, who last year gave evidence against the bill, was in favour of the scheme now proposed. As to the theory that the works of the promoters would fix the channel on the Cheshire side, he said, unless the opponents could show that the promoters intended to curve, corry, crib, and confine the fresh water as they intended to do last I year, and to prevent its operation, their COO of a fixity of 1 channel distppeared. The canal would begin half a mile above Eastharn Ferry, and the promoters proposed to cut a trench, trumpet shaped, 600 feet wide at the mouth and narrowing to 300 feet in the tube. In this they were not doing anything to attract the flood to the Cheshire side. The truth was the opponents feared not a revolution in the regime of the river, but a revolution in the transit charges Mr Pember offered, en the part of the promoters, to post• pone the operation of the 31st clause relating to dredging until the canal was made, and to distinguish all operations that might be condncted under the clause. . _

At the close of 51r Pember's speech the room was cleared. On the public being re.admitted, the Chairman announced that the Co:nmittee would proceed with the Bill, but suz- rested that the opponents should begin the commercial evidence.
On Thursday the Select Committee of the house of Lords presided over by Earle Cowper eat to heat; eyidenoe

in support of the commercial case of the promoters of the scheme. The first witness was Mr Daniel Adamson, chair- man of the Provisional Committee, who explained in detail the various advantages whit h would accrue from the con- struction of the canal. He stated that within a district measured by a radios of 45 mile. there was a population ef 7,400,000 persons who would, directly or indirectly, receive benefits from the cheapening of rates and the improved facilities for the transit of goods. Mr Adamson said theV had already spent £130.000 in trying to get the bill, and he had no doubt whatever that the necessary capital would be raised. He estimated the saving La carriage on goods enter- ing and leaving the district at 50 per cent, which was of enormous importance in view of the State of trade at present. The cross-examination of Mr Adamson by counsel represen- ting opponents was of a formal character. Mr Marshall Stevens, shipowner and agent, also gave evidence in support of the Bill.

div.head: MEETING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MEETING AT RUNCORN.

At Bank Chambers, Runcorn, on Miend—a.y, a meeting of the merchants and traders of the port was held to consider the Mancheeter Ship Canal Bill. Mr G L Davies, J.P., presided. Ile remarked that he thought the port and trade of Roncorn should have the same facilities as those that at present exist, and that the Commissioners should use every means in their power to get the clauses inserted in the Bill for the protection of the town and trade. The following resoultions were passed unanimously :—" We, the traders of Runcorn, having considered the plans of the Manchester Ship Canal as they affect this port, are of opinion that the construction of a wall in front of the docks for the purposes of the canal will create a serious interference with the trade passing to arid from the estuary, and will prevent its being eonducted with the same facility as we at present possess with the freedom of the estuary." **Toe imposition of dues upon ship and cargo, as proposed by the Bill of the promo- ters upon traffic corning to this port and passing along the said Ship Canal, will be such an additional tax upon the co:anterce of the port as to force it into other channels and destroy competition with the ports in the district, and this meeting therefore urges upon the Improvement Commis- sioners of Runcorn the importance of obtaining clauses for the free use of the canal for craft that can now pass between the port and Liverpool, and the non-imposition of any charges upon traffic arriving at or departing from the port or the town, and it pledges itself to render the Commission- ers all possible help to obtain those ends." Mr Beckett, who acted as secretary, was instructed to forward a copy of the resolutions to the Board of Commissioners. •

div.head: EARLES'TOWN.
div.p: EARLES'TOWN.

CROW-LANE BAND OF Horn.—On Wednesday evening over 50 members and friends of the adult and juvenile sec- tions of the Earlestown Good Templars gave an entertain- ment in the Crow-lane Congregational Sunday School under the auspices of the Crow-lane Band of Hope. There was a good attendance, and Mr E Newman presided. Following the Chairman's address an excellent programme was gone through. At the close, 01 the motion of Mr Jones, seconded by Mr Blake, and supported by Mr E Mort, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to the entertainers. NEWTON CRICKET AND BOWLING Cum.—The season in connection with the Newton Cricket and BowliLig Club was opened on Saturday afternoon. It was intended to play the opening game at cricket, but owing to the unfavourable weather the match was abandoned. The green was well patronised. however, and several games at bowls were played. Mr John Betts, of Sutton-in-Ashfield, Notts., has been engaged as cricket professional for the ensuing season, and matches have been arranged with Havton, Birch, War- rington, Leigh, Tyldeeley, ilaydock, and other clubs. The club has prospects of a successful season. A BLACKBURN MAN'S ADTENTURES.—Thomas Pick- up, described as a cotton mill manager, of Blackburn, was, On Saturday, charged at the Newton Town Hall with having been drunk and dismderly and assaulting P.C. Sinev, at Golborne. The oonstable stated that at an early hour in the morning he found the prisoner blowing a whistle in the streets of Golborne. It was very dark, and when he turned his lamp on the prisoner, the latter said "This is the way I solve policemen." Ho then struck the officer a violent blow with his fist. The Bench inflicted a fine of 5s and coats for the drunkenness, and a similar fine for the assault.. .

GOOD TEMPLARY.— On Saturday evening a special session of the Hope of Barlestown Lodge of Good Template was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, for the purpose of initiating candidates who are unable to attend on Monday evenings. There was a very large attendance of members. A programme of songs, readings, and recitations was gone through. The usual weekly session on Monday evening was well attended, and Bro James, W.C.T , again occupied the chair. The evening's programme was " Our own auction night," and a miscellaneous assortment of articles were put under the " hammer," the W.C.T. acting as auctioneer. The proceeds of the sale were in aid of the funds of the lodge and a fair sum was realised. BRUTAL ATTACE ON AN HOTEL MANAGER.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Martin Craighan, a young fellow, was charged under a warrant with refusing to quit the Wellington Hotel, Earlestown, on the 23rd June last ; and also with assaulting Daniel Cullen, manager, at the same time. Daniel Cullen stated that on the date men- tioned there were several men in one of the rooms. They were very disorderly and he told theta to leave, but they paid no attention. Two of the men began fighting, and while he was attempting to separate them the prisoner and two others knocked him to the floor and kicked him several

times. They gave him two black eyes, and otherwise in- jured him.—The Bench inflicted a fine of 40e and costa, or one msnth's imprisonment with hard labour. THE WELLINGTON FOOTBALL CHALLENGE CUP. A meeting of Attociation football club representatives was held at the Committee-rooms of the Barlestown Football

Club, Earle-street, on Thursday eyening, for the purpose of making arrangements for the first competition for the Wet. lington Challenge. Cup. The cup was exhibited at the gathering, and drew forth expressions of admiration from all present. It stands about 12 inches high, and is of

- a . splendid workmanship. On one side is the engraved repre- sentation of a football match, and on the reverse side is the inscription" The Wellington Cup: Presented by Mr J W Thorp. Earlestown." The cup, it csay be stated, wall pre- sented by Mr Thorp to the Earleetown Football Club as a mark of his admiration for their prowess in winning the Liverpool and Distriot Challenge Cup and Gold Medals. With the consent of Mr Thorp, the oonamittee of the Earle's- town Club are offering the cup for competition amongst the various clubs in the district. At the preliminary meeting on Thursday evening there was a large attendance ; clubs from Ilaydock, Golborne, Newten,and Earlestown being re-. presented. CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL TEA PARTY.—The anniversary servieee in connection with the Congregational Sunday school, Crow-hue. Newton, were held on Sunday, when the Rev James Allatt, resident minister, preached two excellent sermons. 'I here were large congregations. The choir effi- ciently sang two anthems, the sole parts in whioh were finely rendered by Miss Wallington, of Warrington. The collections realised about £2O. The annual congregational tea meeting was held in the schoolroom on Thursday. A considerable number of persons partook of an excellent tee; and at the meeting subsequently held there was an insreaaed attendance. The chair was oceupied by the Rev Jame' Allatt (pastor), and amoag other gentlemen present were ithe Bev J T Came (Golborne), Rev H Wilson (Ashton), Rev J M Fairbourne (Earlestown Wesleyan), Rev F N Shinamin (Earlestown Primitive Methodist). After the Chairman had announced that a letter of apology for non- attendance had been received from the Ray W C Tayler (Baptist), the choir rplendidly sang the anthem "Behold, bow good mad joyful." The Pastor then gave his address. With respect to the school during the past year the attendance of the *cholera had been well maintained, and the management and the staff of teachers might be deseribed as thoroughly effieient. With respect to the services and their Christian worship the attendance had been very gratifying, and when they had had occasion to appeal to outsiders, and desire the attend- ance of friend& from other churches they had net been disappointed. He regretted that daring the year they had lest eight members through deeth and four by removal, bat on the other hand there had been eight additions to the church. Mr Alfred Caldwell had been appointed organist of the church, and everybody bad been satisfied with the appointment. The collections during the year had been of a satisfactory character. In concluding he remarked that he had that week entered on the 23rd year of his ministry —(applause)--and that was a long time in a man's life. Looking upon the whole course of his ministry, he had al- ways found sympathy and co-operation with him on the part of those around birn.—Mr F J Holmes, in the absence of Mr B B Glover (treasurer) read a financial statement, from which it appeared that during the year the receipts front all sources were £1,136 Us Cti, of which £429 Os 5d had been raised in connection with the organ fund.—Miss Glover sweetly sang " 'lb. Quaker's daughter," after which the Rev J T Camm, in an address, urged young people to appreciate Christian evi- dence and value Christian teaching. "The broken pitcher" was then sung by Mies Owen.—Rev J M Fair- bourne expressed his sympathy with their pastor, personally as well as well as with the work in which he was engaged. —The duet" A rippling stream " was effectively given by Miss Glover and Miss Wood.—The Rev F N Skimmin urged the desirability of a brotherly feeling among the differ- ent churches, and raid they ought to recognise each other on the ground of character and not simply on account of riches. If there was more union among the various denomi- nations they would have a disposition for mutual assistance and a stimulus to Christian work.—The Rev If Wilson (Ashton) also addressed the merting, remarking that he re- garded denominationalism as only the scaffolding round the great spiritual temple, and while .the scaffolding would some day fall, the great spiritual temple would stand for ever.—The choir then sang "I will lift up mine eyes," and the gathering was shortly afterwards brought to a close.
THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH SCANDAL. ILLEGAILITY OF THE LATE VESTRY MELTING.

At the annual meeting of the I;ariit-h-i-c;tera—W-ti;;;-.Chnrch of St John the Baptist, Earlestown, held on Easter Monday, several of the parishioners maintained that the meeting was illegal on the ground that the notice calling the meeting had not been posted on the church doors for a sufficient length of time. It was elicited that the notice was posted at noon on Good Friday, while the meeting was held on the afternoon of the following Monday'. At the vestry the curate (the Rev G Lovett)who presided in the absence of the vicar (the Rev T R Matthews), held that due notice had I,een given, but in order to test the question, Mr 11 Corlett laid the circumstances before the Bishop of Liverpool, in a communication which be addreseed to his Lordship. The Bishop has since replied to the effect that his secretary (Mr

Gamon, solicitor,) was attending to the tatter; and Mr Gamon afterwards wrote to Mr Corlett that he was in oomrn munioation with the Hey G Lovett. The latter gentleman, during the present week, has called upon Mr Corlett and stated that the former vestry meeting was illegal, and con- sequently the appointments thee made fell through. He intimated that another meeting of the parishioners would be called.

After the stormy proceedings at the vestry meeting some doubt was entertained as to the course which the " new oftioers of the church would pursue in regard to the services In the church. On Sunday last they abstained from attend- ing, and tho services proceeded as usual. The officiating clergyman was the ROY G Lovett, curate, the lessons being read by Mr J.-,13n Matthews, son of the vienr. There were only moderate attendances.

NEWTON COMMISSIONERS: MONTHLY MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Com- missioners WAS held at the Town Hall, on Monday, when there were present: Mr W F Gooch (chairman), Coptiel George McCorquoilale, Messrs T J Gillespie, J W Immett, J Yalu:lough, T Forster, J E Worsley (law clerk), and R Briarley (surveyor). The minutes of the last meeting were read and con- frmed.

Tan STATE OF THE Ges.—Mr Emmett asked if there had lately been any alteration in the pressure of the gas.—The Surveyor replied that there had been no alteration except when the gas in the lamps had not been lighted. When they were not lighted the pressure was taken off a little. On other occasions the pressure was the same.—Mr Emmett said he had noticed that the gas had not been very good and that made him ask the question. HIGHWAYS AND SANITAUY Cowarriess.—The Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee held a meeting on the 16th March.—The Surveyor reported that Mr 11 H Wright had by instructions of Mr Legh's agent threatened to summons the workmen for trespass if they interfered with I the gateways leading into the fields near Green Man's Pits. It was ordered that as such stoppage would not inconve- nience the public that the work remain in abeyance during his pleasure. Dr Watkins attended to confer with the com- mittee upon a site for cottage hospital and the pending liti- gation with the Guardians of the Warrington Union. The Law Clerk also read counsel's opinion thereon, and instruc- tions were given accordingly. The Surveyor submitted , plan and alternative estimates for dealing with:the sewage I at Earlestown (west) outlet, when it was ordered that Mr Glover and Mr Emmett with the surveyor do visit Golcar I sewage works to inspect the working of Hanson's automatic ne;xing machine and report to a future meeting. It was ordered that notices be served upon the property owners at Wargrave, between the church gates and Vulcan Villa, call- ing upon them, within one month, to sewer, pave, flag, &c, the said road in accordance with section 150 Public Health Act, 1875. The Surveyor having certified the sum of £3OO due to Mr Bothwell on his contract for cemetery buildings and the sum of .£7O to 'Mr J Pennington on his sewer con- tract at Wargrave, cheques for those amounts were ordered to be signed.—On the motion of Mr Gillespie, eeconded by Mr Forster, the minutes were passed. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr J W Watkins, medi- c-al officer of health, read his report for the first quarter of the present year. There were registered in the quarter : Births, 52 males, 45 females, total 97; deaths 42 males, 32 females, total 74. The excess of births was 10 males, 13 females, total 23. The birth rate was, on an annual aver- age computation, 32 98, and the death tate 25.16 per thou. sand of the estimated population. The per centage of in- fantile deaths (a: e., under one year) was 29 72, the death rate 5-14 per cent. The percentage of deaths under 5 years of age was 56 75. The deaths from zymotic diseases were 29 72 per cent : measles 10, scarlet fever 9, croup 2, and fever 2, total 23; rate 197 per 1,000. Of these 23 deaths four were cases of measles, and three of scarlet fever exist.l ing in the last quarter of 1884. During the quarter 20 new cases of scarlet fever were notified, and there were three (fatal) cases not notified, total 23, rate 1.97 per 1,000. There were six deaths (one at the infections diseases hospi- tal, at Warrington), or .51 per 1 000. Measles had been extremely prevalent. No approximate estimate could be given of the number of the cases.-Dr Watkins remarked that it was painful to see the large infantile death rate, which was about 25 per cent of the children born, since the let April, last year. The whole of Ecgland was about 15 per cent, and Liverpool for last year was only about 21 per cent. —Mr Emmett : How do yon account for it 7—Dr Watkins replied that many of the deaths were from zymotic dis- eases. The increase in the population, they would observe, was only small. The births were 97 and the deaths 74 In reply to Colonel McCorquodale. Dr Watkins added that measles had been very prevalent. There had been 10 deaths from measles, and 8 from scarlet fever. Of the deaths from scarlet fever three were from last quarter, so that they had really only had five deaths from scarlet fever in the mew cases since let January. He hoped there would be a more favourable report for the mid-summer Quarter. Geis AND Weeset.—A meeting of the Gas and Water Committee was held on the 16th March, at which the sur- veyor reported that the removal of tar and ammoniacal liquor from the gasworks was suspended in consequence of the financial difficulties of Messrs Meadows and Son. It was ordered that Mr Brierlay do make temporary arrange- ments for its disposal, and that the same be again adver- tised. The carbonising account for the past month gave fuel used 253 tons 14 cwt. gas made 2,539,900 cubic feet, averaging 100 feet per ten of feel used. Mr Geoele submit- ted a letter he had received from Mr Brown, chemist, re- specting the water supply to his premises, and it was or- dered that the chairman and the surveyor see Mr Brown thereon. Another meeting of the same committee was held on the 7th lust, when the surveyor reported that Mr Edward Oldham, of Railway View, Chemical-street, Earlestown, had been fraudulently consuming the Commissioners' gas, and it was ordered that the law clerk be instructed to prose- cute Oldham for stealing gas. Tenders for the purchase of tar and ammonlacal liquor were considered, and it was re- solved that the quotations of Mr Win B. Dale. of Tvldes- ley, be aommted for the year ending March 315t,1886, and that the law clerk prepare the necessary agreement. It was ordered that a claim be made upon the estate of W Mea- dows and Son, in bankruptcy, for the loss sustained in the non-fnlfilment ef their tar and liquor contract. It was or- dered that the surveyor prepare a sketch plan for a line of rails from Meeste Evans and Company's siding, Crow-line, to the gasworks.—The minutes were passed. BminuoL ATTENDANCE.—At a meeting of the School At- tendance Committee, ea the 10th nit, Mr Ball, the school attendance officer, read his report. Complaints having been made from St Peter's school of the irregular attendance of two • children, Mr Ball was directed to inquire into the Giese of their ahsense, and report to the next meeting. FINANCE.—At a meeting of the Finance Committee on the lath March, it was ordered that the disputed items of assessment to income tax be appealed against unless the Sur- veyor of Taxes could see hie way to adjust the discrepancy. Accounts amounting to £1,539 7e 8.1 were examined and palmed for payment. —The minutes were confirmed. Tins CEMETERY Br-Lews.—The Law Clerk reported that the by-laws for the Cemetery had been before the Local Government Board, and they bad returned the draft sent to them with some alterations and suggestions. He (Mr Worsley) had altered the form and arrangement of the by- laws, Indite thought he might venture to do so as the words of the by-laws bad not been touched. Tvhs Fuerformeerr USE OF Gera—Alluding to an item ' mentioned in the minutes of the Highway, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee, Mr Worsley stated that in accord- ance with the instructions et the committee the case against ' Edward Oldham was brought before the magistrates at New- ton on Saturday, and Oldham was fined .1310 and costs, or in default of payment two months' imprisonment. Remern OF Paoannev.—Mr Worsley said Mr Brierley ' had instructed hint to write to the Bedford Brewery Com- pany with respect to the state of their heuse property. He ' bad sinew written, and the property had been repaired ac- oerdingly. BANgutrrretv FBOCEEDINGS.—AI the suggestion of the Law Clerk, a motion was passed that Mr Brierley., clerk and earveyor, be authorised under the seal of the Board to make proofs of debts swing to the Commissioners in any future bankraptey proceedings. Mr Woraley stated that that had become necessary under the new Bankruptcy Act. THE COMMISSIONERS T. THE WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS —The Law Clerk reported that the Case Of the Commissioners against the Warrington Guardians had been heard in the County Court, and had been adjourned until Thursday, the 16th inst. CHARGE AGAINST THE SURVEYOR.—The Chairman read a long latter from Mr J E Pardey, agent to Mr W J Legit. M.P., stating that from the agenda of the minutes of the Highways and Sanitary Committee it appeared that Mr Wright had, be instructions of Mr Leglee agent, threatened to summons the workmen for trespass if they interfere with the gateways leading into the fields near Green Man's Pit." He (Mr Pardey) begged to say distinctly that no such Instructions were given by him, and he had been in- formed by Mr Wright that they were never given by him. The Commissioners were not to enter the land before satis- factory arrangements bad been made with him (Mr Pardey), but he had not been supplied with plans or specifications. He added that the Surveyor seemed determined to withhold Information, and entered upon property without leave or licence, and he (Mr Pardey) felt it hie-duty to resist such action. He was s Wiled no member of the Board would submit to have their land or property entered without leave or license.—Mr Brierley observed that hailed been told by the foreman of the works that Mr Wright had threatens Ito take proceedings on the instructions of Mr Legh.—After some conversation, Colonel MeCorquodale moved, and Mr aillespie seconded, that the Surveyor and the Law Clerk be. instructed to see Mr Pardey with the view of coming to some arrangement in order to prevent litigation.-The motion watt carried. Sciaoca. Arrnernamen AND THE RECENT EPIDEMICS. The Chairman stated that he had received a letter from the Bev Canon Whitley a of Wargrave Schools, which stated that the menagerie of- the schools, would feel obliged if the Commissioners would communicate with the Educatio* Department in London intimating to them the compulsony absence of chi:Aron from school owing to the continued pre- valence of fever and other infectious diseases during the current year, and asking the Department to give that fact due consideration when the Government examination took place.—Ma Worsley A very reasonable request. The Chairman added that there was another similar latter from the Earieetown Wesleyan School.—Mr Woralety read the letter which had been written by Mr Gooding, at Earle street. —Mr Emmett moved that the Law Clerk wrlte to the Education Department 89 suggested in the letters.—Mr For- ster : iWilt the motion include all the schools in the town- ship 2—Chairman Yes, it will apply to all schools.—Col. McCorquodale seconded the motion, which was passed. Tan EAntefrows FOOTBALL CLun.—A discussion look place with reference to an alleged enclosure of a public foot-
b • a red path in the Manes by the Earlestown Foothill ' port of which will be found elsewhere, This was the whole of the business.

When Anthony Trollope was a young clerk in the Post- Office, he made the acquaintance of a girl in the country who determined to marry him, whether he liked it or net. He declined to do so, and then, he tells us in his autobiog- raphy, "At last the mother appeared at the Post-Office. My hair almost stands on my head now as I remember the figure of a woman walking into the big room in which I sat with six or seven other clerks, having a large basket on her arm and an immense bonnet on her head. The messenger had vainly endeavoured to persuade her to remain in the ante-room. She followed the man in, and, walking up the centre of the room, addressed me in a lend voice 'An- thony Trollope, when are you going to marry my daughter ?' We have all had our worst momenta, and that was one of my worst. I lived through it, however, and did not marry the young lady." A gentleman was travelling in a smoking-compartment on the Midland line the other day, and at a certain station a German entered the carriage and took his seat opposite to him. When the train had started, the foreigner, noticing the other's bavana, inquired if he could oblige hint with a cigar. The Englishman, astonished at the request, reluct- antly pulled out his case, and saw with disgust the other select the beet cigar he could find and produce a match from his pocket and light it. After taking a few puffs, with evi- dent er.joyment, the German, beaming at his companion through his spectacles, continued affably, "1 vould not bar droubled you, but I had a match in mein beggit, and I did not know vat to do mit it." "A newspaper man," relates Mr. Barnum," called on me when first I opened my great museum in New York, and, after going over the building with me and admiring my ex- hibits, he suggested that, if I could but obtain the club with which Captain Cook had been killed by the Sandwich Islanders, it would prove a great attraction. I had at the time several war-clubs in a lumber-room upstairs; so, seiz- ing on the idea, I told him that, curiously enough, I had secured the treasure yesterday, and that I would fetch it for his inspection. Having procured a descriptive label, I came down triumphantly and placed the club in his hand. He turned it over and over; he almost shed tears, I thought; but at length he spoke. "Poor Cook," he said—"poor fellow! I'm glad you have shown me this; but I expected it. I have been to all the smaller museums in the city, and they all had it, so I felt sure that a gigantic establishment like this would not be without it." A Fran CALIFORNIA !SCHEME. A crowd of summer Unifies were on the beach at Loa Angela one day, watching some fancy rifle-shooting by a party of party of otter- hunters, who had come over from the Channel Islands. These really wonderful marksmen, most of them native Califor- nians, were killing gulls on the water, breaking bottles, and hitting dollars thrown into the air, with great eclat, when a "dudish "-looking young man from 'Frisco yawned in a bored manner, and remarked in a very audible voice to a companion that he did not see anything very wonderful in that sort of shooting. This produced a series of sarcastically polite retorts on the part of the original lords of the soil. Perhaps the gentleman could show them something better ? "Well, I don't know," replied the young man, languidly taking one of the hunters' Winchesters. "I might, if some- body would hold a cork or something on his head for me." The riflemen showed their white teeth with amusement. "Doubtless." said one of them, winking at his companions " doubtless, the gentleman's friend would Oblige him." "Why, to be sure !" drawled the " dude " looking round. But his fellow "dude" had sauntered away, and was standing some three hundred yards further along the beach, meditatively smoking a large cigar. " Ah, there's Cholly!" said the languid party, cocking the gun. "Let me see. You observe he has a cigar in his mouth. Very well, I'll put a hole through it ;" and, taking a careless sight, he fired. At the report the smoker gave a sudden start, took out and examined his Havana, and then shook his fist angrily. The entire crowd ran towards him. Bare enough there was a hole right through the centre of the cigar, cutting it almost in half! "That's the fourth cigar you've spoiled for me," said the smoking "dude," in a vexed tone. "I wish You'd stop that sort of thing." As for the other hunters, they looked at each other in mortified silence for a few minutes, and then climbed into their boat and set sail. "That's the meet wonderful shotl ever saw," said an old gentle-man to the shooter the next morning—asneh a risk too!" "Nothing wonderful nbout it,"eald the Californian Tell confidentially. " jil on have to do 13 to have your confederate cut a hole in the cigar with a penknife beforehand. It's a boss scheme!"

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THVIZSDAY. The probabilities of war with Russia remains the one sub- ject of conversation. It comes up in railway carriages, omnibuses, on river steamers, and at dinner parties. I have noticed that wherever the matter is discussed, by whatever class of society, the persons speaking would be able, if Pro- vidence had placed the matter in their hands, to settle everything off in five minutes. They know where error has been committed, and where danger lies, and would be able—to avoid both. Her Majesty's Government, mean- while, find the task a much harder one. The exceptional difficulty is the character of the nation with which we are at issue. If only the Russians could be trueted matters would be greatly simplified. But, undoubtedly, judging from past histery there is an uneasy feeling that the Rus- sian Government may, behind a friendly attitude, hide de- signs of agreesive war. Even admitting the honesty ef the Russian Ministers there remains the qtfestion whether the Government of the Czar is strong enough to carry out their peaceful protentetions and intentions. The Czar may Pro- pose at St Petersburg, but the fire-eaters on the Afghan Frontier may diepese. Unhappily Russia is not alone in possession of fire-eaters. We have them in bushels in London. "Society" is on the I War path once mere, and the majority of the London news- papers give society its fill every morning with highly spiced defiances of Ruesia and frantic cries to Mr. Gladstone to plunge the couutry into war without another moment's de- lay. It is the old story over again of 187 C it was only by the merest shave that England was then kept out of the =lee, Then, as now, the Times pursued its iniquitous course of iecitiog the country to war, and society—more particularly I note the women--clamoured to be let looee at the throat of Russia. It is tke same to-day, and no one can doubt that, had a Conservative Government teen in power, we should already have been at war. As it is there is still hope. The conduct of the Govern. merit is fairly indicated in a passage from the despetch of the Vienna correspondent of the Times, which hoe to-dav, by some editorial oversight, found aprominent place in that journal must remark," the correspondent telegraph?, "that men who have been blaming the English Govern- ment, and even riling at it for its alleged supineness, have begun to speak with some admiration of the patience and honesty displayed by Mr. Uladstene's Government and Cabinet, in negotiations conducted under the greatest difficulties and provocations." There is profound sateafac- tion in the reflection that it eventually this country is plunged into the horrors of war, of which some people take such light account, it will cnly be after all expede-nts short of sacrificing British hononr will have been tried. England will be able to enter upon war not with a light heart, but with a clear conscience. There .is cue striking coincidence in the condition of affairs to day as compared with the epidemic of Jingoism ; which plagued the country in 1871-5. Whilst the Loedon ; press, with but one exception among the morning journals, ; is wickedly worrying for war, the country press, almost without exception, has assumed an attitude of dignified and impartial iuquiry. When the news came of the affair at Penjieb, the Times, Morning Post, and Standard shrieked to be led instantly to war—or rather urged that so many tens of thousands of honest men should be sent forth to war whilst editors remained at home to criticise the cam- paign. The provincial papers were deeply stirred by this affair. But they recommended that it would be welt to await faller reports before telling an irrevocable decision. It has been the same through all eucceeding stages of events. London pipers have neither investigated nor argued, but Simply cried for war. The country papers have both inves- tigated and adduced argument. They have admitted the necessity of war in certain circumstances, but have protested against bringing about so great a calamity till we are quite sure there is no other way of obtaining the just demands of England. It is a fact within my personal knowledge that it is to the provincial press that Mr Gladstone and his col- leagues in the Cabinet turn for expressions of public opinion. Of course, what the London papers say cannot be ignored, for they as faithfully represent opinion in London, and Lon- don is a big place. Bat Great Britain is bigger, and at national crises has proved itself wiser. It has been remarked that, however undoubted are the advantages of roya'ty, they do not tend in the directien of the preserve; mof international 'peace. This fact is more patent now than it used to be in elder times. When Nineteen married Marie Therese it was simply with the. idea of forming a close alliance with Austria. But this did not prevent Austria from joining the grand ahlance that drove Napoleon from the throne. If it were otherwise, our own Royal Family would be one of the most extensive peace makers in the world. Not only is our Princess Royal married to the heir of the German Imperial Crown, but as between the German people. and the English the links are drawn closer by the provision made for several German princelings by matrimonial alliances with daughters of the English Royal House. The Prince of Wales, it is true, has thrown away opportunities by marriage with the daughter of a King whose military friendship is of no par- ticular consequence. But the Duke of Edinburgh Is married to the sister of the Czar, and the Duke of Connaught again joins hands with the Imperial German Family. Yet, as we know, it was but a few weeks ago that we seemed on the eve of a quarrel with Germany, and at the present moment:are within measurable distance of war with Russia, events which family alliances are wholly impotent to contr. 1. There is one consolatory matter in connection with the war with Russia should it take place. It is no secret that in ordinary hostilities the Duke of Edinburgh would be ap- pointed, over the heads of officers who have fought their way upwards by sheer merit,to important command with the fleet. He would for example, supposing his brother-in-law were not the adversary, take command of the Baltic fleet. Bat that is obviously impossible in view of his near rela- tions with The Czar, and the disposition of this important -command would go to the officer who has the fullest claim upon it. 'thus will be averted sot only much beartburning in the Navy but the possibility of serious drawbacks to the efficiency of the fleet. If it were with our warlike Princes as it is with their German cousins it would be different. Mining the war with France the sons of the German Emperor .not only displayed conspicuous military capacity but .shared with the commonest soldiers the dangers of the -battle field. It is a matter of history what happened in rEgYPt when the Doke of Connaught was there in toe cam- ,paign against Arabi. A crack regiment under his command was kept in ignominious safety in the rear, whilst fighting, such as it was, was going on in the front. This implies no refLction on the courage of the Royal Pierces. They would doubtless like to take their share of what in going forward in the way of knocks or bruises. But they are not free agents in. this matteraand if they will go to war must take the field under the conditions that hampered the Duke of Con-

naught in Egypt. The emphatic rejection of Mr Alderman Cotton's claim for re-election as Lord Mayor completes a singularly un- -fortunate civic career. Mr Cotton was one of the best, most enlightened, and most liberal of Lord Mayors. It is said that during his term of office he vastly exceede I the aver- age expenditure. He graced the office with a portly presence and a pleasant manner. He was, indeed, in all respects a model Lord Mayor. But he failed in one import- ant respect. He was not an out-and-out Tory. Bad he been elected to complete the term vacated by the death of Mr Nottage, a Liberal Government would have been only too glad to seize the opportnnity of recogniaing his claim to a baronetcy. But the flavour of Mr Alderman Fowler's turtle and the aroma of his wine lies more lately on the palate of the Livery, and Mr Cotton had no chance. The other day I accidentally became acquainted with the existence of anew vocation for woman. It is to bite herself out to arrange the flowers on dinner tables. Personally I hear of this with satisfaction, and trust that the band of competent artists may be enlarged and the circle of their clients greatly extended. It is a bold statement to make, but I believe that the art of arranging flowers for the de- coration of a table or a room is one of the raced possersions of womankind. Of course with men it is almost entirely absent. It is an instinct, a species of genius that could never be imparted by tuition, and yet comes as naturally as walking to the favoured few who have received the endowment I have seen in the best houses a lavish abundance of flowers utterly spoilid by their method of arrangement. To put flowers in glasys coloured a bright red Of gren is not un- known in cultured London. From these monstrosities the lady floral decorator will in time deliver us. The prettiest dinner table I know in London is Mr Chamberlain's. He has not only a unique collection of orchids, but they are arranged by a hand that plainly loves and understands flowers,

_ .._.... The party organisations throughout the country are rapidly choosing their candidates for the first general elec- tion under the new' conditions ; and although Liverpool, Birmingham, Bradford, Leeds, and some other of the largest boroughs have yet to make their selection, there is little doubt that when the Press Association issues its promised secoud liat " of candidatee, the gaps will be very few. There is the same difficulty in some parts of the country to find suitable candidates, as has been experienced by am. /salons gentlemen from time immemorial in lighting upon comfortable seats. One of the new county divisions—a Labour constituency in the west of England—is se seriously in want of "a good robust Radical " that the local person- ages of that way of thinking have issued a circular, asking any who can subscribe to their programme and who wish to enter Parliament to put in an appearance. "No prelim i i- nary ntroduction will be necessary, as the field is quite free and oyen to all posseesing the ordinary credentials of re- sponsible Englishmen." This is calculated to tempt a modest anan to Camhorne, for that is where he is wanted. But be may not impossibly be frightened away by being told that "failing initiative on the part of the responsible leaders in questions peculiarly affecting the industries of this country, the cand.date will be expected to lead as well as follow." For who but a Cornishman born could be expected to 'lndef.. stand the laws of the stanneries or the mystery surrounding the production of tin? The halfpenny morning paper which is to revolutionise our present journalistic ideas in London, still hangs fire, but, accmiing to the latest rumours, will see the light next week. If. is generally understood, it intends to favour neither side in politics, its failure may be taken for „grouted.

div.head: Xettexo to the editor.
div.p: Xettexo to the editor.

WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH. Sir,—l have no doubt your readers will be sarprited to bear that the late lively vestry meeting at the Parish Church has not made much impression en that ardent lover of peace, the Rector. After his audacious proposal to elect the people's warden, as well as his own, had been indignantly ' refused by the assembled parishioners, you would have thought the gentleman they have elected would have been treated with at least common courtesy. But lam told on the best authority that the Rector would not allow the war- dens the use of the vestry to count the offertories as usual; i that at the eveoing service the curate informed the people's , warden that the Rector had ordered him to take the offer- tory to the Rectory, and he would count it in the presence of i said curate and parish clerk. Now, air, this may be legal, but iit is not nice. It appears to me that, as the people find the Imoney, their wardens ought at least to have the counting of • their offertories, and until such is the case I for one have decided to contribute nothing further to the Parish Church, \ and believe that many more will do likewise.—Yours, dn., CHURCHMAN.

Sir,—Allow me to thank you for the report touching the "Rector and his curates " that appeared in your last issue. Very likely our townsmen who worship at the Parish Church may feel annoyed at seeing their shortcomings so prominently exposed to the public gaze ; but they must re- member that the doings of a church which claims to be National must always be subject to criticism. One would naturally suppose that the welfare of the peo- ple woeld be the first object of a National Church, yet how woefully disappointed are we on reading the reports of Eas- ter meetings that are yearly given in the public pres. As 3 Liberationiet,l quite sympathise with Mr Francomb in the few earnest words he felt called upon to utter in the Rector's hearieg, and I can assure him that I am strongly of opinion that were those who are working for disestablish- meet to rest on their oars they would soon see the Church party take up the question, "end bless the cause of the Liberation Society, and be thankful to see the Church free from such arbitrary power on the part of the clergy." I have long been of opinion that .it is only from ' pure cussedness" that their objection to liberation from State control arises. In reading over your report, I find one feature stands out I very prominent, that is it reads like a police report of a family brew! in which, as we often notice, the husband, or the wife, as the case may be, refuses to give evidence. In this ease it unfortunately happens that not only the in- terests of the parish are immediately affected, but the in- stincts of our common humanity are outraged. Looking at I the whole question tram an independent standpoint, I can ! but feel a profound sorrow for the Rector and his lady. I notice that a parishioner states that he has no respect for the Rector's wife ; another says " she is at the bottom of everything." When Mr Francomb said "Don't try to frighten us, Re- tor," he implied that the preacher was wanting in that love and kindliness which ehculd form so prominent a feature in the character of a follower of the "meek and lowly." The fact is, Mr Editor, a squabble like this places the clergy in a very awkward position, and for this reason—it proves bow thorough must have been St. Paul's knowledge of women kind. It is well known that the Romish Church I has always considered it to be of vital importance that their priesthood should be celibate; but it has always taken 1 good care that a thorough knowledge of woman's nature I should be inculcated daring the years of youthful study. 1 By the by, what was the Rector going to say when he was interrupted by Mr White ? "When a man comes and says he will make it too hot—" Surely it is not implied that 1 Mr. Montgomery considered it necessary to use such language when addressing a lady. I should like this point clearing up; and should anyone deign to oblige me in this I wish they would alas suggest to Mr. Francomb that he print the Bishop's letter to which he referred. Of course, Mr. Editor, I do not look upon this matter as one of very great importance. It is one of the signs of the times. The days of the church as an establishment are numbered ; of that there can be no doubt. Democratic opinions are not by any means confined to the advanced thinkers of to-day, and those who aspire to control and guide the people must reckon on this as an important factor, and sure to turn up when least expected. It is some- thing gained to have made the Rector sue for peace, "I am for peace—a man of peace." But how pitiable to hear Mr. Davies say that " aelot of young men" had gone there for "mischief," as if" drawing the badger" could be done as well in the Parish Church as in St. Stephene. Of VUTBc my mind was set at rest on this cao3t Uhsemly feature about " young men" by the formidable attitude taken by Mr. Taylor in throwing the terrible charge of youthfulness b:ck at once full into Mr. Davies'e "face." A man who is 42 years of age has surely cut his wisdom teeth, and may be trusted to look well after one who has passed the allotted span. And so, Mr Editor, we may leave these church folks, con- fent to see them prepare the way fcr religious equality, yet sorry to see such bitter fruit, as the result of their teach- ings. In their strivings after privilege and state recognition they have tied their bands by allying themselves to the patronage system, little thinking that the present writer, were he sufficiently wealthy, could coon place himself in a position to snake the next preeentation. Could this be brought tabout just now, I could premise Mr Francomb a "call," and thus rid him of 30033 of his troubles. CLIFFORD DIX.
THE ALLEGED ENCLOSURE OF A FOOTPATH NEAR EAELESTOWN.

Sir,—Will youkindly -ail-rWr-n-e-a-lit6ii space to refer to the alleged enclosure if common land in the Mesnes for the purposes of a foothill field. A question was asked by "A Ratepayer" in your last week's issue, " Where are the com- mon-lookers and Commissioners ?" That will no doubt be answered by the parties to whom it refers, but as one inter- ested in the maintainance of the rights and privileges of the people, I must say I viewed with some alarm the erection of the fence to which your cerreepondent referred. I have personally made some inquiries into the matter, and have been forced to the conclusion that ne public rights are being interfered with. Your correspondent "A Ratepayer "wishes mins abler pen than his would take the matter up. and so do I. Like" A Ritep tyer, 'I am an admirer of the game of foot- ball, but, sir, football must not be allowed to usurp the rights of the people. If it can be satisfactorily proved that a public footpath has been stopped by the Earlestown Football Club, then I say by all means let steps be at once taken to prevent it becoming a permanent stop- page. I should like te ask, however, if it is not a fact that the supposed " public "footpath is only a right of way for the occupier of the land; and does not the footpath pass through a farm yard ? Has it ever been a "free " and open path to the public ? If so, why should the gate at the corner of the blesnee, nearest to the farm, always have been kept locked and securely fastened, and why should the I notice board " Trespassers will be prosecuted " have been erected? Those questions should be satisfactorily answered before anything rash is committed or any extreme measures taken. Everyone will admit that the question is one sur- ronntiedlwith doulit and uncertainty, and, as a necessary consequence, the greatest caution should be exercised in any action that might 413 ta'xen.—Yours, Ac. Earlestewn, 14th April, 1885. SPECTATOR.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING.

Sir,— Under the-a-b-c;;;Weadin-g.-aleitear.appeared in your paper of Saturday Past, signed Peter Plymley, who for coarseness of style very mach resembles another correspond. sot of yours. viz, Clifford Dix. _ . .

_ If the first pazt of his letter means anything it is this, that by closing public-houses on Sundays it Is a direct in- terference with the liberty of the people. Peter wants hi, Sundays as a day of rest, and I have no doubt he would be one of the first to raise an outcry if he were compelled to labour on that day. Then, why object to a measure whose effect will be to enable thousands in this country who ant employed in public-houses to enjoy the same privilege? AS a working-man I am in favour of Sunday Closing, for to adopt it is but to put a check upon the secularizing portion of the community, who advocate no Sunday at all, or, if any, to be modelled upon the continental principle, which means another work day. He not only objects to the means used, but he trys to throw dust into the eyes of your readers by trying to dis- parage the good done in Sunday schools, an-cl for this im- pose he quotes the Hey Caine, late chaplain of Salford Gaol, who in speaking of criminals who have come under his notice as chaplain gives the number of those who have been Sunday school scholars and teachers. After giving the qudtation from the chaplain's re- port, he goes on to say: " From this I gather that mere secular education we . have, the less criminals ; less theology, and less use for prisons." Now, to use his own words, this is mere twaddle, for the only in- ference that can be drawn from the report is that these poor unfortunates have thrown off the restraining influence of the Sunday school, and gone into evil ways. And no won- der when we see exposed for sale the publications that circu- late among the so-ca Led Secularists of this country, whose only tendency is to degrade tie mind to the lowest posaible love. Now, with respect to the work being done by the Salva- tion Army, at which he sneers. However much we may con- demn their eccentric behaviour, still it is a fact that they have succeeded in rescuing thousands from drunkenness and degradation to sobriety and rendectabilitY, and the man who, like your correspondent, calls such good results a fraud, is beyond the reach of argument.—l remain, yours truly, Warrington, April 13th, 1895.
WHIMSICAL WAM.
TYRANNICAL EARLESTOWN ANTI•TACCINATORS.

Sir,—lt is ever an unwelcome duty when one f•iels com- pelled to condemn the action of his own immediate ft iends, and rnoreespecially those with whose views and opinions he is thoroughly in accord and sympathy. But there is a reason- able limit in everything, and tyranny above all is what each individual who values his life and liberty should strive to oppose and suppress. This is absolutely necessary when the principles of a noble cause are at stake. lam a firm and strong believer in the principle of anti-compule•ry vaccination, but, sir, I do not want to be associated with society or class for securing compulsory anti-vaccination. The one would be almost as bad an evil as the other. There is no doubt if the present laws relating to the compul- sory vaccination of children were repealed it would be a good thing. and a blessing ler many chirdren, but then where would be the justice if the Legislature went to the opposite extreme and decreed that no one should have their children vaccinated, and [hit anti-vaccination must he corn pulsory ? Why the thing is ridiculous ! I for one would

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. .-,AP_RIL 18, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. .-,AP_RIL 18, 1885.

oppose it almost as stronaly as I do the imposition of any other obnoxious theory. At least I would oppose it to this extent that any person should be prevented from from hav- ing his children vaccinated if he believed that by so doing he was acting for the good of his own family and the coun- try generally. The Anti-vaccinators cry out for " liberty." and declare that they only want the right to please them- selves. But, sir, after beiog a careful observer of the pro- ceedings of the local anti-vaccinators, I am beginning to doutt if they really only want that. As I have previously remarked, tyranny in any shape or form is objectionable, but it is ten times more repulsive when it is exercised by those who are supposed to be struggling for liberty. There is a certain class associated with the anti-vaccination move- ment in Earlestowneahich by its actions has done more to bar its progress than any other influence or obstacle. It would appear as if, to them, there was nothing else but anti-vaccination. Anti-vaccination appears to be their only end and aim, while other good and important things are baing neglected and unprovided for. This has been shown in many ways—notably in connection with the recent meet- ing of the Liberal "30U" and in connection with the annual meeting of ratepayers at Newton Town Hall. At the last named gathering was this especially the case, where anti- vaccination and anti-vaccination alone was nothing if not everything. One or two fanatical anti•vaccluatore almost shouted themselves hoarse in airing their views ; and it was shown that hewever good a man may be in other things he must be condemned and thrown overboard if he will not submit to the opinions of others. Free thought and liberty, Indeed ! Why such a thing is unknown in the minds of the anti-vaccinators, except for their own purposes. They do not give a man credit for his convictions, but be must go to the winds or anywhere else for what they care, oolong as be does not go band in hand with them. I will not enter into details. A word to the wise is sufficient, and the sin will come home to the minds of thesinners. Let me exhort them to be moderate. Slow and sure progress, based on a just conviction that the, principle i 3 a reasonable and right one, will do fifty times more good than a blind compulsion and intolerant treatment of those who don't happen to see as others do. Your insertion of these remarks will oblige.— Yours, dre, JUNIUS. Earlestown, 13th April, 1885.
