div.head: MR. MeMINN lES, N P ON EDUCATION.
div.p: MR. MeMINN lES, N P ON EDUCATION.

On Thursday afterncon Mr. J. G. MeMinnies, MP., opened a bazaar at the Catholic School, Brownedge, near Preston, which had been organised to clear off a debt of about £7OO in connection with the schools of the Mission. Father Pozzr, in introducing Mr. MeMinnies, said that when he looked around him and saw the extraor- dinary display of goods, both useful and ernamental, he felt so bewildered that he could scarcely compose himself to perform the duty allotted to him. But knowing that England expects every man to do his duty, he very willingly undertook the task, and he had the utmost pleasure in introducing to them hia esteemed friend Mr. McMinnies, the M.P. for War- rington. (Applause.) When that bazaar was .con i• templated, the chief movers in connection with t looked around to see who would be the i most suitable person to take the exalted position of chairman at the opening. They all agreed that Mr. McMin- nies, who was so highly esteemed n that neighbour- hood, was the most eligible person to perform the ceremony of opening. That gentleman, with the kindness of heart that invariably characterised him, ' had at great personal trouble and inconvenience come down to Brownedge for the occasion, and he (Father Pozzi) had no doubt they would give him a hearty welcome. (Applause.) Mr. MeMrsrens, who was very cordially received, said the object of that bazaar, he need hardly tell I them, was to clear off a debt which had been in. in increasing the accommodation of the schools connected with their church. That en- larged accommodation was rendered necessary by the increasing number of scholars, and it was pro- tide d with a view to the better management and de- velopment of the schools. (Hear, hear.) He sup- posed nowadays nobody would deny that the elenieq- tary education of the people was of great import- ! eine, and the schools connected with that Mission had peettliar elaims upon them ; in the first place on account of their antiquity, and secondly because of the good they wer6 Meg in the neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) Doubtless they had schools in cox- nection with that Mission many years ago, in fact he dared say he would not be ex- aggerating if he said the existence of ele- mentary schools in association therewith dated further back than perhaps the memory of any man living. Before education was recognised as a matter of importance by the nation generally, it I was so recognised by that Mission. It was very little more than so years ago since the first grant was , made by Government in aid of education, and that , grant was the very niggardly one ot £20,000. Since then, however, the subject had grown on the public mind, and we had now granted prwery year towards this object the very large sum of ft millions sterling. We had in England and Wales 19,000 elementary schools, 5,000,000 scholars, and 40,000 certificated teachers. (Applause.) In fact so much was being done now that it was becoming a question whether this large sum of money granted annually for school purposes was not too much, whether the pressure of education npon children and young people was not more than their health and strength would bear, and whether our boys were not crammed with informa- tion, up to the age of 13 or 14, most of which they forgot before they were zo. But while so much was being (done by the Govern- ment out of local ratea and Imperial taxa- tion it would be a serious mistake to suppose that a great deal was not being done by volun- tary effort. Hear, hear.) He dared say he was right in supposing that there was no greater or more unpleasant burden upon the clergy than their having to beg pecuniary assistance for their elementary schools (Hear, hear.) School build- ings cost a great deal of money. A great author- ity said recently that the present coat of building schools was about £.5 per scholar provided for. Act- cording to his tMr. MoMinnissea) experience, the coat was S great deal more than that. An infant school with which he had had to do recently had cost £8 per seholar, and then there was the additional burden of maintenance, which was a serious tax upon the clergy and those interested in the management. (Hear, hear.) Well, the enlargements and alterations in connection with those schools had left them with a debt of about £7OO, but it was hoped and expected that by that bazaar they would de something, per- haps a good deal towards diminishing the harden. (Hear, hear.) There were many people who objee, ted to bazaars, and who spoke very dimwit- gingly of those who supported them, likening them. to the money changers of the Temple, and to those who sold doves. (Laughter, and A. voice "It's a shame.") Well, considering the angelic nature of those who presided at the stalls, and who took them willing captives, his idea was that they did not sell doves, but that the doves sold thorn. (Laugh- ter.) He did not believe in those objections to bazaars. He had been connected with them more cif less for over thirty years, and when he considered thsi‘, amount of sickness relieved, ignorance enlightened, religious knowledge imparted, and other benefits con- ferredby institutions that owed their existence to the pecuniary aid they had received from bazaars, he -could not do otherwise than wish success to those instrumentalities. (Applause.) It was sometimes said that those who worked for bazaars did not act with that singleness and purity of purpose that should characterise those who worked for philanthro- pic institutions. That was not his experience. He had seen in young men and women working for bazaars a singleness of purpose and purity of motive which could only be the outcome of a feeling and know- ledge that they were doing good in a good way on behalf of an institution in which they had entire confidence. Again, it was said Christian people would support a religious and charitable object with- out abaaaar. That seemed to him like begging the question. He maintained that working for bazaars was a most generous way of giving help. At a recent bazaar, a screen made by half-a-dozen factory workers sold for £24. It would not have been possible for those girls to have saved this amount in the time it took them to make the screen. It was the working of comparatively raw materials into articles of beauty and utility which increased the value of their efforts. So it had been with that bazaar. The increasing frequency of bazaars, so far from being an argument again 4 them, was a proof of their success, and he hoped they would never come to languish for want of support. (Hear, hear ) He hoped their friends who were present would purchase readily the goods which were marked at ressouable prices, and so reward those who had taken an interest in the work, and at the same time help their friends at the head of the mission to clear off a debt which, if it remained, could not be otherwise than a great discouragement to them. He begged to declare the bazaar now open. (Loud applause.) On the motion of Father O'Brien (Parbold), thanks were accorded to Mr. MeMinnies for his services.

TELEGRAPHY BETWEEN ENOLAND AND THR ISLE OF MAN. —A submarine cable is being laid between England sill the Isle of Man. It will extend from Cornway, south of Rimsey Bay, direct to St. Bees Head. It includes one direct wire te Liverpool, one to Mancbester for the Lan- while and Yorkshire district, and a spire wire to pro- vide for prompt despatch of businsss during the visiting season.

A Foommt DRIVER.—A young man named J R Kemp, a butcher, belonging to 17, Exchange-street, Manchester, was charged with having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and carriage at Lymon on Good Friday afternoon ; and he was further charged with having cruelly ill-treated the horse on the same occasion. It was stated by witnesses that the defendant en the day in question was driving the ani- mal furiously backwards and forwards on the road near the church. He beat the animal so severely that be broke his whip. He was drunk at the time.—A fine o! 5s and costs was imposed for the drunkenness, and 103 and costs for the ill-treatment of the horse, £2 9s in all. div.head: LOCAL BOARD: ANNUAL MEETING.
div.p: LOCAL BOARD: ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of this Board was held in the Board- room on Thursday evening. There were present—Messrs Cameron, Thomason, Appleton, Gibbon, Forger, Woolley, Rogers, Hall. and Ridgway (clerk). Tan Erxerion.—The Chairman said it was his duty as returning officer to announce that he had the election car- ried out in, he believed, proper form. He then mentioned the result of election. ELECTION OF Clerk said the first busi- ness of the Board that evening was to elect a chairman for the ensuing 12 months—Mr Rogers proposed that Mr Cam- eron he re-elected chairman.—Mr Thomason seconded.—Mr Hall said he had been robbed of an opportunity of which he would have been very glad, to propose, in all courtesy, that Mr John Dewhurst should be appointed chairmin of that Board. There was a certain feeling, which he believed he conveyed, not through any ill-feeling—rather the con, trary—that Mr Cameron should not be the chaiman of that Board: Whitt be if lid hesAi(l in ilia greatelt tionrtegya because he believed there viai hip(a genciernati 611 that I Board who could fulfil the duties of the chair better than Mr Cameron. Be only made these remarks because he was conveying, he would not sty the unanimous, but the 1 bulk of the ratepayers' wishes. He was sorry Mr John Dewhurst was not there that night, because if be had been there be (Mr Hall) should certainly have proposed him as chairman. Mr Dewhurst was not there, and consequently he bad no amendment to make. It was not his fault he could assure them ; it was simply the absence of Mr John Dawhuret which took away from him the pleasure—and in another sense not the pleasure. He, however, should not vote for Mr Cameron.—Mr Rogers said he might explain his reasons for proposing Mr Cameron. Mr Cameron was thoroughly well acquainted with the duties of that office ; there was a great deal to be done by the chairman of the Board which did not appear before the Board, a great deal of irksome work which required a great deal of attention. He believed Mr Dewhnrst was away a great deal of his time, and daring that time a deputy chairman would have to be appointed, otherwise the duty would not be performed. He (Mr Rogers) thought it was better the duties of chairman should be performed by the chairman himself, and no better chairman could be, found than the one they had sat under with so much plea- sure for a considerable time.—Mr Hall said Mr Dewhurst had not been absent very many times.—Mr Rogers said he did not mean absent from the Board, he meant absent in the interim between the meetings of the Board. Mr Thomason said there were many things oc- curred between the meetings of the Board. —Mr Hall said he hoped every gentleman would see what he meant and he hoped Mr Cameron would take it kindly. He (Mr Hall) wished to begin his duties in a manner which would be a forerunner of good feeling all through their tenure of office. If they appointed Mr John Dewhuret there might be a deputy-chairman appointed who could fulfil the duties in Mr Dewhuret's abeence, and then the SIIiMUS which had existed for a long tialB in the village would be put a stop to. He might as well tell them that there was a decided opinion expressed pulslicly that. Mr Cameron as the agent of Mr Dewburst, WAS not an eligible party tor the office of chair- man. He would qualify that by saying that Mr Cameron, as far as he had ever met with him, had shown himself very capable of the office, hut, on the other hand, they had to defer to public opinion to a certain extent.—The Clerk : I take it that Mr Hall does not propose an amendment —Mr Hall : I cannot do it; I ans robbed of the opportunity by the absence of Mr Dearborn. lam sorry we cannot put a stop to the little bit—Mr Thomason understands as well as r do. (Laughter.)—Mr Thomason : Don't let us start the first night. (foaughter.)—Mr Cameron was then elected to the chair without opposition—On taking the chair, Mr Cameron thanked them for their renewed expression of con- fidence. He WAS much obliged to Mr Rogers and Mr Thomason, and he was equally *bilged to Mr Hall for the way in which he had' made his remarks. Mr Hall had always consistently objected to him (Mr Cameron) occupying that position, though he htd never quite understood on what principle he based that opposition. He knew that Mr Dewhurst was prepared to undertake any duties that the Board imposed upon him ass member of the Board, bet at the same time his feelings were very much against being put in the choir, for the simple reason stated by Mr Rogers, that he could not be there at all times. He (Mr Cameron) did not think the Board would be disposed to thrust duties upon Mr Dewhaset which he could not per- form without the sacrifice of his own comfort and pleasure. At the same time he (Mr Cameron) thought there might be something gained by having a change of chairman. He had occupied that position for four or five years, and it looked like monopolising the position too much. but as it was the wish of the Board he was willing to put that feel- ing aside. During the past two years they bad had some very heavy work, but as they bad got through the bulk of tlmt he thought they should be able to carry on their future work comfortably. He should think they had got the best- sewered parish in Cheshire. They had got an excellent sewerage farm, their scavenging department was in good working order, and they might say the same of their gas- works. There was therefore no need to feel very anxious about the future if they all put their shoulders to the wheel, and did their best. He again thanked them, and promised that he would do his best to conduct the business satis- factorily,_ and he hoped amicably. _

Tmel -COST OF Tilg Eutcrtn'ts,—The Chairman said the expenses of the recent election were £l3 1.18 6.—Mr Hall : That is cheap.—On the motion of Mr Rogers, seconded by , Mr Appleton, these expenses were passed. THE Column-rms.—The folhowiert committees were ap- pointed :—Building and Fire Engine Committee : Messrs Appleton, Hall, and Woolley.—Finance Committee: Messrs Dawburst, Rogers, Woolley, and Hall.—Gas Committee Messrs Thomason, Dewhuret, and Rogers.—Road Corn- mittee : Messrs Dewhorst, Forster, and Gibbon.—Saatterry Committee: Messrs Hall, Rogers, and Thomason —School Attendance Committee : Messrs Appl4on, Thomason, and Woolley.—Scwage Farm Committee: Messrs Appleton, Fore. ter, and Gibbon. The Chairman to be a member of all the committees. This was all the business.

div.head: LIBERALISM AT STATHAM.
div.p: LIBERALISM AT STATHAM.

_ tinder the auspices of Lynam Liberal Association a meet- ina \TAB held at Statham on Monday ever in, when the choir was occupied by Mr Swanwick, and adSresses were given by Mr Milne and Mr Watford to a fairly good audi- ence.

The ClUIRII&If referred to the serious aspect of affairs with regard to England Russia? If we were forced to a fight our only comfort must be that the quarrel would not in any sense be of our own seekinz, and in the knowledge that cur leaders had done, and would do their uttermost to keep peace. It was impossible in these days for the Liberal leaders to draw the countr3 into an aggressive war, and if we had to fight it would be fer purposes of defence, and the Government would show how ably they could organise, and how they could make the most of the forces at their disposal. There was often a strong tendency on the part of Liberal speakers to evade the guettion of the foreign affairs of the Government, especially in refe-ence to the Soudan, but he thought the more one looked into things the mere one was satisfied that in this respect the Gov,•rnrnent did not need apologists. Mr MiLWE commincsd his speech by a reference to the Franchise Bill, which he did not consider to be a boon to the working classes, but a right which had been withheld. ( Applause.) As a sequence to that AOC they were now en- deavouring to pas l through the Lima of Commons a late

measure which would cistribute electoral power in such a way as to give a very full and fair effect to the votes of the cit,zaine all over the country. The question naturally followed, " What were they going to do with their votes?' For guidance he referred to hietory, and the parts played by the two political parties. Prior to the passing of the Reform Act of 1832 the people were not so well off as now. The power 3 f the country was practically in the hands of wealthy manufacturers and administrators of trusts. In 1833, after the passing of the Act, came the abolition of slavery. (Applause.) The uniform penny postage was es- tablished in me, and the duty was afterwards taken from paper through the efforts of Mr Gladstone. He (Mr Glad- stone) had a hard straggle to get through, but with the country at his back he succeeded in having the tax on knowledge repealed. Then came the great agitation for the repeal of the Corn Laws, which was carried out by Mr Cob- den and Mr Bright, with the effect that beead was cheaper. Now we had practically what Mr Cobden often wished to realise, " a free breakfast table." After the Reform Act of 1332 the death penalty was restricted to punishing the crime of murder, and the influence the Act gave to the large centres of industry resulted in an Ace being passed that reformed municipal corporations, with the exception of that of the city of London, and we were now premised that some day that huge corporation would be dealt with and that the charitable trusts held by the city companies would be transferred to the hands of the pablie administrators, for the public goad. Having referred to the abolition of purchase in the army, the passing of the Education Act, and other measures, Mr. Milner said that these measures showed that ever since the people got power they had used it to in some way better their condition. Let them consider by whom these great measures were passed. During the period of which he hid spoken the Liberals were in power for something like 301 years. The record he bad given them told plainly that the measures of reform that had done so much for the advancement of the people, had been due to Liberal Governments, aided by Liberals out of doors, and lay the strong representations that were made by constita- ences when appealed to on these great questions. Mr. BIRCII, in a short but pointed address, said that the Tories had cast the slur upon them that enfranchisement would be thrown away upon them. They must pay back for that at the next election. (Applause.) With the edit- cational facilities now existing stimulated by the responsi- bility of having a direct voice in the ruling of the countrY, it would not take them long to ehew that they could mas- ter the principles of modern politics and make the Tories realise their position in the future. Mr. WELFORD also delivered an address. In regard to foreign affairs there was nothing in the behaviour of the Liberal Government of which they as Liberals need fear to speak, and he, in all his remarks, world never assume the apologetic tone. He supported the policy of the Govevn- ment in Egypt, and felt that it could not now be left in confusion, undefended against the Mandi. If such men as Gladstone and his colleagues concluded that the re-taking of Khartoum was necessary in the interests of Egypt proper, however unwilling they might be to coincide with that view, they could not withhold their support to the Government. He thought the Government had acted well regarding Afghanistan, and could not be charged with any want of firmness. He himself thought it was possible for the frontieis to meet and the two nations still be friendly. If both were equally disposed, and there was not in either nation a party whose object was war, it would be possible in his opinion to avoid war. In conclusion he urged his hearers to give their votes to the Liberal party. Votes of thanks concluded the meeting.

div.head: PRINCE OF WALES AT KILLARNEY.
div.p: THE PRINCE OF WALES AT KILLARNEY.

The first act of the Prince at Killarney on Friday was to receive the addresses from the locality, which were pre- sented at Kenmore House. Deputations attended from the county magistrates, the grand jury of the county, and a number of the inhabitants, each of which presented the Prince with an address of welcome to the district. 1... at from the inhabitants was signed amongst others by Lord Kenmore, Dr Higgins, the Catholic Bishop of Kerry, and Sir R Blennerhassett, M.P., and expressed a hope that the ! visit would knit closer together the ties which united the people with the Crown, and suggested that a Royal residence in Ireland would conduce to the prosperity and pacifica- tion of the country. The Prince acknowledged the receipt of the addresses; and the Prince and Princess, Prince Albert Victor, Sir Dighton Probyn, and the members of the suite proceeded on an excursion to the Gap of Dunloe. A num- ber of visitors followed the Royal party to the lakes.

div.head: SHIP CANAL 'BILL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL 'BILL.

At the sitting of the Lo-ids' Committee on Friday, Mr Pope, on behalf of the principal opponents, said they had consulted together as tp what had fallen from their lordships respecting the decision of the committee of the Lords last year on the commercial part of the case. They would like to know whether their lordships now felt themselves bound in any way by that decision, and whether they would re- quire evidence of a much strongAr character than what was given by the opponents last year to induce them to reject the scheme. The committee then consulted for half an hour, after which Earl Cowper said the committee were in no way bound by last year's decision, but obviously the probability was that the evidence of last year on the com- mercial part of the case would satisfy the committee. They did not think that a repetition of the whole of the evi- dence of last year WAS necessary, but they must leave the responsibility to the promoters. Mr Pember said he could not aff nd to run any riek, though he would compress his evidence as much 45 possible. The inquiry was then ri Burned,

div.head: TIIE RUSSO AFGHAN DISPUTE.
div.p: TIIE RUSSO AFGHAN DISPUTE.
FRESH • DESPATCH FROM GENERAL
KOMAROFF.

ST. PSTEUSBI7IIO, FRIDAT.—The Official Messenger of this morning states theta despatch which reached St Peters- burg yesterday from General Komaroff reports as follows : —The Afghans have evacuated the posts on the frontier. Our outposts occupy their former positions. Our detach- ment is at Desch Kepri. Shall proceed in a few days to in- spect the troops at the outposts. PROGRESS OF THE NEGOTIATIONS The Standard says the establishment of a previsional Government at Penjdeb by the Russian general will not, it is understood, seriously interfere with the progress of the negotiations. The Standard believes it will be several days before the Government are able to make any definite announcement regarding the negotiations with Russia. THE AMEER AND THE CESSION OF

PENJDEH. The Central News, telegraphirig apparently under Rue- elan inspiration, says :—Although Mr Gladstone stated in the House of Commons last night that the reported inten- tion of the Government to allow Penjdeh to be ceded to Russia was "unauthorised," we are enabled to confirm the annourcement in every particular. In face of the strong disinclination shown by the Amaer to allow Britisk troops to cross the frontier into Afghan territory—even after the slaughter of his troops near Penjdeh—the Government are not indisposed to accept a compromise of the frontier dispute mainly on the lines suggested by Russia, and negotiations with that view have so far progressed that there are grounds for hops that a satisfactory solution may be arrived at.

div.head: FINANCIAL BAROMETER.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL BAROMETER.

-- Owing to the more peaceful aspect of political affairs, tb• London mock Markets opened on Friday with considerable buoyancy, and a sharp rise took place in both home and foreign securities. Consols are now quoted 961 I. or I higher than yesterday. Russian 1873 Loam is up 21 to 87i 88, and. HMS Railways are better all round. WAR PREPARATIONS.

Orders were received at Sheerness on Friday directing the armour-plated turret ship Hydra to be prepared for active service with the least possible delay. Barrack accommoda- tion is being prepared at Chatham for the second b-attalion of the East Kent Militia. Although Mr Gladstone was un- able to give the Commons any delicate isforokation this evening, the prospects of peace are still considered hopeful. There is., however, no abatement of the Govarnmeat's war preparations. The Sheerness correspondent of the Central News tele- graphs that orders have been received there directing the armour-plated turret ship Hydra to be immediately pre- pared for active service. The Hydra is one of the four monitors purchased at the time of the Franco-German war. Slos is equipped with four 18-ton guns.
THE SOUDAN' CAMPAIGN.
OSNIAN DIGNA DENIORALISE.D.

It is reported at Dorgols from native sources that in cou• *twine° of the BritiM troops having occupied the places upon which Osman Dlgna depended for his eupplies of water and forage, the whole of the rebel forces have dispersed. THE REVOLT AGAINST THE MARDI.

Intelligence received at Dongola states that the tribes in revolt aping the Mskdi recently detested the Mihdl's troops, under the Sheikh Ablangs, with heavy loss, at Dar- el.ahamdeh,so miles north of El Obeid.

TRIPLE MURDERER.-A Dutch landowner named Tim- mertnans, who bad ruioed himself by lawsuits, has as- sassinated, out of revenge, the two barristers Van Oppen, father and son, and a female member of their family, at their houses in Maesaricht. He used a revolver and a dageer. TiiE HOME IRON TRADE —Notwithstanding the political uncertainty and the unsettled state of business generally arising from it, and notwithstanding the not altegethor sat- isfactory course of the quarterly meetings, we find the Eng- lish iron market in about the same condition thia week as when we wrote last. The fact is that the more active demand in certain branches of the inn and related trades has assisted in counterbalancing depressing influences. The Scotch warrant market continues firm, but it is at present entirely under the control of holders of a large yfroportion of the warrants, so that the state of trade and the fears of a Russian war are not allowed to have any ffect upon prices, and the bears are being frightened into covering their sales. Scotch pig-iron warrants are now rela tively much higher than either hematite or Middlesborough iron, and thus both the shipments and home consumption are fal.ing off. Scotch ironmasters find it very difficult to make sales, and are quite unable to obtain higher prices for their iron. Closing quotations for warrants were 04.
